# How Operational Platform Works — The Complete Guide

**A single-file, end-to-end guide to the *Operational Platform* package: what it is, why it exists, how its six-phase methodology works, how the `operational-platform` tool implements that methodology, how to use it, how it is built internally — and, importantly, what was verified by actually running it and where it behaves differently from its own documentation.**

---

## About this guide

**Subject.** The archive `operational-platform-a-2a.zip`. It contains a task-execution *methodology* (the "Operational Platform") and a working *implementation* of it for one domain, `operational-platform` — a Python command-line engine, packaged as an installable Claude skill, for line-precise, batch, auditable editing of source code and text files.

**How this guide was produced.**

1. All five files of the delivered archive were read in full, and so were all twelve files inside its nested skill package. (The archive of this edition differs from it in names only; see the next paragraph.)
2. All seven Python modules (3,044 lines) were read line by line.
3. The tool was then exercised in 174 isolated throwaway projects, made by scenario scripts and by a crash harness — happy paths, every plan-time gate, conflict and cycle detection, protected zones, cross-batch locks, undo for every operation, export/import, crash simulation at three points inside a single `apply` call, text-handling edge cases (CRLF, missing trailing newline, form feeds, empty payloads, non-UTF-8 files) and more. The full list is in [Appendix D](#appendix-d--how-this-guide-was-verified). The environment was CPython 3.13.16, with Node.js v22.22.0 present for the optional JavaScript syntax check.

**About this edition.** The package was delivered under several names for one thing: the tool, its folder and its state directory, the project, and the file names that carry them. In this edition they are all one name, **Operational Platform**, in file names and in text, and the guide describes the package under that name. Only names changed. Of the seven modules of the tool one differs from the delivered one, in three strings — the name of the state directory and two docstrings — and the syntax trees of all seven, with the strings blanked, are equal. Every scenario of Appendix D was run on the renamed tool and printed what the delivered tool had printed, apart from the names and from what differs in every run by design; every transcript in this guide was then recorded again on the renamed tool. An example in the text that was captured before the rename has its names changed by the same rules. What was renamed, and the evidence, is in [D.2](#how-the-package-was-renamed); a project that already holds state under the old directory name needs one command to carry it over, and the same place says which.

Every console transcript in this guide is real output. Absolute filesystem paths were shortened, some long outputs were trimmed, short JSON objects that the tool prints over many lines are collapsed onto one line, and `# …` comments are annotations added for this guide; nothing else was edited.

**What you will not find here.** The archive ships no test suite, and the authors' statement that documented behavior is "backed by an automated test" could not be checked. The "source protocol" that the documentation repeatedly mentions as the origin of some design decisions is not included either. Where this guide states that something was *verified*, it means it was observed in the scenarios of Appendix D, not inferred from the documentation.

### Conventions

- **`operational-platform`** is the tool, and the name of its skill, its folder and its `.skill` package. **Operational Platform** is the name of the project, which covers both the methodology and the tool.
- `cli.py <command>` is shorthand for `python3 /path/to/operational-platform/scripts/cli.py <command>`, run with the **current directory set to the project you are editing** (see [section 6](#6-requirements-installation-and-invocation) for why this matters).
- Callouts:
  - **Note** — clarification.
  - **Caution** — easy to get wrong.
  - **Verified** — observed while testing for this guide.
  - **Docs vs. reality** — the bundled documentation and the shipped code disagree.
- References of the form **V1 … V31** point to the numbered entries of the register in [Part VIII, section 56](#56-verified-behaviors-and-deviations-from-the-documentation); **S1 … S10** to the trust findings of [section 57](#57-trust-model-and-security-notes); **L1 … L23** to the limitations that the tool's own documentation states ([section 55](#55-stated-limitations-and-their-verification-status)); **BP1 … BP52** to the best-practice rules of [section 58](#58-best-practices). The minor findings **m1 … m15** are in [section 56.9](#569-minor-findings), and the text edge cases **E1 … E10** in [D.4](#d4-text-edge-cases); [Appendix E](#appendix-e--glossary) lists every label family.
- IDs shown in examples (`f_568470d013`, `d0001`, `dm0001`, `ri0001`, `batch_0001`) are real values generated by the tool for the example files.
- "Docs" means the bundled documentation. The documentation calls the current feature set **v2.6**; the code itself contains no version constant.

## Part I — Orientation

### 1. What this is

#### 1.1 The short answer

The archive contains **one project in two layers**:

```
┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  Operational Platform                                                  │
│                                                                        │
│  Layer 1 — METHODOLOGY  (abstract, implementation-agnostic)            │
│    A six-phase way to execute any non-trivial task:                    │
│    0 Context Loading → 1 Analysis → 2 Task Map →                       │
│    3 Execution Plan → 4 Execution → 5 Validation                       │
│    built on one rule:  ANALYSIS → PLAN → EXECUTION  never merge.       │
│                                                                        │
│  Layer 2 — IMPLEMENTATION for one domain:  operational-platform        │
│    A Python 3 command-line engine (standard library only, 7 modules,   │
│    3,044 lines) packaged as a Claude "skill", for line-precise batch   │
│    editing of text and code, with an on-disk audit trail.              │
└────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

In one sentence: **the model decides *what* to change; the engine owns *where* it is, *whether it is still safe*, *how* it is written, and *proof* that the whole job is finished.**

#### 1.2 What `operational-platform` does in practice

Suppose an agent (or a person) is asked to rename a function everywhere in a codebase, restructure a document, or sweep a code base for a class of problems and fix them. Done by ad-hoc editing, such work tends to fail quietly: line numbers drift after the first insertion, one occurrence is missed, a session is interrupted and nobody knows how far it got, a plan is silently applied to a file that changed in the meantime.

`operational-platform` replaces ad-hoc editing with a small, strict pipeline:

1. **Register** every file you will touch. Each line gets a permanent *line ID*.
2. Open a **batch** and record each change as a **descriptor**: one atomic edit that names its target by line ID and carries a hash of the content it expects to find there.
3. **Trace cascades** ("domino"): for every finding, the engine searches *all* registered files for other places the same change might affect, and refuses to continue until every finding has been looked at.
4. Declare **invariants** — completeness criteria that live outside the plan ("zero occurrences of `old_name` must remain").
5. **Validate the plan**: schema, conflicts, cycles, protected zones, locks held by other batches. Nothing has been touched yet, so a mistake costs nothing.
6. **Apply** one descriptor at a time. Before each write, the live content is hashed and compared with what the descriptor expects. A mismatch aborts, leaving the file exactly as it was.
7. **Validate the result** from the files on disk: syntax checks and every invariant, with concrete matches listed for review.

Everything the process learns is written to a state directory (`.operational-platform/`), so a dropped or compacted conversation resumes by *reading state*, never by remembering.

#### 1.3 A ten-command taste

```text
cd my-project
cli.py register app.py                                    # give every line a permanent ID
cli.py new-batch --shape rename                           # open a batch; commit it to domino tracing
cli.py add-descriptor-template batch_0001 \
       --find old_name --replace new_name                 # one descriptor per matching line
cli.py sync-domino-queue batch_0001                       # queue every finding for a cascade check
cli.py domino-next batch_0001                             # candidates elsewhere? judge them…
cli.py domino-resolve batch_0001 dm0001                   # …then mark each finding traced
cli.py add-invariant batch_0001 --file app.py \
       --pattern old_name --expected-count 0              # independent completeness criterion
cli.py validate-plan batch_0001                           # check everything before touching anything
cli.py apply-all batch_0001                               # apply, with a hash check before every write
cli.py validate-post batch_0001                           # syntax + invariants, re-derived from disk
```

Part IV walks through this with real output.

#### 1.4 What it is *not*

| It is not… | Because… |
|---|---|
| A version-control system | It keeps no history of file contents. It records hashes, a write-ahead log and enough of the "before" text to reverse a single descriptor. Use Git as well (the authors themselves advise working on a copy or a version-controlled checkout for anything you would regret losing). |
| A semantic or AST-aware refactoring tool | It understands *lines*. It can search for text and check syntax of `.py` and `.js` files, but it does not know what a symbol, scope or type is. |
| A transactional system | There is no whole-batch rollback. A failed post-condition leaves applied descriptors applied. Undo exists per descriptor only, and has sharp edges (see V1, V12). |
| A sandbox or a permission system | It writes wherever the registered paths point and has no access control. The "separate writers" design of its logs is a convention, not enforcement. |
| An agent framework | It is a passive CLI. Something else (a model, a person, a script) calls it. |
| Concurrent-writer safe | State is plain JSON files with atomic replace for each write, but there is no cross-process locking. Run one session per project directory. |

#### 1.5 Mental models the authors lean on

The documentation repeatedly explains mechanisms by analogy to tools most engineers already know. They are useful shorthand:

| Mechanism | Analogy |
|---|---|
| `line_id` | A database row ID: identity that does not change when position does |
| `expect_hash` | Compare-and-swap; the context lines of a `git patch` that make it refuse to apply to text that moved on |
| `payloads/<hash>.blob` | A Git object store: content-addressed, writing the same text twice is free |
| `.operational-platform/` | `.git/`: state directory discovered by walking up from the current directory |
| `wal.jsonl` + `checkpoint.json` | A database write-ahead log and checkpoint |
| `validate-plan` / `validate-post` | Pre-flight check and post-condition, with a validator that never authors what it validates |

### 2. What is in the archive

#### 2.1 Files

`operational-platform-a-2a.zip` contains five files (210,071 bytes uncompressed):

| File | Bytes | Lines | What it is |
|---|---:|---:|---|
| `README.md` | 4,459 | 87 | Explains that the delivery holds **two independent packagings of the same work** |
| `operational-platform-task-execution-methodology-full-in-one-file-md.md` | 67,638 | 1,210 | **Set A** — methodology and implementation merged, phase by phase, in one document |
| `operational-platform-task-execution-methodology.md` | 32,968 | 397 | **Set B** — the methodology alone, with no mention of text editing, code, JSON or any implementation |
| `operational-platform.md` | 29,191 | 520 | **Set B** — the tool's operating instructions; a readable copy of the `SKILL.md` inside the package (**verified byte-identical**) |
| `operational-platform.skill` | 75,815 | — | **Set B** — the tool itself: a zip archive that is the installable skill |

The nested `operational-platform.skill` (226,707 bytes uncompressed, 12 files) unpacks to a single folder:

```
operational-platform/
├── SKILL.md                       29,191 B  520 lines   operating instructions (YAML front matter + workflow)
├── references/
│   ├── cli-reference.md           22,222 B  474 lines   every command and flag
│   ├── file-formats.md            15,884 B  405 lines   every state file
│   ├── limitations.md             13,432 B  223 lines   deliberate scope cuts, stated plainly
│   └── methodology-mapping.md     14,825 B  205 lines   which command satisfies which methodology phase
└── scripts/                                              the engine — Python 3, standard library only
    ├── cli.py                     27,495 B  679 lines   the only interface; 38 subcommands; JSON in/out
    ├── engine.py                  39,340 B  814 lines   descriptors, batches, apply, undo, taxonomy, constraints, invariants
    ├── validator.py               27,415 B  605 lines   plan-time and post-condition validation; locks; ordering
    ├── storage.py                 11,324 B  344 lines   all filesystem I/O; state layout; hashing; blobs
    ├── domino.py                  11,024 B  253 lines   cascade-tracing queue
    ├── registry.py                10,041 B  246 lines   line-ID ↔ position bookkeeping; pattern scan
    └── inventory.py                4,514 B  103 lines   region inventory (content assembly)
```

#### 2.2 Set A versus Set B

The README is explicit that the two sets are **not sequential**: Set B does not supersede Set A, and Set A is not a summary of Set B. They hold the same underlying content, organized for different uses.

| | **Set A** — one merged document | **Set B** — separate, reusable layers |
|---|---|---|
| Files | one | three documents plus the installable package |
| Methodology and implementation | woven together, each abstract requirement immediately followed by the concrete command or file that satisfies it | kept apart on purpose |
| Best for | reading everything in one place; handing the whole thing to someone else | reusing the methodology in a domain that is *not* line-oriented text; installing and running the tool; reading one short focused document at a time |
| Self-contained? | Yes; nothing else in the package is needed to understand it | The methodology document stands alone; the tool's instructions live in `SKILL.md` and its references |

The README also says how the names relate, and in this edition the answer is short: **Operational Platform is the one name of everything in the package** — the project, the methodology and the tool. In file names and in the skill's `name:` field it is written `operational-platform`, and the tool keeps its state in a `.operational-platform/` directory.

#### 2.3 What is not in the archive

- **No test suite.** The documentation says that stated behaviors have "an automated test backing" them; none is shipped, so that could not be checked. (The behaviors exercised for this guide are listed in Appendix D.)
- **The "source protocol".** `limitations.md` and `methodology-mapping.md` repeatedly refer to a "source protocol" from which some design decisions were taken or deliberately declined (for example, an "in-progress" descriptor status). It is not part of the delivery.
- **No license or authorship information.**
- **No example project.** The worked examples in this guide were built for it.

---

### 3. The problem it solves

LLM-driven editing fails in a small number of predictable ways. Each mechanism of `operational-platform` exists to close a specific one. (The authors' own closing note says the same: every mechanism "exists because of a specific, statable failure mode it closes".)

| # | Failure mode | Typical symptom | Mechanism that closes it |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | **Position drift** | Insert two lines near the top and every later line number is wrong — including those in the plan. A later edit silently lands on the wrong line. | Permanent `line_id` per line; descriptors address ids, never numbers; one module (`registry.py`) is the only code allowed to write positions. |
| 2 | **Unreliable long-sequence arithmetic** | Off-by-one errors compound across dozens of edits. | Position arithmetic, hashing and file writes live in deterministic code. |
| 3 | **Internally consistent but incomplete plans** | Every descriptor is valid, nothing conflicts — and one occurrence was missed. | The *domino* queue (every finding must be traced, gated) plus *invariants* declared independently of the plan. |
| 4 | **A plan that grades itself** | Whoever composes a plan shares its blind spots with whoever checks it. | Validator never authors descriptors; invariants and descriptors live in separate files; `domino-resolve` recounts cascades itself instead of trusting a self-report; `--checked-against` warnings flag "I re-counted my own payload". |
| 5 | **Interruption and context loss** | Session dropped or conversation compacted; the model "remembers" progress incorrectly. | Every phase's output is a durable artifact: batch files, WAL, checkpoint, `resume`. |
| 6 | **Stale plan applied to changed material** | A file was edited by someone else between planning and applying. | `expect_hash` compare-and-swap before every write; a four-way result (`applied` / `skipped` / `recovered` / `abort`); `abort` leaves the file untouched. |
| 7 | **Contradictory or overlapping edits** | Two descriptors both rewrite the same line; one depends on the other but nobody said so. | Conflict graph over resolved id-sets, `--depends-on`, cycle detection, cross-batch locks. |
| 8 | **Touching what must not be touched** | Vendored code or an owned section gets modified. | Protected-range constraints, checked at plan time, project-wide if desired. |
| 9 | **Silent omission** | When assembling a document from several sources, the well-behaved, conflict-free parts are quietly dropped. | The region inventory: every declared source range needs an explicit disposition before the plan validates. |
| 10 | **Claiming completion without proof** | "All done" is asserted, not demonstrated. | `validate-post` re-derives syntax validity and every invariant from the files on disk and lists concrete matches. |
| 11 | **No way back** | A single wrong edit cannot be reversed. | `pre_payload_ref`, `created_ids` and `undo_anchor` are captured at plan/apply time; `undo-descriptor` reverses one descriptor through its own inverse. |

---

### 4. When to use it

#### 4.1 Decision guide

| Situation | Use it? |
|---|---|
| A single, obvious one-line fix | **No.** Edit the file directly. The authors say so explicitly: the overhead buys nothing when there is nothing to get inconsistent. |
| Rename an identifier everywhere it appears | **Yes** — the canonical case (`--shape rename`). |
| Multi-file refactor, restructuring a block, moving code between files | **Yes.** |
| Inserting, deleting, moving or replacing many lines that must stay consistent with each other | **Yes.** |
| An audit or conformance sweep with categories and priorities | **Yes** (`--shape audit` / `conformance`). |
| Building one document from parts of several others | **Yes** (`--shape assembly`). |
| Work that might be interrupted, or must survive a dropped conversation | **Yes.** |
| You need to *show* the work was complete, not merely assert it | **Yes** — that is what invariants are for. |
| Semantic refactors that need to understand types, scopes or symbols | **Not alone.** Pair it with language tooling; the engine only sees lines. |
| Binary files, or text that is not valid UTF-8 | **No.** Registration fails (exit code 2) on invalid UTF-8. |
| Files that contain form-feed or other unusual line-separator characters | **Careful.** See V7. |

#### 4.2 What it costs

- **Ceremony.** Registering, opening a batch, recording descriptors, tracing, validating: many more tool calls than a direct edit.
- **Verbose output.** Every command prints a JSON object (indented), including whole descriptors.
- **Discipline.** Several protections only work if you use them: invariants are optional; the domino queue is opt-in; `--checked-against` is advisory; path spelling must be consistent (V3); after adding descriptors you must re-run `validate-plan` (V4).

---

### 5. Design principles

Eight ideas explain nearly every design choice in the engine.

1. **The model decides *what*; code owns *where* and *how*.** Judgment (what is wrong, whether a candidate is a real cascade, whether a surviving match is a legitimate exception) stays with the model or person. Bookkeeping (positions, hashes, ordering, writes, logs) is mechanical and lives in code.
2. **Position is an identity resolved at the moment of use.** A line's ID never changes; where it *is* is looked up in the registry each time it is needed. No cached position is ever trusted.
3. **Compare-and-swap before every write.** A descriptor carries the hash of the content it was authored against. If live content no longer matches, nothing is written.
4. **Durable artifacts, not mental state.** A phase "in progress" is exactly what its output files say. Resuming means *reading* them, not re-running the phase or recalling it.
5. **Independent verification.** Completeness criteria (invariants) are declared separately from the plan; the validator only inspects what the engine wrote; two append-only logs have different writers; counts are recomputed from disk, not taken from a caller's word.
6. **Gates, not suggestions.** `validate-plan` refuses; there is no "apply anyway". Shape gates, taxonomy gates, domino gates and inventory gates all stop the plan until satisfied.
7. **Fail safe, never clever.** When reality matches neither the "before" nor a plausible "after", the engine reports `abort` and leaves the file as found. It never patches over a mismatch.
8. **Honest about the line between mechanical and judgment.** Each mechanism is explicit about what it checks and what it cannot ("a shape gate checks that a mechanism was *used*, not that it was used *well*").

---

### 6. Requirements, installation and invocation

#### 6.1 Requirements

- **Python 3**, standard library only — no packages to install. No minimum version is declared in the package; this guide's tests ran on CPython 3.13.16.
- **Node.js** (optional): only for the post-condition syntax check of `.js` files, which shells out to `node --check`. If `node` is absent the check is reported as *skipped*, not failed.
- Text files encoded in **UTF-8**.

#### 6.2 Installation

The package is a *skill*: a folder with a `SKILL.md` (YAML front matter with `name: operational-platform` and a long `description` that tells an agent when to reach for it), a `scripts/` folder and a `references/` folder. To make it available to an agent, install the `.skill` package (or place the unpacked `operational-platform/` folder) the way your Claude environment installs skills. To use it **without any agent**, no installation is needed at all: it is a plain script — unzip the `.skill` file and call `scripts/cli.py` directly.

The `description` in `SKILL.md` is what triggers its use: reliable, auditable batch editing; stable line IDs immune to line-number drift; idempotent atomic descriptors; protected-zone constraints; a three-phase validator; a write-ahead log and checkpoint for safe resumption; and a CLI that keeps position tracking, hashing and file writes in deterministic code. It ends with "Skip for a single one-line fix".

#### 6.3 Invocation — and the one thing the docs gloss over

The documentation writes commands as `python3 scripts/cli.py <command> ...` and says to "run from inside the project you're editing". Those two instructions only fit together if you read the first as shorthand for *the path to `cli.py`*. What actually matters:

> **Verified:** the state directory is located from the **current working directory**, not from where the script lives. `cli.py` finds the nearest ancestor directory (starting at the current directory) that contains `.operational-platform/`, exactly like Git finds `.git/`; if none exists, the current directory is used and `.operational-platform/` is created there on first use. Running `python3 scripts/cli.py …` from *inside the skill folder* would therefore create state inside the skill folder.

So the correct pattern is:

```text
cd /path/to/the/project/you/are/editing
python3 /path/to/operational-platform/scripts/cli.py register src/app.py
```

Even read-only commands (`checkpoint`, `resume`, `status`, `show-file`) create an empty `.operational-platform/` directory with `payloads/` and `batches/` inside if none exists yet.

#### 6.4 Paths: one spelling, relative to the project root

> **Caution (V3).** A file's identity (`file_id`) is a hash of the path *string exactly as you typed it*. `app.py` and `./app.py` are registered as **two different files with two disjoint sets of line IDs**, even though they are the same file on disk. Nothing warns you and the conflict graph cannot see the overlap. Pick one canonical spelling — relative to the project root, no `./` prefix — and use it in every command, including `--file`, `--checked-against`, `--files` and `--src-file`/`--dest-file`.

#### 6.5 Input and output conventions

- Every command prints **one JSON object** to standard output (with the single exception of `dry-run`, which prints the simulated file as plain text — V16).
- **Exit codes:** `0` success; `1` a reported failure worth stopping for (a validation failure, a conflict, an `abort`); `2` a usage or programming error. Uncaught exceptions inside a command are converted to `{"error": "<ExceptionName>: <message>"}` with exit code `2`.
- Argument-parsing errors (unknown flag, invalid `--severity`, invalid `--shape`) are produced by `argparse`: a usage message on standard error and exit code `2`.
- `--payload-file`, `--depends-on` (comma-separated), `--descriptor-ids` (comma-separated) and `--files` (comma-separated) are the multi-value conventions.

---
## Part II — The methodology

This part explains the **Operational Platform methodology** itself, and for every requirement shows how `operational-platform` satisfies it. The methodology document in Set B is deliberately free of implementation detail so that it can be re-applied to other domains; here the two are read side by side, which is exactly what Set A does.

### 7. Core philosophy: three stages, six phases

Any non-trivial task decomposes into three stages that **must never be merged**:

```
ANALYSIS  →  PLAN  →  EXECUTION
```

Merging them is described as "the primary source of error": acting before the full scope of work is understood leads to omissions, cascading failures and rework. The three stages expand into six operational phases:

| Stage | Phase(s) | One-line purpose |
|---|---|---|
| Preparation | **Phase 0 — Context Loading** | Establish complete, confirmed situational awareness before any work |
| Analysis | **Phase 1 — Analysis** | Find *every* deviation against the reference — without acting on any |
| Plan | **Phase 2 — Task Map** | Turn findings into a structured, verifiable artifact |
| Plan | **Phase 3 — Execution Plan** | Turn the map into an ordered, validated, trackable plan |
| Execution | **Phase 4 — Execution** | Apply changes in a controlled, risk-minimizing sequence |
| Verification | **Phase 5 — Validation** | Confirm the intended state was reached and nothing new broke |

**In `operational-platform`**, the separation is structural rather than a matter of discipline: no command both analyzes and applies. `add-descriptor` only *records* a finding; `apply-next` only acts on a batch that `validate-plan` has already passed and given an `apply_order`. They are different calls with different preconditions.

### 8. Interruption is not a special case

A methodology that only describes a clean, uninterrupted run through six phases "is describing the easy case and leaving the common one undefined". Any phase can be interrupted: Phase 0 mid-load, Phase 1 partway through its sweep, Phase 4 mid-batch. Two properties make interruption survivable:

1. **Every phase's output is a durable artifact, not a mental state.** A phase is "in progress" exactly to the extent its recorded output says so. Nothing that matters lives only in the reasoning that produced it.
2. **Resuming means reading that artifact, not restarting the phase.** The correct response to an interruption is to determine from the artifact exactly how far the phase got and continue from there — never to re-run "to be safe", never to guess from memory.

A methodology satisfies this only when each phase's required output is specified precisely enough that "how far did this get" is *a fact you can read, not a judgment you reconstruct*.

**In `operational-platform`**, each phase has a concrete on-disk output:

| Phase | Durable artifact (under `.operational-platform/`) | How progress is read |
|---|---|---|
| 0 Context loading | `registry.json`; `batches/<id>/materials_manifest.json`; `constraints.json` | `show-file`; `validate-plan` reports `materials_missing` |
| 1.1 Taxonomy | `batches/<id>/taxonomy.json` (and `project_taxonomy.json`) | `taxonomy_incomplete` gate |
| 1.2 Cross-examination | descriptors with `provenance: direct` in `descriptors.json` | `status` |
| 1.3 Domino | `batches/<id>/domino_queue.json` | `domino-status` → `pending` / `traced` / `ready_for_plan` |
| 2 Task map | `descriptors.json`, `invariants.json`, optional `region_inventory.json` | `status`, `explain`, `find-pattern` |
| 3 Execution plan | `apply_order` in `descriptors.json`; `active_locks.json`; `validation_log.jsonl` | `validate-plan`, `status` |
| 4 Execution | per-descriptor `status`; `wal.jsonl`; `checkpoint.json` | `resume`, `checkpoint`, `status` |
| 5 Validation | `validation_log.jsonl`; batch `status` (`committed` / `failed`) | `validate-post`, `report` |

`resume` is the command that turns these artifacts into a recommendation. [Section 35](#35-the-eleven-step-workflow) shows it in each state.

---

### 9. Phase 0 — Context loading

**Purpose.** Establish complete, confirmed situational awareness before any analytical or productive work begins.

**Required tasks**
- Load the **governing reference** against which correctness will be judged.
- Load **all materials** that are the subject of the work.
- Establish **constraints**: what must not be touched, what is critical, what takes priority.
- **Explicitly confirm** that loading is complete before proceeding.

**Governing rule.** No transformation or corrective work happens in this phase — only intake and confirmation.

**Rationale.** Incomplete or misunderstood context invalidates every downstream conclusion, and errors introduced here propagate through every later phase.

**On constraints specifically.** Establishing a constraint is not enforcing it. A constraint that is only ever written down and never mechanically checked against the plan is "a note, not a guardrail". The check belongs in Phase 3.

**In `operational-platform`**

| Requirement | Concrete answer |
|---|---|
| Load the governing reference | **No command.** Ordinary reading, with whatever tool already holds the spec, ticket or standard. The authors judge nothing here specific enough to mechanize. (Consequence: `--rule-ref` can cite a clause but nothing can verify the citation.) |
| Load the subject material | `register <path>` once per file the task will touch. Idempotent. Every line gets a permanent `line_id`. |
| Establish constraints | `add-constraint <batch_id> --file --start --end --reason`. Needs an open batch, so in practice it is called right after `new-batch`; the ordering that matters is *before any descriptor could violate it*. `--project` makes it apply to every future batch. |
| Confirm that loading is complete | `show-file <path>` reads every registered line back with its ID and position (and records a `file_inspected` event). `require-file <batch_id> <path>` declares a file that *must* be registered; `validate-plan` fails with `materials_missing` otherwise. |

> **Note.** The `materials_missing` gate only checks that a required path was *registered*. It does not check that the file was read, or that it is the right file.

---

### 10. Phase 1 — Analysis

**Purpose.** Systematically examine all loaded material against the reference, identifying every deviation — without acting on any of them yet.

#### 10.1 Category taxonomy (1.1)

Establish an exhaustive, named classification of possible deviation types **before** examining individual material. *A category that is never defined can never be searched for; an analysis without a taxonomy is structurally incomplete.*

**In the tool:** `add-category <batch_id> --code CODE --description TEXT`, declared **before** any descriptor references the code. This is enforced immediately: `add-descriptor --category` rejects an undeclared code at the moment it is added (not later at plan time). A taxonomy is optional — "a plain rename doesn't need a category system" — and worth declaring when the task is shaped like "find and classify issues" rather than "make this one specific change". Categories can be project-wide (`--project`).

Closing the loop (Phase 5's "never silence" rule): at plan time, every declared category must either be used by at least one descriptor or be explicitly closed with `close-category` (a "checked, nothing found" record). Otherwise `validate-plan` fails with `taxonomy_incomplete`.

#### 10.2 Systematic cross-examination (1.2)

Examine each unit of material against each defined category, in a fixed, sequential order — **unit × category**, never skipping ahead — using structured, layered questioning rather than opportunistic scanning.

**In the tool:** *not a command.* `show-file` supplies the material; the taxonomy supplies the categories; deciding "does this line violate that category" is "the reasoning step this whole skill exists to support, not replace". The mechanical backing is optional and opt-in: `set-category-scope --code C --files a.py,b.py` demands that category C be accounted for **per file** — a descriptor with that category on that file, or `close-category-file` — before the plan validates (`unit_category_matrix_incomplete`). Whether the file was *really* examined stays a human/model judgment.

#### 10.3 Dependency analysis — "domino" (1.3)

For every identified deviation, determine **everything else that would break or become inconsistent if only that single point were corrected in isolation.** The cascade analysis must be exhaustive; an incomplete cascade produces a broken or inconsistent result once execution begins.

**Three distinct activities, only one of which resists automation:**

| Activity | Nature | In the tool |
|---|---|---|
| **Searching** the material for places that might be affected | Mechanical — a matter of *coverage* | `domino-next`: literal/regex search across **every** registered file, minus places already covered by a descriptor in the batch |
| **Judging** which candidates are genuine cascades and which are coincidental | Not mechanical — needs *understanding what the material means* | **Stays with the model/person.** No command. A wrongly accepted or wrongly dismissed candidate is not compensated by a perfect search or ordering |
| **Ordering** the resulting dependencies | Mechanical — respect them, refuse cycles | `--depends-on` on `add-descriptor`, honored as a hard constraint by `validate-plan`, which refuses cycles |

Treat these as three separate reliability problems.

**Five rules about this phase:**

1. **It is its own pass, sequenced strictly after 1.2 closes** — never interleaved with it. Cross-examination produces a finished, stable list; domino analysis traces each item against that finished list. Interleaving makes deduplication unreliable and progress impossible to measure or resume. (The tool enforces this structurally: `sync-domino-queue` queues only findings that already exist as descriptors.)
2. **It is durable and resumable.** Each deviation becomes an item with its own traced-or-not status, recorded as it happens. (`domino_queue.json`; `domino-resolve` is WAL-backed and idempotent.)
3. **Nothing proceeds past it with an untraced item.** It is a *gate*: a plan built from an incompletely traced list is invalid, like a plan with a dependency cycle. (`validate-plan` → `domino_incomplete`.)
4. **For material that carries its own embedded logic, judging requires reading that logic, not only searching text.** A dependency can exist with no shared wording at all — a script that silently assumes a sibling element still exists in a specific place — and no search, however exhaustive, will surface it. Judging it means reading the dependent logic for what it hard-codes or assumes. (The tool cannot help here; the docs say so plainly.)
5. **Domino tracing does not recurse** in the tool: a descriptor added with `--provenance domino` is never itself queued for its own trace.

> **Caution — what the gate does and does not guarantee.** `domino-resolve` records that a finding was *traced*, "not that nothing was there". It will happily resolve a finding while mechanical candidates remain uncovered. It records the number of cascade descriptors it finds linked to the finding and whether candidates existed (`had_candidates`), so a reviewer can see how much of the queue "needed a real look" — but nothing forces you to add a descriptor for every candidate. See [section 30](#30-the-domino-queue).

---

### 11. Phase 2 — Task map

**Purpose.** Convert the analysis into a **structured, verifiable artifact — not a narrative list** — that captures every issue and its relationships.

**Conceptually required attributes of every recorded issue**

| Attribute | Function | `operational-platform` field |
|---|---|---|
| Unique identifier | Reference from elsewhere, especially dependencies | `descriptor_id` (`d0001`, `d0002`, …, sequential per batch) |
| Category | Ties the issue to the Phase 1.1 taxonomy | `category` — validated against the taxonomy when added |
| Severity | Determines execution priority | `severity` ∈ `critical` / `major` / `minor` / `cosmetic` |
| Change type | Nature of the transformation (creation, removal, substitution, addition, relocation …) | `op` ∈ `insert_after` / `delete_range` / `replace_range` / `move_range` / `copy_range` |
| Location reference | Precise enough to find and re-verify without re-deriving | `start`/`end` or `after` — a `line_id`, never a line number |
| Current state / expected state | Two distinct values, never one blended description | `expect_hash` (current) / `payload_ref` (expected) — machine-checkable hashes and blob references rather than prose |
| Dependencies | Verifiable references to other issue identifiers, not free text | `depends_on` — list of `descriptor_id`s, checked to exist at plan time |
| Status | Progress through the workflow | `status` ∈ `pending` / `applied` / `undone` |
| *(not in the abstract table)* | Where a finding came from | `provenance` (`direct` / `domino`) and `domino_of` — added because the Phase 5 report "can't honestly break down 'found directly' versus 'found by domino'" without it |

For conformance-shaped tasks an issue may also carry a pointer to the **specific clause of the governing reference** responsible for it — distinct from Category, which groups by *this task's* taxonomy rather than locating a requirement in an external document. The methodology notes that, because Phase 0 loads reference material by ordinary reading rather than parsing, such a pointer "is necessarily an unverified citation, not a checkable reference the way a dependency is checkable". In the tool: `--rule-ref` (free text; never validated; the only check is a non-blocking `validate-plan` warning when two `rule_ref` values normalize to the same string but are spelled differently).

**Severity** is "what makes execution order determinable". The methodology's four tiers, from highest priority down, are: violations of fundamental/architectural invariants; violations of standards carrying broad structural or scaling risk; "noise" that does not affect function but degrades quality; purely cosmetic deviation. The tool's closed vocabulary has four levels — `critical`, `major`, `minor`, `cosmetic` — which correspond naturally to those tiers (the documentation does not spell out the pairing).

**Change type** is a fixed, closed vocabulary because different change types carry different risk and dependency profiles. The tool's vocabulary is the five ops (see [section 24](#24-descriptors-the-five-operations)).

**The map is a snapshot, not a promise.** A task map records the state of the material *as understood when Phase 1 examined it*. Writing an issue into the map guarantees nothing about the material still being in that state when Phase 4 reaches it. Phase 4 states what re-validation requires.

---

### 12. Phase 3 — Execution plan

**Purpose.** Convert the task map into an actionable, trackable, hierarchically organized plan.

**Structure**
- Top-level grouping: one natural unit of work per group → **one batch per logically related set of edits** ("a batch's job is to let you check that *these specific* edits are mutually consistent, not to be a container for everything you do in a session").
- Subgrouping: one category/type per subgroup → the `category` field; `status --group-by file_id,category` produces the nested view.
- Leaf items: individual issues, each with a trackable status → descriptors.
- **Dependency items execute together with their parent issue** — never as independent, separately scheduled items → they are in the same batch and the same `apply_order`; `--depends-on` edges are hard constraints.

**Execution priority**
1. Primary ordering by severity, most fundamental first.
2. Secondary ordering within a severity tier by **number of dependencies** — items with more cascading effects first, since they affect more of the system.

*In the tool, this is a tie-break inside a topological sort, not a separate step.* Every hard dependency edge and every conflict-forced ordering is respected regardless of severity; severity only decides between descriptors that are *already free to run in either order*. The second key is how many other descriptors list this one in their own `depends_on` — **declared** edges only (the tool does not infer that a domino-derived descriptor "depends on" its finding). Details in [section 45](#45-validatorpy).

**Plan validation** — before *any* item is acted on, the *complete* plan is checked once:
- every dependency reference resolves to an issue that exists;
- no dependency ordering is contradictory (no cycle);
- no planned change targets a constraint established in Phase 0 as off-limits.

This is "the last point at which finding a problem costs nothing", because nothing has been changed yet; the same check mid-execution is strictly more expensive. In the tool this is `validate-plan`, which does considerably more (a dozen ordered checks, see [section 45](#45-validatorpy)), and which has **no "apply anyway" path**: `apply-next` refuses to run on a batch that has no `apply_order`.

---

### 13. Phase 4 — Execution

**Purpose.** Apply planned changes in a controlled, risk-minimizing sequence.

**Six governing principles**

| # | Principle | In `operational-platform` |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | **Reality is checked before it is changed.** Immediately before acting on an item, confirm the material still matches what Phase 1 recorded — not what the plan assumes; what is actually there *right now*. | `expect_hash`, recomputed from the live file and compared before **every** write. |
| 2 | **Single-unit focus.** Finish one unit completely before the next; never interleave mid-way. | `apply-next` applies exactly one descriptor and stops. Looping it (or `apply-all`) is an explicit choice. |
| 3 | **Immediate dependency resolution.** An issue's dependency items are resolved in the same pass — never deferred to "later". | There is no "later" queue: dependent descriptors are in the same `apply_order`. Domino-derived descriptors are ordinary descriptors; discovering *which* are needed happened in Phase 1.3 "precisely so this phase never has to go looking". |
| 4 | **Layered passes.** Process complex units through sequential passes, each addressing one logical dimension. | Multiple batches run in sequence, each scoped to one dimension. |
| 5 | **Specific-before-general ordering.** When changes could overlap, apply the most specific first so a general change cannot silently absorb a more specific case. | **Deliberately not mechanized.** Express it with `--depends-on`. With line-ID addressing the classic failure (a naive "replace every occurrence" making a more specific string stop existing) mostly cannot occur: ranges that do not overlap cannot affect each other's content in any order, and overlapping ranges are already a conflict the graph catches. |
| 6 | **Incremental validation.** Validate each unit immediately after it is applied, never only at the end. | `validate-post` is meant to run **per batch**, not once at the end of a multi-batch task. |

**Three outcomes, not two.** The result of attempting a planned item is not simply success or failure:

| Abstract outcome | Meaning | Tool result |
|---|---|---|
| **Confirmed** | Reality matched the plan; the change was applied | `applied` |
| **Already satisfied** | Reality no longer matches the plan's *starting* state but matches what its *ending* state would have been; not a failure — the plan's record just needs updating | `recovered` (and `skipped`, an idempotent no-op on a descriptor already marked applied) |
| **Unresolvable** | Reality matches neither start nor end; something unanticipated changed. The only outcome that stops forward progress — and it must stop *cleanly*, leaving the material exactly as found | `abort` (exit code 1) |

Treating "already satisfied" like "confirmed" risks re-applying a change that should not be re-applied; treating it like "unresolvable" halts progress that did not need to halt. The tool therefore returns a four-way result, not a boolean.

> **Note (V18).** `skipped` can only be produced through the Python API. The CLI's `apply-next` and `apply-all` select descriptors whose status is not `applied`, so they never call apply on an already-applied one.
>
> **Caution (V2).** The "already satisfied → recovered" mechanism is the tool's crash-recovery path. Simulating a crash inside a single apply showed that it works for some operations and crash points but not others — notably `insert_after` and `copy_range` can be applied twice. See [section 48](#48-concurrency-atomicity-and-crash-windows).

---

### 14. Phase 5 — Validation

**Purpose.** Confirm that execution achieved the intended state and introduced no new problems.

**Three validation levels**

| Level | What it is | In `operational-platform` |
|---|---|---|
| 1. **Automated check** | A systematic, repeatable check for the *absence* of the originally identified deviation patterns | `validate-post`: syntax check of every touched file (`.py` via `compile()`, `.js` via `node --check`) and every declared **invariant**, re-derived fresh from disk |
| 2. **Semantic / contextual review** | Not every surviving match is a violation; each must be judged in context. This cannot be delegated to the automated check — it produces *candidates*, not the judgment. The check owes the reviewer enough context per candidate (not just a count) to judge without re-deriving where it is | `validate-post` returns up to 20 concrete matches (line + text) per invariant. `accept-match` records a reviewed exception — excluded from the failing count but **kept listed with its note and `accepted: true`**, so "reviewed and accepted" stays distinguishable from "never found" |
| 3. **Final report** | Structured status per unit, fully clean units distinguished from those with remaining issues, by severity. For **every** declared category: at least one finding *or* an explicit "checked, nothing found" — never silence. When citing a methodology phase as the basis for a decision, state separately what the citation supplied (a process step, a required check, a structural rule) versus what came from applying it to the specific material | `status <batch_id>` and the last `validate-post` result; `report --batches b1,b2,…` rolls several batches up (issues by severity, before/after line counts); `status --group-by` breaks one batch down. `close-category` enforces the "never silence" half. |

---

### 15. Requirements for specifying a task map

Before a task map can be produced, the request that defines it must explicitly specify ten things. The Set A document pairs each with its concrete answer:

| # | Requirement | How `operational-platform` satisfies it |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | **Scope** — the exhaustive set of units, and for region-targeted transformations the exhaustive *partition* of the relevant region: every line or block assigned a disposition | Every file `register`ed before planning; for region-scoped work, a range map built before descriptors exist (`add-source-range`) |
| 2 | **Reference** — the specification being analyzed against | Read directly; no mechanism |
| 3 | **Category taxonomy** — exhaustive, coded | `taxonomy.json` via `add-category` |
| 4 | **Severity scale** — explicit criteria per tier | The closed vocabulary `critical`/`major`/`minor`/`cosmetic` |
| 5 | **Change-type vocabulary** — closed set | The five ops |
| 6 | **Output structure** — exact structure and field types | The descriptor schema ([section 24](#24-descriptors-the-five-operations), [Part VII](#part-vii--state-file-formats)) |
| 7 | **Identifier rules** | `descriptor_id` = `d0001`… per batch; `line_id` = `<file_id>_l<seq>`, permanent |
| 8 | **Dependency reference rules** | `depends_on`: a list of `descriptor_id`s, checked to exist and acyclic at `validate-plan` |
| 9 | **Location / context requirements** | A `line_id` resolved through the registry; optionally `--context` (≤120 characters, verified once at add time) |
| 10 | **Explicit exclusions and protected material** | `add-constraint` for in-scope-but-protected; anything never registered is out of scope by omission |
| *(11)* | **Reference-clause traceability** (conformance tasks) | `--rule-ref`, free text and unvalidated |

**Gaps in a naive specification, and what closes each**

| Gap | Closed by |
|---|---|
| No defined output structure | An explicit structure with typed fields and worked examples |
| No unique identifiers | A defined identifier format; ids assigned by the tool, never by hand |
| No current/expected separation | `expect_hash` and `payload_ref` as two distinct fields (plus optional `--context`, since "a hash alone tells code what to check but tells a person nothing to look at") |
| Dependencies only as text | Reference-based `depends_on` pointing at verifiable ids |
| No structural validation of the map itself | Every referenced dependency id must exist — `validate-plan` checks it |
| No bound on location precision | `line_id`, immune to the drift a raw line number suffers |
| No severity | No way to determine execution order → the `severity` field and its tie-break role |
| No change type | No way to tell operations of different risk apart → the five-op vocabulary |
| No re-verification before acting | `expect_hash`, checked live at apply time |
| No account of interruption | `checkpoint.json` + `wal.jsonl` + `resume` |

---

### 16. Task shapes

The phase architecture is constant; its emphasis shifts with the shape of the task. `new-batch --shape X` turns the matching advice into a **gate**: it commits the batch to the mechanism that shape cannot responsibly skip, and `validate-plan` refuses a batch that claims a shape without having used it.

| Shape | Goal | Methodology emphasis | Gate (`--shape`) | Concrete practice in the tool |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Conformance transformation** | Bring material into line with a reference standard | Analyze unit × category; group the plan by unit | `conformance` → needs a **taxonomy** | One category per deviation type from the reference; batch by unit; an invariant per category confirming its defining pattern is gone |
| **Diagnostic audit** | Assess quality or risk across dimensions | Analyze by *dimension*; group the plan by dimension; prioritize by impact × effort (high-impact/low-effort first) | `audit` → needs a **taxonomy** | Lean on `severity` more than `category` ("what's worth doing first", not "what kind of thing is this"); batch by dimension |
| **System transition** | Move material from one system/interface/approach to another | Find all usages first; isolate breaking changes in their own batch; validate after every unit | `transition` → needs **domino tracing** *and* declared **constraints** | `register` everything that references what is moving *before* writing descriptors; `add-constraint` what is not ready; `validate-post` after every batch |
| **Global identifier / terminology change** | Rename or redefine something referenced throughout | Search exhaustively incl. secondary material; order from definitional to surface layers; close with a final exhaustive check | `rename` → needs **domino tracing** | Give each rename a `--domino-hint` of the exact old name; one `add-invariant --pattern <old> --expected-count 0` per touched file. "Caught twice, not once" |
| **Content assembly / transplant** | Build a new unit from material in two or more existing units, none of which is the reference | **Partition every source region into a complete inventory** before extraction; a region with no conflict is an inventory item with the disposition "transfer as-is", not an item with no disposition | `assembly` → needs a **region inventory** | `add-source-range` / `inventory-resolve`; prefer an invariant that cross-checks two *independently sourced* facts over one whose count was grepped from the same payload the descriptor was built from |

Without `--shape`, nothing is required. All gates are satisfied by *existence* of the mechanism's state — which the authors call out as a limit: "a gate that confirms a mechanism was used does not confirm it was used well" (verified: an empty `sync-domino-queue` on a batch with no descriptors satisfies the `rename` gate).

---

### 17. Requirements that building a tool made explicit

The methodology's later revisions state five requirements that a first implementation had to decide one way or the other. They are stated as requirements on *any* implementation:

1. **Reversal needs the before-state, recorded when the change is planned.** A fingerprint (hash) of the original lets you *detect* that something changed, not *undo* it — undoing needs the original content plus a record of what the change created. Reversal is a per-unit property (one change through its own inverse is well-defined; "the whole task" is larger) and must itself pass "reality is checked before it is changed". *In the tool:* `pre_payload_ref`, `undo_anchor`, `created_ids`; `undo-descriptor`; per descriptor, not per batch.
2. **Plans in flight are checked against each other.** Two internally consistent plans can target the same material; validation must consider plans that already passed and have not finished, and an abandoned plan must neither silently keep nor silently lose its claim. *In the tool:* `active_locks.json`, `cross_batch_conflicts`; an abandoned batch keeps its lock on purpose.
3. **A reviewed exception is recorded and stays visible.** *In the tool:* `accept-match`.
4. **Constraints have a scope.** Standing constraints belong above any single task; one-off restrictions with the task. *In the tool:* `--project` on `add-constraint`/`add-category`.
5. **Declaring the task's shape commits the plan to what that shape needs.** *In the tool:* `new-batch --shape` and the `shape_incomplete` gate.

---

### 18. Anti-patterns

Twelve named failure patterns, each with the tool's answer. "Prevented" means the structure of the tool makes it hard to commit; "Supported" means the tool provides the means but judgment remains; "Not mechanized" means only discipline helps.

| Anti-pattern | The harm | Tool's answer |
|---|---|---|
| **Simultaneous analysis and correction** — fix each issue the moment it is found | No complete picture, so no prioritization and no judgment of completeness | **Prevented.** No command both analyzes and applies. |
| **Interleaved cross-examination and cascade tracing** | Unreliable deduplication; progress through either pass cannot be measured or resumed | **Prevented.** `sync-domino-queue` only queues descriptors that already exist. |
| **Descriptive rather than referential dependencies** | Free text cannot be verified | **Prevented.** `depends_on` and `domino_of` hold real ids, checked; cascade counts are recomputed, not claimed. |
| **Incorrect operation ordering** — general before specific | The specific case becomes unreachable | **Not fully prevented.** Specificity is not inferred; use `--depends-on`. Line-ID addressing removes the classic form of the risk. |
| **End-only validation** | An early error surfaces much later | **Prevented by convention:** `validate-post` per batch. |
| **Ignoring legitimate context during validation** | False alarms | **Supported.** Concrete matches + `accept-match`; the review itself stays a judgment. |
| **Location-less mapping** | Cannot be found, re-verified or confirmed resolved | **Prevented.** Every location is a `line_id`; there is no "approximately here". |
| **Trusting the map without re-checking reality** | A correct analysis yields an incorrect result when acted on late | **Prevented.** `expect_hash`, live, before every write. |
| **Binary success/failure on execution** | Needless rework or needless halting | **Prevented.** `applied` / `skipped` / `recovered` / `abort`. |
| **No resumption path** | Wasted work, or silent redoing | **Prevented.** `checkpoint.json` + `wal.jsonl` + `resume` (with the crash-window caveats of V2). |
| **Conflict-filtered inventory** — building the transfer inventory from the items that raised a decision, so well-behaved material silently disappears | The best-behaved content vanishes precisely because it needed no decision | **Prevented** for assembly: partition first (`add-source-range`), every range needs a disposition; open decisions are a filter on top, never a substitute. |
| **Unprompted substitution** — replacing material that will not resolve (a broken path, a missing dependency) with a working alternative nobody asked for | The mirror of the previous one; fails quietly and is discovered by whoever asked for the work | **Not mechanized.** Carry an unresolvable reference forward exactly as written and say so. |

---

### 19. Large bodies of material, quality assessment and the checklist

#### 19.1 Working with large bodies of material

- Read the entire unit before transforming it; do not proceed sequentially from the start without first understanding the whole (`show-file` before `add-descriptor`, not instead of it).
- Apply matching changes in batches grouped by pattern or category, not one at a time.
- Split work into passes aligned with the natural dimensions of the material, not arbitrary chunks (separate batches per dimension, not one batch chunked by line count).
- Confirm each pass before the next (`validate-post` before opening the next batch).

#### 19.2 Quality assessment

Completion questions, and where the tool answers them:

1. Does the number of issues recorded equal the number marked resolved? → `status <batch>` counts.
2. Does a systematic recheck for all originally identified patterns return none remaining, excluding legitimate exceptions? → `validate-post` invariants, reviewed against their `matches`.
3. Do all elements conform to the reference's structural rules? → the syntax half of `validate-post`, where a checker exists.
4. Have all violations of fundamental/architectural invariants been eliminated? → filter descriptor results by `severity: critical`.
5. Has the underlying meaning or behavior stayed unchanged where only structural or naming changes were intended? → **not mechanically checkable in general**; the closest proxy is the syntax check plus a manual review of a representative sample.

Numerical indicators to record before and after: total units, total volume of material, issue count by severity, units with zero remaining issues. `new-batch` snapshots `{files, lines}` automatically, and `report` compares it with the live registry, but no single command aggregates *all four* across a multi-batch task.

#### 19.3 Checklist upon receiving a task

- [ ] Has the entire reference specification been loaded and read — not only its beginning?
- [ ] Have all materials referenced by the task been loaded?
- [ ] Has an exhaustive taxonomy of deviation types been compiled?
- [ ] For every identified issue, has its cascade been traced as its own resumable pass — checkable per item?
- [ ] Does the map contain precise, unambiguous location references rather than approximate ones?
- [ ] Do all dependency references in the map correspond to entries that actually exist?
- [ ] Is execution order determined by severity?
- [ ] Does each unit have a defined plan of sequential passes?
- [ ] Is validation planned incrementally, after each unit, rather than only at the end?
- [ ] Is it clear, for every category, what constitutes a legitimate exception versus a genuine violation?
- [ ] If this task is interrupted partway through any phase, can it resume from what is recorded rather than restarting that phase?
- [ ] Before a planned change is applied, is the material re-checked against what the plan expected?
- [ ] Does execution distinguish "already done" from "not yet done" from "cannot proceed"?

---

### 20. The dividing line: what is mechanized and what stays judgment

The whole design rests on a deliberate split. This table is the single most useful summary of the methodology as implemented.

| Concern | Mechanized by the engine | Left to the model / person |
|---|---|---|
| Where a line is now | Registry lookup by `line_id` | — |
| Whether the file still matches the plan | Hash compare before every write | Deciding what to do about an `abort` |
| Order of application | Topological sort; severity tie-break; cycle refusal | Declaring `--depends-on` for semantic ordering (e.g. specific-before-general) |
| Finding other places a change might affect | Exhaustive text search across every registered file | **Judging** whether each candidate is a real cascade; spotting logic-level dependencies with no shared text |
| That every finding was looked at | Queue + gate | That each look was *thorough* |
| That a category / file / source range was addressed | Gates (`taxonomy_incomplete`, matrix, `inventory_incomplete`) | Whether the examination was real; whether a disposition is correct |
| That the job is complete | Invariants re-derived from disk; syntax checks | *What* the invariants should say; judging surviving matches |
| Surviving matches | Listed (≤20) with line and text | Deciding legitimate exception vs. real problem |
| Interruption | WAL, checkpoint, `resume` | Reading `resume` and acting on it |
| Reversal | Per-descriptor inverse | Deciding what to undo and in what order |

---
## Part III — Core concepts and data model

Part II described the methodology in the abstract. This part defines the **vocabulary and the data model** of `operational-platform` precisely enough that every later part can use it without restating it: what a line ID is, what a descriptor contains, what a batch goes through, what each kind of gate checks. Facts here come from the code and were checked by running it; where the shipped behavior differs from the bundled documentation, a callout points to the numbered entry in [section 56](#56-verified-behaviors-and-deviations-from-the-documentation).

### 21. The mental model on one page

#### 21.1 The pieces

```
  YOUR PROJECT (the only files the tool ever edits)
  ├── app.py
  ├── util.py
  └── .operational-platform/                    ← the state directory (found like .git/)
        ├── registry.json                  line_id → current position, per file
        ├── payloads/<sha256[:16]>.blob    content-addressed text: new content, "before" text
        ├── batches/
        │     └── batch_0001/
        │           ├── descriptors.json     the edits, their order, their status
        │           ├── invariants.json      "what complete means" — kept apart on purpose
        │           ├── taxonomy.json        declared categories (optional)
        │           ├── constraints.json     protected ranges (optional)
        │           ├── domino_queue.json    findings still owing a cascade check (optional)
        │           ├── region_inventory.json  source ranges needing a disposition (optional)
        │           ├── materials_manifest.json  files that must be registered (optional)
        │           └── snapshot.json        file/line counts when the batch was opened
        ├── project_taxonomy.json          categories inherited by every batch   (optional)
        ├── project_constraints.json       protected ranges inherited by every batch (optional)
        ├── active_locks.json              line IDs claimed by validated batches
        ├── wal.jsonl                      append-only: what started / what finished
        ├── validation_log.jsonl           append-only: validator verdicts
        └── checkpoint.json                overwritten: where things stood last
```

Only a few files exist in a simple job (`registry.json`, one batch with `descriptors.json` and `invariants.json`, the blobs, the three logs). The rest appear when the matching feature is used.

#### 21.2 The nouns

| Noun | One-line definition | Stored in | Detailed in |
|---|---|---|---|
| **file ID** (`file_id`) | `f_` + first 10 hex digits of the SHA-256 of the path *string* | `registry.json` | [§22](#22-files-and-lines-identity-that-never-changes) |
| **line ID** (`line_id`) | Permanent name of one line: `<file_id>_l<5-digit seq>` | `registry.json` | [§22](#22-files-and-lines-identity-that-never-changes) |
| **registry** | The only record of where each line *is now* | `registry.json` | [§23](#23-the-registry) |
| **descriptor** | One atomic edit: an op, a target by line ID, the content it expects there | `batches/<id>/descriptors.json` | [§24](#24-descriptors-the-five-operations) |
| **payload / blob** | Text a descriptor will write (or the "before" text it replaces), stored by content hash | `payloads/` | [§25](#25-hashes-payloads-and-the-compare-and-swap-check) |
| **`expect_hash`** | Hash of the exact content the descriptor was authored against | in the descriptor | [§25](#25-hashes-payloads-and-the-compare-and-swap-check) |
| **batch** | A set of descriptors meant to be checked and applied together | `batches/<id>/` | [§26](#26-batches-and-their-lifecycle) |
| **`apply_order`** | The dependency-safe order `validate-plan` computed | in `descriptors.json` | [§26](#26-batches-and-their-lifecycle), [§45](#45-validatorpy) |
| **taxonomy / category** | A declared, closed list of issue types | `taxonomy.json` | [§27](#27-taxonomy-categories-and-severity) |
| **severity** | `critical` / `major` / `minor` / `cosmetic` — decides order among free choices | in descriptors, invariants | [§27](#27-taxonomy-categories-and-severity) |
| **constraint** | A protected range no descriptor may touch | `constraints.json` | [§28](#28-constraints-and-protected-zones) |
| **invariant** | An independent completeness criterion checked after applying | `invariants.json` | [§29](#29-invariants-and-accepted-matches) |
| **finding / domino queue** | A direct descriptor that still owes a cascade check | `domino_queue.json` | [§30](#30-the-domino-queue) |
| **region inventory** | Source ranges that each need an explicit disposition | `region_inventory.json` | [§31](#31-the-region-inventory) |
| **shape / gate** | A declared task type that commits the batch to certain mechanisms | in `descriptors.json` | [§32](#32-shapes-and-gates) |
| **lock** | A validated batch's claim on specific line IDs | `active_locks.json` | [§33](#33-cross-batch-locks) |
| **WAL / validation log / checkpoint** | The audit trail and the resume pointer | three files | [§34](#34-the-audit-trail-wal-validation-log-and-checkpoint) |

#### 21.3 The life of one edit

```
 1. add-descriptor   reads the file NOW → computes expect_hash, stores payload/"before" blobs
        │            (nothing on disk in your project changes)
        ▼
 2. validate-plan    resolves every target through the registry → ID sets;
        │            runs the gates, conflict graph, topological sort, lock check;
        │            writes apply_order, status "validated", takes locks
        ▼
 3. apply-next       picks the next descriptor in apply_order →
        │              WAL op_start
        │              re-reads the file, hashes the target range, compares with expect_hash
        │                 match     → write the file → update the registry → save registry
        │                             → WAL op_applied → status "applied" → checkpoint
        │                 no match  → "recovered" (post-state already there) or "abort"
        ▼
 4. validate-post    only when everything is applied: syntax of every touched file, every
                     invariant re-derived from disk; status "committed" or "failed"; locks released
```

Two properties are worth fixing in mind. **Hashes are taken at authoring time and enforced at apply time — never at plan time** (§25). And **the descriptor is the unit of everything**: one write, one WAL pair, one status, one undo.

#### 21.4 Who writes what

The documentation stresses that each state file has a single writer, so that "nothing can forge a verdict". This is how it is actually wired:

| File | Documented writer | Actual writers in the code |
|---|---|---|
| `registry.json` | `registry.py` only | `registry.register_file`; `engine.apply_descriptor` / `undo_descriptor` (which call `registry.apply_*`, then `storage.save_registry`) |
| managed files (yours) | `engine.apply_descriptor` only | `engine.apply_descriptor` and `engine.undo_descriptor` |
| `wal.jsonl` | `engine.py` and `domino.py` | `engine.py`, `domino.py`, **`registry.py`** (`file_registered`), **`cli.py`** (`file_inspected`) |
| `validation_log.jsonl` | `validator.py` only | `validator.py` and **`cli.py`** (the `per_op` abort record written by `apply-next` / `apply-all`) |
| `checkpoint.json` | "overwritten on every phase transition" | `engine.py`, `validator.py`, `domino.py`, `inventory.py`, `cli.py` |
| `batches/<id>/*.json` | the module that owns the feature | `engine.py`, `domino.py`, `inventory.py`, `cli.py` (`require-file`, `new-batch` snapshot) |

> **Note.** Every JSON file is written by `storage._write_json`, which writes `<name>.tmp` and then `replace()`s it over the target — atomic on POSIX, so a state file is never half-written (there is no `fsync`, so a power loss can still lose the latest write). The managed files are the exception: they are written with a plain `Path.write_text`, not through a temporary file. See [section 48](#48-concurrency-atomicity-and-crash-windows).

---

### 22. Files and lines: identity that never changes

#### 22.1 File identity

```
file_id = "f_" + sha256(path_string.encode("utf-8")).hexdigest()[:10]
```

The input is **the path string exactly as it was passed to the command**. It is not resolved, normalized or made absolute. Paths are *resolved against the project root* when the file is read or written, but the ID is derived from the spelling.

> **Verified (V3).**
> ```
> $ cli.py register app.py      → "file_id": "f_568470d013"
> $ cli.py register ./app.py    → "file_id": "f_4c5dadafcc"     (the same file on disk)
> ```
> The registry then holds two independent entries for one physical file, each with its own set of line IDs. Nothing warns you.

Practical rule: **one canonical spelling, relative to the project root, everywhere.** That includes `--file`, `--checked-against`, `--src-file`, `--dest-file`, `--files` (for `set-category-scope`), `require-file`, and the positional path of `register` and `show-file`.

#### 22.2 Line identity

```
line_id = "<file_id>_l" + 5-digit zero-padded sequence number      e.g. f_568470d013_l00004
```

Properties, all enforced by `registry.py`:

- **Permanent.** Once minted, a line ID never changes meaning. It carries no position information.
- **Never reused.** Each file has a counter, `next_seq`, which only ever increases — even across deletions.
- **Dead IDs stay in the registry as tombstones** (position `null`). A stale reference to a deleted line therefore fails with a precise message instead of silently resolving to whatever now occupies the old position.
- **Positions are 1-based** and live only in `registry.json`.

A fragment of a real registry, after the rename walked through in [section 36](#36-worked-example-1--a-global-rename):

```json
"f_568470d013": {
  "path": "app.py",
  "lines": {
    "f_568470d013_l00001": null,     ← replaced: tombstone
    "f_568470d013_l00002": 2,
    "f_568470d013_l00003": 3,
    "f_568470d013_l00004": null,     ← replaced: tombstone
    "f_568470d013_l00005": 1,        ← its replacement: a NEW id, at the old position
    "f_568470d013_l00006": 4
  },
  "next_seq": 7,
  "line_ending": "lf"
}
```

#### 22.3 How IDs and positions change

| Event | New IDs minted | IDs tombstoned | Positions affected |
|---|---|---|---|
| `register` | one per line, `l00001…` in file order | — | — |
| `insert_after`, K lines | K, at the anchor + 1 … + K | — | every line below shifts by +K |
| `delete_range`, k lines | — | the k lines | every line below shifts by −k |
| `replace_range`, k → K lines | K, at the old start | the k old lines | every line below shifts by K − k |
| `move_range` | — | — | the block and the lines it jumped over swap; **IDs survive** |
| `copy_range`, K lines | K, after `dest` | — | every line below `dest` shifts by +K |
| undo of `replace_range` | as many as the restored text has (**fresh**) | the lines the replace produced | as a replace |
| undo of `delete_range` | as many as the restored text has (**fresh**) | — | as an insert |
| undo of `insert_after` / `copy_range` | — | the lines it created | as a delete |
| undo of `move_range` | — | — | block moves back; IDs unchanged |
| `register --force` | all lines re-minted from `l00001` | the whole entry is replaced | reset |

> **Verified.** Replacing `L2..L3` (two lines) with three lines `X Y Z`, then undoing it, on a five-line file:
>
> ```
> after replace  L1 X Y Z L4 L5
> after undo     L1 L2 L3 L4 L5
> registry       l00001:1  l00002:∅  l00003:∅  l00004:4  l00005:5
>                l00006:∅  l00007:∅  l00008:∅  l00009:2  l00010:3       next_seq 11
> ```
>
> The text is back, but **the two original lines now have new identities** (`l00009`, `l00010`); the original `l00002`/`l00003` remain tombstones forever. Anything still holding the old IDs — another descriptor, a constraint, an inventory range — can no longer resolve them. This is the root of V12 (an undone `replace_range` or `delete_range` poisons its batch).

> **Verified.** `move_range L2..L3` after `L5` on a six-line file keeps the IDs and only reassigns positions: `l00001:1  l00004:2  l00005:3  l00002:4  l00003:5  l00006:6`.

#### 22.4 Resolving an ID

`registry.resolve_pos(file_id, line_id)` is the single lookup everything goes through. It fails in exactly three ways:

| Condition | Exception | Message |
|---|---|---|
| file not in the registry | `LineNotFound` | `file_id '…' is not registered -- register it first` |
| line ID not in that file's table | `LineNotFound` | `<line_id> is not in the registry for <path>` |
| line ID present but tombstoned | `LineNotFound` | `<line_id> was deleted earlier and is no longer addressable` |

A **range** `start..end` is resolved to a *position interval* and then to the **set of all live line IDs whose positions fall inside it** (`registry.ids_in_range`). If `end` resolves before `start` the call raises `RangeInvalid: … resolves to an inverted range (3..1)`.

Two consequences follow from ranges being position intervals rather than stored lists of IDs:

1. **A range automatically includes lines inserted inside it.** If an earlier descriptor inserts a line between a range's two endpoints, the later descriptor's range now covers that line too. The hash check (§25) catches this at apply time (the range content no longer matches), and the conflict graph (§45) catches an `insert_after` anchored *inside* the range at plan time.
2. **The conflict graph compares ID sets, not endpoints.** This is why an insertion that names neither endpoint but lands inside someone else's range is still detected.

> **Verified (V6).** `add-descriptor` accepts an inverted range without complaint: it hashes the empty slice (`e3b0c44298fc`, the SHA-256 prefix of the empty string). The error appears only at `validate-plan`, as an *uncaught* exception — a JSON `{"error": "RangeInvalid: …"}` with exit code **2** rather than a regular validation failure with exit code 1.

#### 22.5 What a "line" is

The tool's line model is Python's: `Path.read_text(encoding="utf-8").splitlines()`. Writing is the inverse: join the lines with the file's line ending, and add one terminator after the last line (an empty file stays empty). This is simple and mostly invisible — until the content is unusual.

| Situation | What the tool does | Reference |
|---|---|---|
| File does not end with a newline | Reads fine; **gains a trailing newline** on the first write | V7 (E1) |
| CRLF file | `\r\n` detected once at `register` time (`line_ending: "crlf"`) and used for every write; an LF payload is written as CRLF | V7 (E2) |
| Mixed LF/CRLF | **Normalized to a single style** on the first write, touching lines the batch never targeted | V7 (E6) |
| A line containing a form feed (`\x0c`), vertical tab, `\x1c`–`\x1e`, `\x85`, ` ` or ` ` | `splitlines()` treats these as line breaks: the registry sees *more* lines than an editor does, and **the separator is rewritten as a newline** on the next write | V7 (E3) |
| Lone `\r` | Treated as a line break | V7 |
| File that is not valid UTF-8 | `register` fails: `UnicodeDecodeError …` (exit 2). Binary files are out of scope | V7 (E10) |
| Empty file | 0 lines | — |
| File with only `\n` | 1 line, the empty string | — |
| **Path that does not exist** | `register` **succeeds with 0 lines**; an `insert_after … --after START` then *creates* the file (and its parent directories) | V19 (E7) |

Payload text is split with `str.split("\n")`, which has its own consequences ([§24.4](#244-payload-text-and-newlines)).

---

### 23. The registry

#### 23.1 Format

```json
{
  "files": {
    "f_568470d013": {
      "path": "app.py",
      "lines": { "f_568470d013_l00001": null, "f_568470d013_l00002": 2, … },
      "next_seq": 7,
      "line_ending": "lf"
    }
  }
}
```

| Field | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `path` | The path string as registered (also the input of `file_id`) |
| `lines` | `line_id → 1-based position`, or `null` for a tombstone |
