### 38. Worked example 3 — assembling a document

**Task.** Build `out.md` from material in two source files, deliberately keeping some of it and deliberately dropping the rest — and be able to show that no region of either source was silently lost.

```
s1.md                      s2.md                   out.md (the target)
# Title A                  # Title B               # Combined
intro A                    intro B                 (blank line)
## Install                 ## Usage
step 1                     use it
step 2
## Legacy
old stuff
```

Decisions: keep `s1`'s intro and Install section (drop its title); drop `s1`'s Legacy section; keep `s2`'s Usage section (drop its title and intro).

#### Partition first

```
$ cli.py new-batch --shape assembly
$ cli.py validate-plan batch_0001
{… "result": "fail", "shape_incomplete": ["shape requires a region inventory, but add-source-range was never used"],
 "detail": "batch declared shape='assembly', which requires: ['inventory']"}      [exit=1]

$ cli.py add-source-range batch_0001 --file s1.md --start f_8bb7300d37_l00001 --end f_8bb7300d37_l00005    → ri0001
$ cli.py add-source-range batch_0001 --file s1.md --start f_8bb7300d37_l00006 --end f_8bb7300d37_l00007    → ri0002
$ cli.py add-source-range batch_0001 --file s2.md --start f_2a89e9a9b4_l00001 --end f_2a89e9a9b4_l00002    → ri0003
$ cli.py add-source-range batch_0001 --file s2.md --start f_2a89e9a9b4_l00003 --end f_2a89e9a9b4_l00004    → ri0004
```

Between them, the four ranges cover **every line of both sources** (7 + 4). That is the whole point of the gate: a region with no open question still gets an entry, so it cannot vanish quietly. (Each call prints the new range: `{"range_id": "ri0001", …, "status": "pending", "disposition": null, …}`.)

```
$ cli.py inventory-next batch_0001
{"range_id": "ri0001", "file_id": "f_8bb7300d37",
 "content": ["# Title A", "intro A", "## Install", "step 1", "step 2"]}

$ cli.py validate-plan batch_0001
{… "result": "fail", "inventory_incomplete": ["ri0001", "ri0002", "ri0003", "ri0004"],
 "detail": "declared source range has no recorded disposition"}                    [exit=1]
```

#### A first attempt that fails instructively

The natural way to write the plan is two inserts after the same anchor — the blank line 2 of `out.md`:

```
$ printf 'intro A\n## Install\nstep 1\nstep 2' > edited.txt
$ cli.py add-descriptor batch_0001 --op insert_after --file out.md --after f_9edf618823_l00002 --payload-file edited.txt     → d0001
$ cli.py copy-across-files batch_0001 --src-file s2.md --start f_2a89e9a9b4_l00003 --end f_2a89e9a9b4_l00004 \
        --dest-file out.md --dest-after f_9edf618823_l00002                                                              → d0002
```

Both descriptors carry `expect_hash: e3b0c44298fc` — the hash of the **empty anchor line**, since line 2 of `out.md` is blank. After resolving all four ranges (`inventory-resolve … --disposition transferred_with_edit --descriptor-ids d0001 …`, two `excluded` with notes, one `transferred_with_edit` for `d0002`) and adding an invariant, the plan is checked:

```
$ cli.py validate-plan batch_0001
{… "result": "fail", "conflicts": [
  "d0001 and d0002 both target overlapping lines ['f_9edf618823_l00002'] in f_9edf618823 with no declared order between them -- either they must not both apply, or one needs depends_on the other"]}   [exit=1]

$ cli.py apply-all batch_0001
{"applied": []}                                                                    [exit=0]

$ cli.py validate-post batch_0001
{"phase": "post", …, "result": "fail", "error": "2 descriptor(s) not yet applied: ['d0001', 'd0002']"}   [exit=1]
```

Three lessons are packed into that failure:

1. Two inserts anchored on the **same line** overlap, and the planner will not pick an order for you.
2. `apply-all` on a batch that never passed `validate-plan` does **nothing and exits 0** (`{"applied": []}`); only `apply-next` complains (V4). Always read the *contents* of `applied`, not the exit code.
3. `copy-across-files` / `move-across-files` accept no `--depends-on`, so the ordering has to be expressed through the *other* descriptor.

#### The corrected flow

The rule for stacked inserts: **the insert applied last ends up closest to the anchor.** To get "Install, then Usage" at one anchor, the Usage block must be applied **first**, and the Install insert must depend on it:

```
$ cli.py copy-across-files batch_0001 --src-file s2.md --start …_l00003 --end …_l00004 \
        --dest-file out.md --dest-after f_9edf618823_l00002                                     → d0001  (Usage block)
$ cli.py add-descriptor batch_0001 --op insert_after --file out.md --after f_9edf618823_l00002 \
        --payload-file edited.txt --depends-on d0001                                            → d0002  (Install, applied second)
$ cli.py inventory-resolve batch_0001 ri0001 --disposition transferred_with_edit --descriptor-ids d0002 --note "title dropped"
$ cli.py inventory-resolve batch_0001 ri0002 --disposition excluded --note "legacy section dropped"
$ cli.py inventory-resolve batch_0001 ri0003 --disposition excluded --note "title+intro of 2nd source not needed"
$ cli.py inventory-resolve batch_0001 ri0004 --disposition transferred_verbatim --descriptor-ids d0001 --note "copied as-is"
$ cli.py add-invariant batch_0001 --file out.md --pattern '(?m)^## ' --expected-count 2 \
        --description "Install + Usage headings, no Legacy"

$ cli.py validate-plan batch_0001
{"phase": "plan", …, "result": "pass", "apply_order": ["d0001", "d0002"],
 "warnings": ["invariant on pattern '(?m)^## ' has no --checked-against, and this batch has payload-carrying descriptors -- confirm the expected count came from the untouched source, not from re-counting the payload you just built"]}
```

Preview before touching anything:

```
$ cli.py dry-run batch_0001 --file out.md
# Combined

intro A
## Install
step 1
step 2
## Usage
use it
```

Then `apply-all`, and:

```
$ cli.py validate-post batch_0001
{"phase": "post", …, "result": "pass", "syntax": {"…/out.md": "skipped (no checker registered for this file type)"},
 "invariants": [{"type": "occurrence_count", "description": "Install + Usage headings, no Legacy", "pattern": "(?m)^## ",
                 "expected": 2, "actual": 2, "raw_matches_before_exceptions": 2, "result": "pass",
                 "matches": [{"line": 4, "text": "## Install"}, {"line": 7, "text": "## Usage"}], "matches_truncated": false}]}
```

#### What the example shows

| Point | Detail |
|---|---|
| **Dispositions are a record, not a proof.** | `transferred_with_edit` demands existing descriptor IDs but does not check they target the range; `excluded` and `transferred_verbatim` are on your word. What is guaranteed: no declared range is left without one |
| **The invariant is independent of the payload.** | `expected_count: 2` came from the *intended result* ("Install and Usage, no Legacy"), not from grepping `edited.txt`. The warning is the tool asking you to confirm exactly that. An invariant whose count is grepped from the same payload "checks that the plan agrees with itself, not that it is complete" |
| **The regex needs `(?m)`.** | Without it `^## ` would anchor only at the start of the file and the count would be 0 (V8) |
| **No syntax check for Markdown.** | `validate-post` reports `skipped (no checker registered for this file type)` — honestly, not "OK" |
| **A move/copy between files is two descriptors.** | `copy-across-files` composed the `insert_after` from the *verified* source text; nothing makes the pair atomic ([§40.4](#404-moving-and-copying-across-files)) |

---

### 39. Failure, conflict and recovery in practice

#### 39.1 Reading a failure

| Signal | Meaning |
|---|---|
| exit `0` | the command ran. **Not** necessarily that anything useful happened (`apply-all` on an unvalidated batch exits 0) |
| exit `1` | a *reported* failure worth stopping for: a failed `validate-plan` / `validate-post` / `check`, an `abort` |
| exit `2` | a usage error **or any uncaught exception** (bad regex, unresolvable `dest`, inverted range, unknown ID…). The JSON is `{"error": "<Type>: <message>"}` |
| `result: "fail"` + a key | the key names the category of failure ([§32.2](#322-all-gates-in-the-order-validate-plan-runs-them), full catalog in [§51](#51-the-validate-plan-diagnostic-catalog)) |

`validate-plan` stops at the first failing check, so fixing one problem may reveal the next.

#### 39.2 Conflicts — and why a declared order is obeyed, not judged

Two descriptors whose resolved ID sets overlap, without a declared order, fail the plan:

```
$ cli.py validate-plan batch_0001
{… "result": "fail", "conflicts": ["d0001 and d0002 both target overlapping lines ['f_e4723ca566_l00002'] in f_e4723ca566 with no declared order between them -- either they must not both apply, or one needs depends_on the other"]}
```

(`d0001` replaced line 2; `d0002` replaced lines 2–3.) Two replaces of the same text usually mean "they must not both apply": since descriptors cannot be removed, the way out is a new batch. When both *should* apply, declare the order — but the planner **obeys the order you declare without judging whether it is meaningful**:

| Plan | `validate-plan` | Result |
|---|---|---|
| `d0001` insert after L2, then `d0002` (depends on `d0001`) replace L2 | pass | applies; file: `l1 L2-new inserted l3 l4 l5` |
| `d0001` replace L2, then `d0002` (depends on `d0001`) insert after L2 | **pass** | `d0001` applies; `d0002` → `abort: target no longer exists in the registry (…_l00002 was deleted earlier and is no longer addressable). This batch needs re-planning, not a retry.` |

In the second plan the anchor of `d0002` is tombstoned by `d0001`. The planner does not simulate the batch forward, so this is only discovered mid-apply, leaving the batch half-applied. Check by hand that each descriptor's target **still exists when its turn comes**.

Other plan-time failures with the same shape:

```
dependency_cycle:  ["d0001", "d0002"]
conflicts:         ["d0001: depends_on unknown descriptor d0099"]
protected_zone_violations: ["d0001 targets protected lines ['f_e4723ca566_l00003'] (vendored, do not touch)"]
cross_batch_conflicts:     ["batch_0002 overlaps already-locked ranges from batch_0001: [('f_e4723ca566', 'f_e4723ca566_l00003')]"]
```

#### 39.3 The two most useful questions after any failure

1. **What did the tool actually change?** `status <batch>` (counts), `cat` of the file, `show-file` for current IDs. Nothing is written by a failed plan or an `abort`.
2. **Is the state still consistent?** The one case where the answer can be *no* is a failed `move_range` with an invalid `dest` (V5) — there the file changed and the registry did not. Detect it with `check <batch> <id>`: a move that "should" still match but fails the hash means the registry is stale.

#### 39.4 Protected zones

A descriptor that reaches into a constraint fails the plan before anything is touched; fix the target or remove the descriptor by abandoning the batch. If the zone is stale ("declared constraint is stale and could not be re-resolved"), the protected lines were replaced by an earlier change; a *batch-level* constraint is simply recreated in a new batch, but a **project-level** one has no removal command (hand-edit `project_constraints.json`).

#### 39.5 Cross-batch locks

`cross_batch_conflicts` names the other batch. Finish it (`apply`, then `validate-post`, which releases its locks even on a `failed` result) or — if it is abandoned — remove its entry from `active_locks.json` by hand, the one hand-edit the authors endorse. Never delete the whole file blindly: it may hold other batches' live claims.

#### 39.6 Abort: the file changed under the plan

An `abort` means *the live content at the target matches neither what the descriptor expected nor a plausible result of applying it*: something changed the file outside the batch. The file is left exactly as found. A complete, real sequence:

```
$ cli.py validate-plan batch_0001
{… "result": "pass", "apply_order": ["d0001", "d0002"]}
$ cli.py apply-next batch_0001
{"result": "applied", "descriptor_id": "d0001"}
              ── someone edits line 4 outside the tool: print(old_name(1)) → print(old_name(999)) ──
$ cli.py apply-next batch_0001
{"result": "abort", "descriptor_id": "d0002",
 "detail": "d0002: live content matches neither the expected pre-state (4532a463920b) nor a plausible post-state. live hash f9e49c7473ff. Someone or something changed this file outside the batch -- re-plan rather than retry."}      [exit=1]

$ cli.py resume
{"checkpoint": {"active_batch": "batch_0001", "last_interrupt_cause": "abort", …},
 "batch_status": "validated", "applied": 1, "total": 2,
 "suggested_next_command": "investigate the abort detail, fix the underlying cause (re-register the file and re-plan a fresh batch if the file changed out of band), do not just retry apply-next",
 "last_abort": {"phase": "per_op", "batch_id": "batch_0001", "descriptor_id": "d0002", "result": "abort", "detail": "…"}}
$ cli.py check batch_0001 d0002
{"phase": "per_op", …, "result": "fail", "detail": "live hash f9e49c7473ff"}            [exit=1]
$ cli.py validate-post batch_0001
{"phase": "post", …, "result": "fail", "error": "1 descriptor(s) not yet applied: ['d0002']"}
```

The tool recommends "re-plan a fresh batch". Here is what actually happens when you do:

```
$ cli.py new-batch                                   → batch_0002
$ cli.py add-descriptor batch_0002 --op replace_range --file app.py --start …_l00004 --end …_l00004 --payload-text 'print(new_name(999))'
$ cli.py validate-plan batch_0002
{… "result": "fail", "cross_batch_conflicts": ["batch_0002 overlaps already-locked ranges from batch_0001: [('f_568470d013', 'f_568470d013_l00004')]"]}
```

> **Verified (V21).** An aborted batch can **never be closed**: `validate-post` refuses while any descriptor is unapplied, so `batch_0001` keeps its locks — even the one for the line it *did* apply — and blocks the very re-plan the tool recommends. The `resume` suggestion does not mention this. The way out is the documented hand-edit:

```
# remove "batch_0001" from .operational-platform/active_locks.json, then
$ cli.py validate-plan batch_0002      → pass
$ cli.py apply-all batch_0002          → applied
$ cli.py validate-post batch_0002      → pass
```

(`batch_0001` stays `validated` with one applied and one pending descriptor for good — a permanent open item in the audit trail.)

**What to do after an abort**, in order:

1. Read `detail` and `last_abort`. Find out *what* changed the file (a person, a formatter, another tool, a second session).
2. `show-file` the file. If the new text is what you want, the *plan* is out of date, not the file; if the outside change was a mistake, restore the file from version control.
3. If lines were added or removed outside the tool, **the registry no longer matches the file** — re-register with `register <file> --force` (this re-mints every ID, so nothing may still reference the old ones).
4. Open a fresh batch and re-author the descriptors against current content. Release the stale locks first (hand-edit).
5. Do not "retry `apply-next` expecting a different result".

> **Note.** `check` and `abort` use the same comparison. `check <batch> <descriptor>` before `apply-next` is a cheap way to find out whether the file has drifted since planning.

#### 39.7 A failed post-condition

`validate-post` returning `fail` marks the batch `failed` and **releases its locks**, but does not undo anything. Decide per failing item:

| The failing item is… | Do |
|---|---|
| a surviving match you have reviewed and judge legitimate | `accept-match`, then `validate-post` again (do this as the last step — accepted matches are keyed by line number) |
| a genuine miss | a small follow-up batch closing that specific gap, planned and validated like any other. The old batch is `failed` and its locks are gone, so nothing blocks the new one |
| a syntax error | fix with a follow-up batch (e.g. `replace_range` of the offending line); or `undo-descriptor` for the one change that caused it |
| an error instead of a result (`PatternError`, `LineNotFound`) | the invariant itself is broken — see V8; the batch stays `validated` with its locks held. **Unregistered file** (`LineNotFound: file_id … is not registered`): `register` it and run `validate-post` again — verified: it then passes and commits. **Bad regex** (`PatternError`): the batch cannot be committed; open a new batch |

#### 39.8 Undo in practice

`undo-descriptor <batch> <descriptor>` reverses **one applied descriptor** through its own inverse: replace restores the original text, insert/copy delete what they created, delete re-inserts what it removed, move moves the block back. It works for all five ops:

```
replace: applied -> L1 X Y Z L4 L5      after undo -> L1 L2 L3 L4 L5
delete:  applied -> L1 L4 L5            after undo -> L1 L2 L3 L4 L5
insert:  applied -> L1 L2 N1 N2 L3 …    after undo -> L1 L2 L3 L4 L5
copy:    applied -> L1 L2 L3 L4 L1 L2 L5   after undo -> L1 L2 L3 L4 L5
move:    applied -> L1 L4 L5 L2 L3      after undo -> L1 L2 L3 L4 L5
```

For replace, insert and copy it first checks that the live content still equals what the descriptor produced and refuses otherwise ("something else changed it since"). Delete and move have **no such check**. The descriptor's status becomes `undone`. Errors: `d0001 has status 'pending', not 'applied' -- nothing to undo` (the same text for `undone`).

What undo does **not** do, all verified:

| Expectation (from the docs) | Reality |
|---|---|
| "An undo followed by `apply-next` is a redo" | `apply-next` reports `recovered` — "WAL shows this already completed; status reconciled, nothing re-applied" — and flips the status back to `applied` **with the file still in its original state**. `validate-post` then **passes**. A false green (**V1**) |
| The batch can continue after an undo | For `replace_range` / `delete_range` the descriptor's target IDs are now tombstones: the next `validate-plan` fails with `schema_errors: ["d0001: …_l00002 was deleted earlier and is no longer addressable"]`. The batch can no longer be re-planned (**V12**). Undoing an `insert_after` / `copy_range` / `move_range` leaves the plan valid, but re-applying still hits V1 |
| Undo restores identities | It restores *text* with **new IDs** (§22.3). Anything holding the old IDs breaks |
| Undo order is enforced | Not at all: undoing an early descriptor while later ones are applied is allowed. Undo in the **reverse order of application** yourself |
| A crash mid-undo is recovered | `undo_start` without `undo_applied` in the WAL tells you it happened; re-running is not guaranteed safe |

**Practical rule:** treat undo as an *emergency back-out*, not a redo mechanism. After an undo, abandon the batch (do not re-apply, do not try to commit it) and express the corrected change as a new batch. For anything you would regret losing, work on a version-controlled checkout.

#### 39.9 Interruption

Because every transition is recorded, an interrupted session resumes by *reading*: `resume` → follow the suggestion. Typical situations:

| Where it stopped | State on disk | Next |
|---|---|---|
| before `validate-plan` | descriptors present, `planning` | continue authoring; `sync-domino-queue` again; `validate-plan` |
| mid-trace | queue partly `traced`; checkpoint has `domino_pending` | `domino-next` → continue (`domino-resolve` is idempotent) |
| between applies | some descriptors `applied` | `apply-next` continues with the next one |
| **inside** one `apply-next` (killed process) | one of four crash windows, [§48](#48-concurrency-atomicity-and-crash-windows) | `apply-next` again — and read the result carefully: `recovered` is the good outcome, but for `insert_after` and `copy_range` two of the windows silently apply the change **twice** (V2). After any crash, `show-file` and compare |
| after all applies, before `validate-post` | all `applied` | `validate-post` |

---

### 40. Recipes

Short, concrete answers to "how do I…". Outcomes quoted are from real runs.

#### 40.1 Several edits in one file whose line counts differ

The reason the tool exists. Three edits authored against the *original* numbering of an eight-line file — insert three lines at the top, delete original lines 2–3, replace original line 6:

```
$ cli.py add-descriptor batch_0001 --op insert_after  --file f.txt --after START --payload-text $'H1\nH2\nH3'
$ cli.py add-descriptor batch_0001 --op delete_range  --file f.txt --start …_l00002 --end …_l00003
$ cli.py add-descriptor batch_0001 --op replace_range --file f.txt --start …_l00006 --end …_l00006 --payload-text 'SIX (edited)'
$ cli.py validate-plan batch_0001        → pass, apply_order ["d0001","d0002","d0003"]
$ cli.py apply-all batch_0001
```

```
before: one two three four five six seven eight          after: H1 H2 H3 one four five SIX (edited) seven eight
```

Each descriptor named an ID, so `d0002` and `d0003` hit the right lines although `d0001` had already pushed everything down by three. The registry afterwards: `l00001:4  l00002:∅  l00003:∅  l00004:5  l00005:6  l00006:∅  l00007:8  l00008:9  l00009:1  l00010:2  l00011:3  l00012:7`.

#### 40.2 Choosing the right operation

| I want to… | Use |
|---|---|
| add lines at the top | `insert_after --after START` |
| add lines at the end | `insert_after --after <ID of the last line>` |
| add lines in the middle | `insert_after --after <ID of the line above>` |
| change lines (any number of lines → any number) | `replace_range` (an empty payload makes **one blank line**, not a deletion) |
| remove lines | `delete_range` |
| reorder lines inside one file | `move_range --dest <ID of the line it should follow>` (`START` for the top) |
| duplicate lines inside one file | `copy_range --dest <ID>` |
| take lines from one file into another | `move-across-files` / `copy-across-files` |
| create a new file | [§40.5](#405-creating-a-new-file) |
| delete or rename a file | **not supported** — the tool never removes a file (deleting every line leaves an empty one), and a file's identity is its path |

#### 40.3 Moving a block within a file

`dest` means "immediately after this line". On a six-line file `L1…L6`:

| Descriptor | Result |
|---|---|
| move `L2..L3` after `L5` (later) | `L1 L4 L5 L2 L3 L6` (IDs preserved: `l00001:1 l00004:2 l00005:3 l00002:4 l00003:5 l00006:6`) |
| move `L5..L6` after `L1` (earlier) | `L1 L5 L6 L2 L3 L4` |
| move `L3..L4` to `START` | `L3 L4 L1 L2 L5 L6` |
| copy `L1..L2` after `L4` | `L1 L2 L3 L4 L1 L2 L5 L6` |
| delete `L2..L3` | `L1 L4 L5 L6` |
| insert two lines at `START` and one after the last line | `top1 top2 L1 … L6 bottom` |

> **Caution (V5).** Make sure `dest` lies **outside** the block and is still live when the move runs. `dest` is validated by nothing before apply; a `dest` inside the block (or equal to its first/last line) makes `apply-next` return `RangeInvalid: move destination falls inside the block being moved` **after the file was already rewritten** — verified: `L1 L2 L3 L4 L5` became `L1 L3 L2 L4 L5` while the registry kept its old positions. `check` then fails and the registry must be rebuilt. `copy_range --dest START` is accepted but fails at apply (`LineNotFound: START is not in the registry`). A `dest` that an earlier descriptor of the batch deletes fails the same way (`LineNotFound … was deleted earlier`, exit 2).

#### 40.4 Moving and copying across files

```
$ cli.py move-across-files batch_0001 --src-file a.txt --start …_l00002 --end …_l00003 \
        --dest-file b.txt --dest-after …_l00001
{"delete_descriptor": {"op": "delete_range", …, "descriptor_id": "d0001"},
 "insert_descriptor": {"op": "insert_after", …, "after": "f_ffa0da5d88_l00001", "descriptor_id": "d0002"}}
$ cli.py validate-plan batch_0001   → pass, apply_order ["d0001","d0002"]
$ cli.py apply-all batch_0001
```

```
a.txt: a1 a2 a3 a4  →  a1 a4          b.txt: b1 b2  →  b1 a2 a3 b2
```

The two descriptors share one blob (the verified source text). They touch different files, so no order is needed and none is added. They are **not atomic**: one can apply while the other aborts, leaving the lines in both places or in neither — `descriptors.json` shows which applied. `undo-descriptor` reverses each half separately (verified: undoing `d0002`, then `d0001`, restored both files). These commands accept no `--depends-on`, `--category` or `--severity` (they pass no extras), so shape the plan through other descriptors if you need ordering.

#### 40.5 Creating a new file

There is no "create file" operation, but registering a path that does not exist yields a zero-line file, and an insert at the top then creates it — including missing parent directories:

```
$ cli.py register brand/new.txt
{"file_id": "f_40799742e0", "path": "brand/new.txt", "line_count": 0}
$ cli.py add-descriptor batch_0001 --op insert_after --file brand/new.txt --after START --payload-text $'hello\nworld'
$ cli.py validate-plan batch_0001 && cli.py apply-all batch_0001
```

The file now holds `hello⏎world⏎`. Two cautions: a **typo in a path** at `register` time silently registers an empty phantom file instead of failing (V19), and the new file is written with LF endings.

#### 40.6 Several inserts at the same anchor

Inserts anchored on the same line overlap (§39.2) and need a declared order. The **last-applied** insert lands closest to the anchor:

| You want, below anchor `L3` | Apply order |
|---|---|
| `ins-A` then `ins-B` | `ins-B` first, then `ins-A` (`ins-A` `--depends-on` `ins-B`) |

Verified: with `d0002 --depends-on d0001`, `d0001 = ins-A`, `d0002 = ins-B`, the file read `L1 L2 L3 ins-B ins-A L4 …`. Two inserts at **`START`** do not conflict at all (START is excluded from the overlap test) and simply stack the same way — `second-added first-added L1 …` when applied in insertion order (V17).

#### 40.7 Mechanical find-and-replace

```
cli.py add-descriptor-template <batch> --find old_name --replace new_name [--file app.py]
```

The text is matched **literally** (not as a regex), and the template writes **one `replace_range` per matching *line***, replacing every occurrence within the line and keeping its indentation. Verified: a line `foo foo bar` became `BAZ BAZ bar` through a single descriptor; two files, one `--file` filter respected. A line another descriptor already targets is not skipped — it shows up as a conflict at `validate-plan`. Because the template covers every match across **all registered files**, a following domino pass will typically find nothing new; the invariants are what check the job.

#### 40.8 Scouting and previews

| Command | Use |
|---|---|
| `show-file F` | current IDs and text (also records `file_inspected` for `--checked-against`) |
| `find-pattern --pattern REGEX [--file F]` | per-line regex search across registered files; test an invariant's or a hint's pattern here first (mind that invariants evaluate over the whole text — V8) |
| `explain <batch> <d>` | `before` / `after` text of one descriptor (`before` exists only for delete/replace; move has neither) |
| `dry-run <batch> --file F` | the file as it would look after all pending descriptors — plain text, one file, **no hash checks** |
| `check <batch> <d>` | would this descriptor still apply right now? |
| `status <batch> [--group-by a,b]` | counts; `--group-by file_id,category` for a breakdown |

#### 40.9 Batch size, and several batches in sequence

- One batch per logically related set of edits; split a big job by **dimension** (rename first, then restructuring), not by line count.
- Keep batches small: a failed post-condition is easier to diagnose at ten descriptors than at fifty.
- Run `validate-post` after **each** batch, not once at the end — it also releases the locks that would otherwise block the next batch on the same lines.
- A breaking change belongs in its own batch.
- Two batches can exist at once, but they cannot claim the same lines once both are validated; `resume` follows only the most recently active one.

#### 40.10 Moving a batch to another project

```
$ cli.py export-batch batch_0001 --out /path/exp.tar.gz
{"exported": "batch_0001", "path": "/path/exp.tar.gz"}
$ cli.py import-batch /path/exp.tar.gz            # in the other project
{"imported_from": "/path/exp.tar.gz"}
```

The archive holds the batch directory and the **entire** shared `payloads/` store (not only the blobs the batch needs). The import merges blobs by name and refuses to overwrite an existing batch ID. Cautions:

- The destination must have registered **the same files, in the same state** — IDs derive from the path and registration order; nothing is remapped. Verified: after an import into a project with the same `f.txt`, the batch validated and applied; where content differs, hash checks fail at apply.
- **Check the numbering before the next `new-batch`** (V13): importing `batch_0003` into a project that has one batch makes the next `new-batch` allocate `batch_0003` again and overwrite it. Verified — the imported batch's descriptor vanished and a stray `taxonomy.json` stayed behind.
- A failed import leaves `.operational-platform/_import_tmp/` behind, and the extraction applies no tar filter (Python 3.12–3.13 prints a `DeprecationWarning`).
- **Export a batch before you apply it.** Descriptor statuses travel in the archive (V31): a batch exported *after* `apply-all` — and a committed one — arrives as `applied`/`committed` in a project whose files were never edited, and `validate-post` passes there. After any import, `status` should show the descriptors as `pending`; if it shows `applied`, re-plan in the destination.
- Import only archives you made yourself: extraction is unfiltered ([section 57](#57-trust-model-and-security-notes)).

#### 40.11 Awkward file contents

| Situation | Behavior (§22.5) |
|---|---|
| CRLF files | preserved; LF payloads are written as CRLF |
| no trailing newline | one is added on the first write |
| mixed line endings | normalized to one style, touching untargeted lines |
| form feed, vertical tab, U+2028 … inside a line | the line is split in the registry and the character is rewritten as a newline — **do not use the tool on such files** |
| non-UTF-8 files | `register` fails with `UnicodeDecodeError` |
| a trailing newline in `--payload-text` | an extra blank line is written |

#### 40.12 Payloads and shell quoting

- For anything longer than a line or two, use `--payload-file`. It strips exactly one trailing newline.
- A value that starts with two dashes must use the `=` form, or argparse mistakes it for a flag: `--domino-hint=--the-value`, `--payload-text=--text`.
- `$'a\nb'` (bash ANSI-C quoting) is the quick way to pass a multi-line `--payload-text`.
- `--payload-text` is **not** trimmed; `--payload-file` is.

#### 40.13 Shape gates as a checklist

Declare `--shape` when you want the tool to refuse to plan until you have done the thing that shape depends on. Because a gate only checks that the mechanism was used (§32.1), treat it as a reminder, not a certificate.

---
## Part V — Inside the engine

This part walks through the code. It is for readers who want to understand *why* the tool behaves as it does, to extend it, or to judge how far to trust it. Everything is derived from reading the seven modules as shipped in the archive; statements that were additionally confirmed by running the code are marked **Verified**, and statements that follow from the code but were not exercised are marked **Code-derived**. File and line references (`engine.py:442`) are to the copy in the archive's `operational-platform.skill`; the standalone `operational-platform.md` is byte-identical to its `SKILL.md`.

---

### 41. Module architecture

#### 41.1 The seven modules

| Module | Lines | Bytes | Responsibility | Principal functions |
|---|---:|---:|---|---|
| `storage.py` | 344 | 11,324 | The gateway to the disk: root discovery, JSON/JSONL/blob I/O, hashing, line reading and writing, the checkpoint file | `_find_root`, `state_dir`, `_write_json`, `_append_jsonl`, `store_blob`, `read_lines`, `write_lines`, `save_checkpoint` |
| `registry.py` | 246 | 10,041 | File IDs, line IDs, and every position update | `file_id_for`, `register_file`, `resolve_pos`, `ids_in_range`, `apply_insert/delete/replace/move`, `scan_pattern` |
| `engine.py` | 814 | 39,340 | The descriptor schema, batch bookkeeping, **`apply_descriptor`** (the only code that mutates a managed file), undo, categories, constraints, invariant definitions | `new_batch`, `add_descriptor`, `apply_descriptor`, `undo_descriptor`, `add_invariant`, `accept_match` |
| `validator.py` | 605 | 27,415 | The independent checks: plan-time, per-operation, post-condition; cross-batch locks | `validate_plan`, `check_descriptor`, `validate_post`, `release_locks` |
| `domino.py` | 253 | 11,024 | The domino queue | `sync_queue`, `next_pending`, `resolve`, `status` |
| `inventory.py` | 103 | 4,514 | The region inventory | `add_range`, `next_pending`, `resolve`, `status` |
| `cli.py` | 679 | 27,495 | argparse, 38 subcommands, JSON output, exit codes, export/import, `resume`, `dry-run`, `report` | `main`, `cmd_*`, `_out`, `_err` |
| **Total** | **3,044** | **131,118** | | |

The distribution reflects the design: the "dangerous" part (`apply_descriptor` plus the four position primitives it calls) is roughly 300 lines; the larger share of the code is validation and bookkeeping.

#### 41.2 Dependencies

| Module | Imports (from this project) | What it borrows |
|---|---|---|
| `storage` | — | (standard library only) |
| `registry` | `storage` | file reading, registry load/save, WAL append |
| `engine` | `registry`, `storage` | ID resolution, position primitives, blobs, state files |
| `validator` | `engine`, `registry`, `storage` | from `engine`: `effective_taxonomy`, `effective_constraints`, `BASE_OPS`, `SEVERITY_LEVELS`, `_check_pre_state` |
| `domino` | `engine`, `registry`, `storage` | from `engine`: `target_old_content` |
| `inventory` | `registry`, `storage` | `ids_in_range`, state files |
| `cli` | all six | everything |

The import graph is a clean layering (`storage` → `registry` → `engine` → `validator`/`domino`; `inventory` beside them; `cli` on top) with **no cycles**. Third-party packages: none. The standard-library modules used are `argparse`, `hashlib`, `json`, `os`, `pathlib`, `re`, `shutil`, `sys`, `tarfile`, `time`, `typing`, and — lazily, only for `.js` files — `subprocess`.

`cli.py` starts with `sys.path.insert(0, str(Path(__file__).parent))` so the sibling modules are importable by bare name regardless of the current directory. The consequence is that the scripts directory is a trusted code location: anything placed there that shadows a module name would be imported ([section 57](#57-trust-model-and-security-notes)).

#### 41.3 The process model

Every command is a **fresh Python process**. Nothing is cached in memory between commands; every command re-reads what it needs from `.operational-platform/` and writes back what it changed. This is deliberate ("state exists only when it is on disk") and is what makes the tool resumable by construction — and also what makes it slow for very large inputs (see 41.5), because there is no way to keep a parsed registry in memory across commands.

Inside a single command the pattern is almost always *load → compute → save the whole file*:

```
load_registry()  ──►  mutate the in-memory dict  ──►  save_registry()      # whole file, atomic rename
load_descriptors ──►  mutate                     ──►  save_descriptors()   # whole file, atomic rename
```

There is no partial update of any JSON file, and no locking ([section 48](#48-concurrency-atomicity-and-crash-windows)).

#### 41.4 The claim "all I/O goes through `storage.py`" — and the exceptions

`storage.py`'s header says all filesystem I/O lives there "and nowhere else". Almost, but not literally. Code-derived, by grepping the other modules for file operations:

| Where | Direct file/process operation |
|---|---|
| `cli.py:105` | `Path(args.payload_file).read_text(...)` — reading `--payload-file` |
| `cli.py:432–469` | `tarfile` read/write, `Path.rename`, `shutil.rmtree` — `export-batch` / `import-batch` |
| `validator.py:469` | `path.read_text(...)` for the Python syntax check |
| `validator.py:476–478` | `subprocess.run(["node", "--check", …])` for `.js` |
| `validator.py:523` | `path.read_text(...)` for every invariant |
| `registry.py:240` | `path.exists()` inside `scan_pattern` |

These are all *reads* of managed files (or archive handling); the single place that **writes** a managed file is `storage.write_lines`, called from `engine.py` only (`_mutate_and_update_registry` and `undo_descriptor`). So the important property — "only `apply_descriptor` and `undo_descriptor` change managed files" — does hold. The same cannot be said of the audit files (see the writers table in [section 21.4](#214-who-writes-what)).

> **Note.** `validator.validate_post` reads files with `Path.read_text`, which applies *universal newlines* (so `\r\n` becomes `\n` in the text it searches), whereas `storage.read_lines` uses `splitlines()`. Both agree on ordinary files; they can differ on exotic separators. See [section 22.5](#225-what-a-line-is) and [29.3](#293-evaluation-semantics-what-actually-runs).

#### 41.5 Cost model and measured scale

Because the design is "whole file in, whole file out", the cost of each operation is easy to state and was measured (CPython 3.13.16, a small cloud VM; absolute numbers will differ on your machine, the *shape* will not).

| Operation | What it touches | Cost |
|---|---|---|
| `register` | reads the file; writes the whole registry | O(N) in file lines |
| `add-descriptor` | loads the whole registry; reads the whole target file (to hash a range); loads and saves the batch's whole `descriptors.json` | O(N + D) per call, so O(D·(N + D)) to add D descriptors |
| `validate-plan` | resolves every descriptor's ID set (`ids_in_range` scans *every* ID of the file, tombstones included); compares every pair of descriptors in the same file; Kahn ordering re-scans the remaining edges | O(D·N) + O(D²) + O(D·(D+E)) |
| `apply-next` (one descriptor) | loads the registry; reads the target file; rewrites the whole file; shifts all IDs; saves the whole registry; loads the registry *again* to hash it for the checkpoint; reads the whole WAL to look for `op_applied` | O(N + W) per descriptor (W = WAL records) |
| `validate-post` | reads each touched file; evaluates every invariant over each file's whole text | O(files + invariants × file size) |

Measured on a **20,000-line** file (789 KB; `registry.json` 749 KB) with **200** independent single-line `replace_range` descriptors:

| Step | Time |
|---|---:|
| `register` | 0.13 s |
| 200 × `add-descriptor` (separate processes) | 13.6 s (68 ms per call) |
| `validate-plan` | 0.30 s |
| `apply-all` | 10.8 s (≈ 54 ms per descriptor) |
| `validate-post` | 0.08 s |

Afterwards: `registry.json` 756 KB, `descriptors.json` 135 KB, `wal.jsonl` 45 KB (401 records), 400 payload blobs, and exactly the 200 intended lines changed.

And the growth in the number of descriptors, on a 5,000-line file, calling the engine in-process (so process start-up is excluded):

| Descriptors in one batch | Adding them all | `validate-plan` | `descriptors.json` |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 500 | 4.4 s | 0.27 s | 0.32 MB |
| 1,000 | 14.6 s | 0.54 s | 0.64 MB |
| 2,000 | 50.5 s | 1.69 s | 1.28 MB |
| 4,000 | 190.4 s | 6.11 s | 2.56 MB |

Adding grows towards a quadratic cost (every doubling of the batch cost 3.3, 3.5 and 3.8 times as much, approaching four, because each call loads and rewrites the whole `descriptors.json`); `validate-plan` grows faster than linearly (2.0, 3.1 and 3.6 times per doubling). **Practical limits:** a few hundred descriptors per batch is comfortable; a few thousand is possible but tedious; beyond that, split the work into several batches (which the methodology recommends anyway, [section 40.9](#409-batch-size-and-several-batches-in-sequence)). File size matters mainly through the registry: about 37 bytes of JSON per line ever registered (tombstones included, never pruned), rewritten in full at every apply.

> **Caution — unmeasured.** No benchmark was run for files in the hundreds of thousands of lines, nor for concurrent use. At 1,000,000 lines the registry would be on the order of 40 MB, loaded and rewritten at every apply; the tool is not designed for that.
