### 42. registry.py

`registry.py` is the module the docstring calls "the only code allowed to write positions into `registry.json`". Precisely: it is the only code that *computes* position changes (the `apply_*` primitives); the *saving* of `registry.json` is done by `engine.py` (and `register_file`).

#### 42.1 Function reference

| Function | At | Behavior | Raises |
|---|---|---|---|
| `file_id_for(rel_path)` | :31 | `"f_" + sha256(path.encode("utf-8")).hexdigest()[:10]` — spelling-sensitive (V3) | — |
| `register_file(rel_path, force=False)` | :45 | If the ID is already in the registry and not `force`: return the existing entry (idempotent). Otherwise read the file, assign `{fid}_l00001 …` to its lines, store `line_ending`, save the registry, append `file_registered` to the WAL | `UnicodeDecodeError` (non-UTF-8); nothing for a missing file (V19) |
| `_require_file(reg, fid)` | :81 | the entry or an error | `LineNotFound("file_id … is not registered -- register it first")` |
| `resolve_pos(reg, fid, lid)` | :87 | the current 1-based position of a live ID | `LineNotFound("<id> is not in the registry for <path>")` for an unknown ID; `LineNotFound("<id> was deleted earlier and is no longer addressable")` for a tombstone |
| `ids_in_range(reg, fid, start, end)` | :97 | every **live** ID whose position is in `[pos(start), pos(end)]`, ordered by position | `RangeInvalid("… resolves to an inverted range (ps..pe)")` when `pe < ps`; the two above |
| `range_content(path, ps, pe)` | :113 | `read_lines(path)[ps-1:pe]` — reads the **disk**, not the registry | — |
| `file_path_for(reg, fid)` | :118 | absolute path via `storage.resolve_project_path` | `LineNotFound` |
| `_shift(entry, from_pos, delta)` | :128 | add `delta` to every live position ≥ `from_pos` | — |
| `apply_insert(reg, fid, after_pos, texts)` | :134 | shift ≥ `after_pos+1` by *k*; mint *k* new IDs at `after_pos+1 …` | — |
| `apply_delete(reg, fid, ps, pe)` | :149 | tombstone `[ps,pe]` (`null`), shift ≥ `pe+1` by −*k* | — |
| `apply_replace(reg, fid, ps, pe, texts)` | :158 | tombstone `[ps,pe]`, shift ≥ `pe+1` by `k_new − k_old`, mint new IDs at `ps …` | — |
| `apply_move(reg, fid, ps, pe, dest_pos)` | :178 | reorder positions only; IDs preserved | `RangeInvalid("move destination falls inside the block being moved")` when `ps <= dest_pos <= pe` |
| `snapshot_hash(reg)` | :213 | `content_hash(json.dumps(reg, sort_keys=True))` — a change fingerprint stored in the checkpoint | — |
| `scan_pattern(reg, pattern, file_ids=None)` | :222 | for every registered file (or the given ones) that exists on disk, `re.search(pattern, line)` per line; returns `{file_id, path, pos, text}` with `text.strip()` | `re.error` (shown as `PatternError` on Python ≥ 3.13) |

Two details worth knowing:

- `register_file` stores `"line_ending": "crlf"` if the raw bytes contain **any** `\r\n`, otherwise `"lf"` (decided once; [section 22.5](#225-what-a-line-is)).
- `scan_pattern` reports positions *in the file on disk* and never consults the registry's IDs. It also silently skips an unregistered `file_id` and a path that no longer exists. The caller that needs an ID (`add_descriptor_template`, `domino`) maps position → ID itself.

#### 42.2 The position arithmetic

Each primitive is a few lines, and all of them leave **live positions as the contiguous range `1..N`** (when registry and file agree). With *k* = number of lines moved, inserted or removed:

| Primitive | Effect on IDs and positions |
|---|---|
| insert *k* lines after position *p* | live positions ≥ *p*+1 move down by *k*; *k* new IDs take positions *p*+1 … *p*+*k* |
| delete positions *ps … pe* | IDs in the range become `null` (tombstones); positions > *pe* move up by *k* |
| replace *ps … pe* by *k′* lines | old IDs become `null`; positions > *pe* shift by *k′ − k*; *k′* new IDs take *ps … ps+k′−1* |
| move block *ps … pe* to after *d* (*d* > *pe*) | IDs with *pe* < pos ≤ *d* move up by *k*; the block's IDs move down by *d − pe* |
| move block *ps … pe* to after *d* (*d* < *ps*) | IDs with *d* < pos < *ps* move down by *k*; the block's IDs move up by *ps − 1 − d* |

(The directions above are in terms of position numbers: "down" = larger number.) Worked example for the second-from-last row: six lines `L1…L6`, move `L2..L3` after `L5` (*ps*=2, *pe*=3, *d*=5, *k*=2). `L4`, `L5` (positions 4, 5) take positions 2, 3; the block moves by *d − pe* = 2, so `L2` → 4 and `L3` → 5; `L6` is untouched. Result `L1 L4 L5 L2 L3 L6`, registry `l00001:1 l00004:2 l00005:3 l00002:4 l00003:5 l00006:6` — exactly what the run in [section 40.3](#403-moving-a-block-within-a-file) shows.

The text edit corresponding to a move is done *by the engine*, with the formula `insert_at = pd − k if pd > pe else pd` on the list with the block already removed (`engine.py:621`, `:709`). The registry primitive and the text edit are two independent implementations of the same permutation; they agree when `dest` is outside the block. When `dest` is inside it they do not — the text edit has already been written when `apply_move` raises `RangeInvalid` (V5).

#### 42.3 Complexity and growth

`_shift`, `apply_delete`, `apply_replace`, `apply_move` and `ids_in_range` each iterate the whole `entry["lines"]` dictionary, which holds **every ID the file has ever had** — live and tombstoned. `next_seq` only ever increases and IDs are never reused or pruned. After *n* edits that touch *m* lines in total, the dictionary has *N + m* entries, and each of the next operations pays for all of them. For ordinary use this is invisible; for a file that is churned heavily over many batches, the registry grows without bound (the only reset is `register --force`, which also discards every ID).

#### 42.4 How registry and file can come apart

The registry is a *claim* about the file, not a view of it. They stay in step only while every change goes through `apply_*` + the matching text edit. Known ways they diverge (each is a section elsewhere):

| Cause | Detected by | See |
|---|---|---|
| an external edit to the file | the hash check at apply time (`abort`), or `check` | [39.6](#396-abort-the-file-changed-under-the-plan) |
| a `move_range` whose `dest` lies inside the block | file already written, registry unchanged; `check` fails afterwards | V5 |
| a crash between the file write and the registry save | depends on the op (recovered / double-applied / abort) | [48.3](#483-the-verified-results) |
| the line separator rules of `splitlines()` vs. the file's bytes | not detected: separators like `\f` or `U+2028` split lines and are rewritten as `\n` | V7 |

`show-file` reveals a divergence in one particular form: its `text` is `null` for a registered position beyond the end of the file.

---

### 43. storage.py

#### 43.1 Root discovery and the state directory

`_find_root(start=None)` (`storage.py:50`) resolves the current directory and walks **upward** looking for a directory that *contains* `.operational-platform/`; the first hit is the project root. If none is found, the **current directory** is the root. `state_dir()` then creates `<root>/.operational-platform/`, `payloads/` and `batches/` if they do not exist — on **every** call, with `mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)`.

> **Verified** (and documented: the CLI reference says the first command that needs state creates the directory — what the reference does not stress is that *every* command counts, including read-only ones). There is no `init` command. *Any* command — even the read-only `checkpoint` — run in a directory without state creates `.operational-platform/payloads/` and `.operational-platform/batches/` there:
> ```
> $ ls -A                 (empty directory)
> $ cli.py checkpoint
> {"detail": "no checkpoint yet -- nothing has run in this project"}
> $ ls -A
> .operational-platform
> $ ls -A .operational-platform
> batches  payloads
> ```
> Start the first command from the directory you want as the project root — otherwise a stray state directory is created in a subdirectory, and later commands run *from that subdirectory* will find and use it instead of the real one.

`resolve_project_path(path)` returns the path unchanged if it is absolute, otherwise `<root>/<path>` — the **root**, not the current directory.

> **Verified** (documented behavior with a sharp edge). With state at `<root>`, running `cli.py register app.py` from inside `<root>/src/` registers `<root>/app.py`, which does not exist, and reports `"line_count": 0` (a phantom file, V19). `cli.py register src/app.py` from the same place registers the intended file. Always give paths **relative to the project root**, whatever the current directory.

#### 43.2 The JSON writer

```python
def _write_json(path, data):
    path.parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
    tmp = path.with_suffix(path.suffix + ".tmp")        # registry.json -> registry.json.tmp
    with open(tmp, "w", encoding="utf-8") as f:
        json.dump(data, f, indent=2, ensure_ascii=False)
        f.write("\n")
    tmp.replace(path)                                   # atomic rename on POSIX
```

- A reader never sees a half-written `registry.json`; a crash between writing the temporary file and the rename leaves a stray `*.json.tmp` and the previous version intact.
- The format is two-space-indented, non-ASCII preserved, newline-terminated. That makes the state files diff-friendly and readable by hand.
- There is **no `fsync`** (confirmed: the string does not occur in any module). Atomic with respect to a process crash; **not** durable against power loss or a kernel crash, where the rename may reach the disk before the data does.

#### 43.3 The JSONL appender

`_append_jsonl` adds `"ts": time.time()` as the **first** key and appends `json.dumps(record) + "\n"` with a fresh `open(path, "a")`. Consequences:

- Every WAL / validation-log record carries a float epoch timestamp (`1792568034.6058838`), written by this function, not by the caller.
- A record that already contains a `ts` key would *override* the generated one (the generated value comes first in the dict literal and is replaced by `**record`). No caller does this today.
- Appends are not locked and not synced. A crash during a write could leave a final line that is not valid JSON; `read_jsonl` only skips *blank* lines, so such a line would make every later `json.loads` over the log raise (Code-derived — this was not simulated).

#### 43.4 The blob store

`store_blob(text)` computes `sha256(text)[:16]` (64 bits) and writes `payloads/<hash>.blob` **only if it does not already exist**, with a plain `write_text` (not atomic, not verified afterwards). `load_blob(ref)` reads the file and returns it; it does **not** re-hash it.

Code-derived consequences:

- identical text is stored once, across batches and across descriptors (a `move-across-files` pair shares one blob);
- if a crash left a truncated blob, the *name* still says it contains the intended text, `store_blob` will see the file exists and not rewrite it, and every later use trusts it. Nothing in the tool detects this;
- a 64-bit name makes an accidental collision astronomically unlikely, but there is no collision check either;
- blobs are never garbage-collected — undone and abandoned batches keep theirs, and `export-batch` bundles the *entire* store ([section 40.10](#4010-moving-a-batch-to-another-project)).

Blob content has **no trailing newline** unless the payload itself had one (payloads are stored exactly as handed to `add-descriptor`, after the `--payload-file` trim).

#### 43.5 Reading and writing managed files

```python
def read_lines(path):   # [] if the file does not exist
    return path.read_text(encoding="utf-8").splitlines()

def write_lines(path, lines, line_ending="lf"):
    sep = "\r\n" if line_ending == "crlf" else "\n"
    text = sep.join(lines)
    if lines: text += sep
    path.write_text(text, encoding="utf-8")        # creates parent directories first
```

These two functions define the line model of the whole tool ([section 22.5](#225-what-a-line-is)): the text is decoded as UTF-8; `str.splitlines()` splits on `\n`, `\r\n`, `\r`, `\v`, `\f`, `\x1c`–`\x1e`, `\x85`, ` `, ` `; writing joins with a single separator and **always** terminates the last line. `read_lines` of a missing file is `[]`, which is why a nonexistent path registers as an empty file (V19) and why `insert_after START` then creates it. `write_lines` with an empty list writes a zero-byte file (no terminator).

`write_text` truncates and rewrites in place: **a crash during this call can leave the managed file truncated or empty** (Code-derived; not simulated — the three injected windows in [section 48](#48-concurrency-atomicity-and-crash-windows) all lie *after* a completed write).

`detect_line_ending(path)` returns `"lf"` for a nonexistent file, `"crlf"` if the bytes contain any `\r\n`, else `"lf"`.

#### 43.6 Loader defaults

Every `load_*` returns a default when its file is missing. The defaults define what "a file that was never written" means:

| Loader | Default |
|---|---|
| `load_registry` | `{"files": {}}` |
| `load_descriptors(batch)` | `{"batch_id": batch, "status": "planning", "apply_order": [], "descriptors": []}` |
| `load_invariants` | `{"batch_id": …, "invariants": []}` |
| `load_taxonomy` | `{"batch_id": …, "categories": []}` |
| `load_constraints` | `{"batch_id": …, "protected_ranges": []}` |
| `load_domino_queue` | `{"batch_id": …, "entries": []}` |
| `load_region_inventory` | `{"batch_id": …, "ranges": []}` |
| `load_materials_manifest` | `{"batch_id": …, "required": []}` |
| `load_batch_snapshot` | `{}` |
| `load_project_taxonomy` / `load_project_constraints` | `{"categories": []}` / `{"protected_ranges": []}` |
| `load_active_locks` | `{"batches": {}}` |
| `load_checkpoint` | `None` |

Because `batch_dir(batch_id)` **creates** the directory as a side effect, any command given an unknown batch ID returns this default "planning batch with no descriptors" and leaves an empty phantom directory behind (V13). Also note that `domino_queue_exists` and `region_inventory_exists` test for the *file*, which is what the shape gates rely on: the gate "was `sync-domino-queue` ever run" is "does `domino_queue.json` exist" — and `sync_queue` writes the file even for an empty queue.

---

### 44. engine.py

`engine.py` is the largest module and holds everything that defines *what a descriptor is* and *what applying one does*.

#### 44.1 Constants and exceptions

| Name | Value / meaning |
|---|---|
| `BASE_OPS` | `{"insert_after", "delete_range", "replace_range", "move_range", "copy_range"}` |
| `POSITIVE_CONTENT_OPS` | `{"insert_after", "replace_range", "copy_range"}` — ops whose result can be recognized by reading the file back; the only ones eligible for post-state recovery |
| `SEVERITY_LEVELS` | `["critical", "major", "minor", "cosmetic"]`, most severe first |
| `SHAPE_GATES` | `conformance → [taxonomy]`, `audit → [taxonomy]`, `transition → [domino, constraints]`, `rename → [domino]`, `assembly → [inventory]` |
| `DescriptorError` | invalid input to an `add_*` / `undo` call |
| `Abort` | raised by `apply_descriptor` for a discrepancy it will not resolve alone; "not a bug — the intended, structural way the engine refuses to guess" |

#### 44.2 `new_batch` and descriptor IDs

`new_batch(shape)` (`:61`): validates the shape; counts the existing `batches/batch_*` **directories** and takes *count + 1* (V13: not *max + 1*); writes `descriptors.json` (`status: "planning"`, empty `apply_order`, `shape`, `required_gates`) and `invariants.json`. The CLI then writes `snapshot.json` (`{"files": F, "lines": L}`: the number of registered files and live lines at that moment — the "before" figure for `report`).

Descriptor IDs are `d` + `len(descriptors) + 1` zero-padded to four digits. Because descriptors are never removed, the count is also the next number; the scheme would break if a delete command were ever added.

#### 44.3 `add_descriptor`: the checks, in order

`add_descriptor` (`:80`) validates in this exact order and raises `DescriptorError` at the first problem (the CLI turns it into `{"error": …}`, exit 2):

1. `op` ∈ `BASE_OPS`
2. `severity` (if given) ∈ `SEVERITY_LEVELS`
3. `context` ≤ 120 characters
4. `provenance` ∈ {`direct`, `domino`}
5. `provenance == "domino"` requires `domino_of`
6. the file is registered (`file_id_for(file)` is in the registry) — **the path spelling decides**
7. `category` (if given): the effective taxonomy must be non-empty and contain it
8. per-op required fields and snapshots (next table)

Then it appends the descriptor to `descriptors.json`. What step 8 requires and computes:

| Op | Required | Computed and stored at add time |
|---|---|---|
| `insert_after` | `after`, `payload_text` | `expect_hash` = hash of the anchor line's text (the literal string `"START"` for `START`); `payload_ref` |
| `delete_range` | `start`, `end` | `expect_hash` = hash of the range text; `pre_payload_ref` (the old text); `undo_anchor` = the ID of the line *above* `start` **as of now**, or `null` |
| `replace_range` | `start`, `end`, `payload_text` | `expect_hash`; `pre_payload_ref`; `payload_ref` |
| `move_range` | `start`, `end`, `dest` | `expect_hash`; `undo_anchor` (as for delete) |
| `copy_range` | `start`, `end`, `dest` | `expect_hash`; `payload_ref` = the source text (a snapshot) |

`_check_context` (`:205`) is the only place `context` is ever verified: it must be a substring of the live target text *at this moment*.

What is **not** checked at add time (each is a verified deviation or a documented limit):

- whether `dest` exists, is outside the block, or is a valid anchor (V5);
- whether `start` precedes `end` — an inverted range hashes the empty string and is only rejected, with an uncaught exception, at `validate-plan` (V6);
- `depends_on` — the IDs are not looked at until the plan is validated (and are not trimmed, V26);
- whether the target is already protected, claimed by another descriptor, or locked by another batch;
- that `payload_text` is non-empty.

The "hash" in `expect_hash` is `sha256(text)[:12]` where `text` is the range's lines joined with `"\n"` (no trailing newline). A single blank line therefore hashes as `e3b0c44298fc` — the same value as an *empty* range.

#### 44.4 `apply_descriptor`: the whole algorithm

This is the function the rest of the system exists to protect (`engine.py:442`). In full:

```
apply_descriptor(batch, d)
 │
 ├─ d.status == "applied" ? ──────────────────────────────► return "skipped"          [CLI never calls it: V18]
 │
 ├─ WAL contains op_applied for (batch, d) ? ─────────────► d.status := applied; save; checkpoint
 │                                                          return "recovered"         [R1 — and after an undo: V1]
 │
 ├─ pre-state check  (hash of the live target  vs  d.expect_hash)
 │     ├─ the target ID cannot be resolved ────────────────► raise Abort("target no longer exists …")
 │     ├─ match ───────────────────────────────────────────► normal path ↓
 │     └─ mismatch
 │           ├─ op ∈ POSITIVE_CONTENT_OPS  and  the live text at the expected spot == the payload
 │           │       └─► registry := post-state; WAL op_applied (note "backfilled"); d.status := applied
 │           │           return "recovered"                                          [R2]
 │           └─ otherwise ───────────────────────────────────► raise Abort("matches neither the expected pre-state … re-plan")
 │
 └─ normal path
      1. WAL  op_start
      2. read file → splice lines → write file                 (storage.write_lines — plain write_text)
      3. registry mutation in memory (apply_*)  → created_ids
      4. save registry.json                                    (atomic rename)
      5. WAL  op_applied
      6. d.status := applied; save descriptors.json            (this is the save that records created_ids)
      7. checkpoint := {queue_position, total_descriptors, registry_snapshot_hash, last_interrupt_cause: "post_op"}
      return "applied"
```

Points that are easy to miss:

- **The recovery decision is made from the WAL, not from the file.** `_wal_has_applied` (`:522`) reads the *entire* WAL and looks for a matching `op_applied`. That is what makes undo-then-apply a false "recovered" (V1) — the old record is still there.
- **Pre-state check is a hash of what is at the descriptor's *current* resolved position.** For `insert_after` that is the anchor line; for the other four it is the target range. For `START` it is skipped entirely (`"START anchor always matches"`).
- **Post-state recovery exists for three ops only** (`_check_post_state`, `:544`): it re-reads the payload from the blob store and compares it with the live slice where the descriptor says it should have landed — for an insert, the lines after the anchor; for a replace, from the start of the range; for a copy, after `dest`. For `delete_range` and `move_range` there is none ("no post-state check defined for this op").
- **A false positive is possible in principle** (Code-derived): if an *external* edit changes an insert's anchor line, and by coincidence the following lines already equal the payload, the descriptor is declared `recovered` and the registry gets new IDs for lines this descriptor never inserted. The coincidence needs identical text; it is rare, not impossible.
- `created_ids` is assigned in memory at step 3 and persisted only at step 6, and **neither recovery path sets it** (see 44.7 and V24).
- Exceptions other than `Abort` — `LineNotFound` from a `dest` that no longer resolves, `RangeInvalid` from `apply_move`, I/O errors — propagate uncaught. At that point step 1 (`op_start`) and possibly step 2 (the file write) have happened (V5).

`_mutate_and_update_registry` (`:584`) is the per-op body of steps 2–3:

| Op | Text edit (on the list of lines read in step 2) | Registry call |
|---|---|---|
| `insert_after` | `lines[p:p] = payload.split("\n")` where `p` = 0 for `START` else `resolve_pos(after)` | `apply_insert(p, payload_lines)` |
| `delete_range` | `del lines[ps-1:pe]` | `apply_delete(ps, pe)` |
| `replace_range` | `lines[ps-1:pe] = payload.split("\n")` | `apply_replace(ps, pe, payload_lines)` |
| `move_range` | remove the block; re-insert at `pd − k` if `pd > pe` else at `pd` (`pd` = 0 for `START`) | `apply_move(ps, pe, pd)` |
| `copy_range` | `lines[pd:pd] = payload.split("\n")` (payload = the add-time snapshot) | `apply_insert(pd, payload_lines)` |

In every case the **entire file is re-read from disk and rewritten**, using the registry's stored `line_ending`. That is the code-level origin of the line-model quirks in [section 22.5](#225-what-a-line-is): lines the batch never targeted are re-encoded too.

> **Note — `copy_range` is a copy of the *snapshot*.** The text inserted comes from the blob captured at `add-descriptor` time, not from the live source range. The source range is only *hash-checked* at apply time, so a copy cannot silently pick up a changed source — it aborts instead.

#### 44.5 The recovery helpers

| Helper | At | What it does |
|---|---|---|
| `_wal_has_applied(batch, d)` | :522 | linear scan of `wal.jsonl` for `event == "op_applied"` with this batch and descriptor |
| `_check_pre_state(reg, path, d)` | :530 | returns `(hash == expect_hash, "live hash <h>")`; the same function backs the `check` command |
| `_check_post_state(reg, path, d)` | :544 | positive-content recognition for insert / replace / copy; `(False, "no post-state check defined for this op")` otherwise |
| `_sync_registry_to_post_state` → `_mutate_registry_only` | :560, :567 | re-runs only the registry half (`apply_insert`/`apply_replace`) for insert / replace / copy; **discards the new IDs**, so `created_ids` stays empty |

Because `_mutate_registry_only` is called with the registry in its *pre*-state for replace (the only case in which it is reached for a replace is crash window A, [48.3](#483-the-verified-results)), it recomputes exactly what the interrupted run would have done.

#### 44.6 `undo_descriptor`

`undo_descriptor` (`:637`) reverses one `applied` descriptor. Its structure:

1. `status` must be `applied`, else `DescriptorError("<id> has status '<s>', not 'applied' -- nothing to undo")`.
2. **Append `undo_start` to the WAL** — *before* any of the per-op checks (V25).
3. Per op:

| Op | Preconditions checked | Inverse performed |
|---|---|---|
| `replace_range` | `created_ids` and `pre_payload_ref` exist; the live text at `created_ids[0]..[-1]` equals the payload | replace those lines with the stored old text (`apply_replace` → **new IDs**) |
| `delete_range` | `pre_payload_ref` exists | insert the old text after `undo_anchor` (`null` → top of file) — **no check of the surroundings** |
| `insert_after`, `copy_range` | `created_ids` exist; the live text at `created_ids[0]..[-1]` equals the payload | delete those lines (`apply_delete`) |
| `move_range` | none | move the block `start..end` back to after `undo_anchor` (`null` → top) |

4. `save_registry`, append `undo_applied`, set `status = "undone"`, save descriptors. Returns `{"result": "reverted", …}`.

What this implies, beyond the table in [section 39.8](#398-undo-in-practice):

- **`undo_anchor` is captured when the descriptor is *added*, not when it is applied** (`:162`, `:184`). If an earlier-applied descriptor inserts lines between that anchor and the block, undoing the delete puts the block back **in a different place than it came from** (V23).
- The anchor can have been tombstoned by then; `resolve_pos` raises `LineNotFound`, which `cmd_undo_descriptor` does not catch (only `DescriptorError`), so the user sees the generic `LineNotFound: …` error — after `undo_start` was already logged.
- `created_ids` exists only for descriptors applied through the **normal path**; after either recovery path it is `null`, and undo refuses with the misleading `…missing created_ids, predates undo support` (V24).
- Undo does not call `_advance_checkpoint` — the checkpoint still describes the state before the undo.
- Undo does not touch locks, taxonomy, the domino queue or the inventory.

#### 44.7 Verified: undo after a recovered crash is impossible

> **Verified (V24).** Using the crash harness ([48.2](#482-the-crash-harness)): run `apply_descriptor`, crash, retry (the retry returns `recovered`), then call `undo_descriptor`:
> ```
> insert_after  C (crash after WAL op_applied): retry -> recovered created_ids=None  undo -> DescriptorError: d0001: missing created_ids, predates undo support
> replace_range A (crash before registry save): retry -> recovered created_ids=None  undo -> DescriptorError: d0001: missing created_ids/pre_payload_ref, predates undo support
> replace_range C (crash after WAL op_applied): retry -> recovered created_ids=None  undo -> DescriptorError: d0001: missing created_ids/pre_payload_ref, predates undo support
> ```
> The message says "predates undo support", which is wrong for a descriptor created seconds ago: the real cause is that the recovery path never recorded the IDs that the interrupted run minted.

#### 44.8 Helpers composed from `add_descriptor`

| Function | At | What it really does |
|---|---|---|
| `add_descriptor_template(batch, find, replace, file=None, **kw)` | :323 | `scan_pattern(reg, re.escape(find), file_ids)`; for every matching line, maps its position to an ID, **re-reads the real line** (the scan output is stripped), `live_line.replace(find, replace)`, then `add_descriptor(…, "replace_range", start=id, end=id, payload_text=new_line, **kw)`. The CLI passes no `**kw`, so template descriptors carry no category or severity |
| `move_across_files(batch, src, start, end, dest_file, dest_after, **kw)` | :360 | reads the source range text; `add_descriptor(delete_range, src)` then `add_descriptor(insert_after, dest_file, after=dest_after, payload_text=text)`. No `depends_on` between them |
| `copy_across_files(…)` | :382 | only the second half of the above |

> **Verified (V27).** `add-descriptor-template --find '' --replace X` is accepted: `re.escape('')` is the empty pattern, which matches **every line of every registered file** (or of `--file`), and `"ab".replace("", "X")` is `"XaXbX"`. On a two-line file (`ab`, `cd`) it created `d0001` and `d0002`; `explain d0001` shows `before: "ab"`, `after: "XaXbX"`. Nothing is applied until you validate and apply, but a careless empty value produces a descriptor per line of the whole project.

`add_constraint` (`:395`) validates the range with `ids_in_range` (so the file must be registered and both IDs live and ordered) and appends to the batch's or the project's constraint list. `effective_constraints` (`:418`) is the plain concatenation of both lists — duplicates are possible.

#### 44.9 Categories, invariants and exceptions

| Function | At | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| `add_category` | :291 | refuses a duplicate code *in the same scope*; project scope writes `project_taxonomy.json` |
| `effective_taxonomy` | :310 | batch categories + project categories whose code the batch does not redeclare |
| `close_category` | :744 | requires the code to exist in the effective taxonomy; if it exists only at project scope, **copies** a new entry into the batch file and closes that — so a closure never leaks to other batches |
| `set_category_scope` | :769 | stores `scope_files` (file IDs) and an empty `checked_files` map on the batch's entry |
| `close_category_file` | :790 | requires a scope; records `checked_files[fid] = {status: "closed_empty", note}` |
| `add_invariant` | :256 | validates `severity` and `type`; **does not compile the regex, nor check that the file is registered** (V8) |
| `accept_match` | :724 | finds the **first** invariant with the same `file_id` and the identical `pattern` string and appends `{line, note}`; if two invariants share both, the second can never be annotated |

> **Note — leftovers in the source.** `accept_match` ends with a stray docstring (`:738–743`) that belongs to `close_category`, and `close_category_file` ends with a duplicated, unreachable `storage.save_taxonomy(…); return entry` (`:801–802`). Both are harmless dead code; they are the kind of residue that shows the module was edited by hand over time, and a reason to prefer reading the code to trusting its comments.

#### 44.10 `_advance_checkpoint`

After every applied (or recovered) descriptor, `_advance_checkpoint` (`:805`) reloads the registry from disk, counts applied descriptors, and **overwrites** `checkpoint.json` with `active_batch`, `queue_position` (= applied count), `total_descriptors`, `registry_snapshot_hash` and `last_interrupt_cause` (`"post_op"`) plus `updated_at`. Any `domino_pending` / `inventory_pending` fields written earlier by `domino.py` or `inventory.py` are lost, because the file is replaced, not merged ([section 34.3](#343-the-checkpoint)).

---
### 45. validator.py

`validator.py` never authors a descriptor and never touches a managed file. It reads what `engine.py` wrote and answers three questions: *may this plan run?* (`validate_plan`), *would this one descriptor still apply?* (`check_descriptor`), and *is the finished batch complete and well-formed?* (`validate_post`). It also owns the cross-batch lock table.

#### 45.1 `validate_plan`: the control flow

`validate_plan` (`validator.py:41`) is a sequence of gates; **each failure returns immediately**, so one call reports at most one kind of problem. The order is fixed:

| # | Trigger | Result key (value) | Source |
|---:|---|---|---|
| 1 | a gate in `required_gates` has not been satisfied: `domino` → no `domino_queue.json`; `inventory` → no `region_inventory.json`; `taxonomy` → no category in the batch **or** project; `constraints` → no protected range in the batch **or** project | `shape_incomplete` (list of messages) + `detail` | :46–62 |
| 2 | a file named with `require-file` is not registered | `materials_missing` (list of paths) | :64–71 |
| 3 | an effective category is neither used by any descriptor (of **any** status) nor `closed_empty` | `taxonomy_incomplete` (list of codes) | :73–84 |
| 4 | a category with a scope has a `(file, category)` pair with neither a descriptor of that category on that file nor a per-file closure | `unit_category_matrix_incomplete` (list of `CODE × path`) | :86–91, :266 |
| 5 | an inventory range with `status == "pending"` | `inventory_incomplete` (list of `ri…`) | :93–99 |
| 6 | a domino-queue entry with `status == "pending"` | `domino_incomplete` (list of `dm…`) | :103–110 |
| 7 | `_schema_errors` found problems; or resolving a descriptor's IDs raised `LineNotFound` | `schema_errors` (list) | :112–123 |
| 8 | a descriptor's resolved IDs intersect a protected range | `protected_zone_violations` | :125–127 |
| 9 | an unknown `depends_on`, or two overlapping descriptors with no declared order | `conflicts` | :129–131 |
| 10 | the dependency graph has a cycle | `dependency_cycle` | :133–135 |
| 11 | the resolved IDs intersect another batch's locks | `cross_batch_conflicts` | :137–139 |

Every failure goes through `_log_and_return(batch_id, "plan", False, {…})`: it appends `{"phase": "plan", "batch_id", "result": "fail", …details}` (plus `ts`) to `validation_log.jsonl` **and overwrites `checkpoint.json`** with `{active_batch, last_interrupt_cause: "plan_check", updated_at}`. A failed validation does **not** touch `descriptors.json`: the batch keeps its previous `status` and `apply_order`. (That is why, after a failed *re*-validation of a half-applied batch, `apply-next` still follows the old order — V22.)

If all eleven gates pass, in this order:

1. `apply_order` and `status = "validated"` are written to `descriptors.json`;
2. `_acquire_locks` records the claimed ID sets in `active_locks.json` (replacing this batch's previous entry);
3. the two non-blocking warning generators run (45.7) and their messages are added to the result as `warnings`;
4. `_log_and_return(…, True, result)` logs a `pass` record and overwrites the checkpoint with cause `plan_check`.

Note the order in 1–3: the plan is committed and locked *before* the warnings are computed. A warning therefore can never block anything.

**Which descriptors are validated?** `descs = [d for d in descriptors if d["status"] != "applied"]` (`:101`) — everything that is **not applied**, i.e. `pending` **and `undone`**. Gates 3 and 4 look at *all* descriptors (including applied ones); gates 7–11 look only at `descs`. Two consequences, both verified:

- an `undone` replace/delete is re-validated, and its tombstoned targets fail gate 7 (V12);
- a pending descriptor that `depends_on` (or is `domino_of`) an **applied** one fails, because `by_id` is built from `descs` only (V22).

> **Verified (V22).** Batch of two: `d0001` insert after `L1`; `d0002` replace `L3`, `--depends-on d0001`. After `apply-next` applies `d0001`, re-running the plan check reports
> ```
> "conflicts": ["d0002: depends_on unknown descriptor d0001"]                                  [exit=1]
> ```
> and, for a domino link,
> ```
> "schema_errors": ["d0002: domino_of references 'd0001', which isn't a descriptor in this batch"]
> ```
> Both are wrong: `d0001` exists; it is merely already applied. The batch is not damaged — the old `apply_order` is still in force and `apply-next` continues — but a half-applied batch **cannot be re-validated** to pick up newly added descriptors as soon as any pending one points at an applied one. Practical rule: do not extend a half-applied batch; finish it, then open a new one.

#### 45.2 `_schema_errors`

For each non-applied descriptor (`:320`):

| Rule | Message |
|---|---|
| `op` ∈ `BASE_OPS` | `unknown op '…'` |
| `file_id` is registered | `file_id … is not registered` |
| `insert_after` has `after` | `insert_after missing \`after\`` |
| every other op has `start` and `end` | `<op> missing start/end` |
| `move_range` / `copy_range` has `dest` | `<op> missing dest` |
| `insert_after` / `replace_range` / `copy_range` has `payload_ref` | `<op> missing payload_ref` |
| `expect_hash` is non-empty | `missing expect_hash -- was this added via add_descriptor?` |
| `provenance == "domino"` has `domino_of`, and it names a descriptor among the non-applied ones | `provenance=domino but domino_of is not set` / `domino_of references '…', which isn't a descriptor in this batch` |

It checks *presence*, not meaning: it does not look inside the blob store, and **it never inspects `dest` for move/copy** beyond "is not empty" (V5). After it passes, the loop at `:116–123` resolves each descriptor's ID set; a tombstoned or unknown ID becomes a `schema_errors` entry (`"<id>: <LineNotFound message>"`). `RangeInvalid` (inverted range) is **not** caught there — it escapes `validate_plan` as an uncaught exception and the CLI prints `{"error": "RangeInvalid: …"}` with exit 2 (V6).

#### 45.3 What a descriptor "claims"

`_resolve_ids` (`:350`) defines the set of IDs a descriptor occupies. Everything downstream — protected zones, the conflict graph, the locks — is computed from it:

| Op | Claimed set |
|---|---|
| `insert_after` after `START` | `{"START"}` (discarded in every comparison) |
| `insert_after` after an ID | `{that ID}` — only the **anchor line**, although the insert is a change *between* two lines |
| `delete_range`, `replace_range` | every live ID between `start` and `end` |
| `move_range` | the **source block only** — the destination is not claimed |
| `copy_range` | the source block — which the copy only reads, but is claimed anyway |

Three behaviors follow, and all of them are consequences of the table rather than separate features:

- two inserts anchored on the same line overlap and must be ordered ([section 40.6](#406-several-inserts-at-the-same-anchor));
- an insert after the **last line of a protected range** claims a line inside it and is refused, while an insert after the line *above* the range does not (it lands just above the zone) — and a move *into* a protected zone is not caught at all (V5);
- a `move_range` and an edit of its destination line do not conflict at plan time.

#### 45.4 The conflict graph

`_build_conflict_graph` (`:364`) returns `(edges, conflicts)`:

- for every `depends_on` entry: an unknown ID becomes a `conflicts` message, a known one an **edge** `(dependency, dependent)`;
- for every **pair** of descriptors on the same `file_id` (double loop, O(D²)): if their claimed sets share an ID other than `START`, and neither lists the other in `depends_on`, a `conflicts` message is produced.

So a declared dependency in *either* direction waives the overlap complaint, and the engine does not judge whether the declared order makes sense (the "replace then insert after the replaced line" trap of [section 39.2](#392-conflicts--and-why-a-declared-order-is-obeyed-not-judged)). Overlap is only ever evaluated against the **current** registry — the plan is not simulated forward.

#### 45.5 The topological order

`_topological_order` (`:398`) is Kahn's algorithm, restructured: each round recomputes the set of *ready* descriptors (no remaining incoming edge), sorts them, takes the first, removes it and its outgoing edges. Complexity is O(D·(D+E)), which is the second reason `validate-plan` slows down quickly as D grows ([section 41.5](#415-cost-model-and-measured-scale)).

The sort key decides the order among simultaneously ready descriptors:

| Situation | Key |
|---|---|
| no descriptor in the batch has a severity | `(insertion index,)` |
| at least one has a severity | `(severity rank, −number of edges that start at it, insertion index)` where the rank is the index in `["critical", "major", "minor", "cosmetic"]` and **4** for "no severity" |

So severity is only a *tie-breaker among ready descriptors*; it never overrides a dependency, and a batch that does not use severity is ordered purely by insertion. The "number of edges that start at it" is the count of descriptors that declared this one as a dependency — "most depended upon first".

When no descriptor is ready but some remain, the function returns `([], remaining)` and `validate_plan` reports `dependency_cycle: remaining`.

> **Verified.** `remaining` is *everything left*, not just the cycle. With `d0001 → d0002 → d0001` (each depends on the other) and `d0003` depending on `d0001`, the report is `["d0001", "d0002", "d0003"]` — `d0003` is only *downstream* of the cycle. Read the list as "the part of the graph that can never start", then look for the actual loop.

#### 45.6 Locks

| Function | At | Behavior |
|---|---|---|
| `_cross_batch_lock_conflicts` | :219 | builds `{(file_id, id)}` for this batch's claimed IDs (minus `START`); for every *other* batch in `active_locks.json`, intersects with its claimed `{(file_id, id)}`; reports `"<this> overlaps already-locked ranges from <other>: [first five sorted pairs]"` |
| `_acquire_locks` | :243 | stores `locks["batches"][batch] = [{"file_id", "ids": […]}, …]` — **replacing** any previous entry of this batch, i.e. a re-validation after a partial apply *shrinks* the lock to the non-applied descriptors |
| `release_locks` | :254 | deletes the entry; called only by `validate_post`, when the batch reaches `committed` or `failed` |

So the lock lifecycle is exactly: *taken by the first passing `validate-plan`; refreshed by every later passing one; released by `validate-post` when all descriptors are applied.* An abandoned or aborted batch holds its lock forever (V21; [section 39.6](#396-abort-the-file-changed-under-the-plan)).

#### 45.7 The two warning generators

Both are non-blocking and are computed from the non-applied descriptors.

**`_invariant_independence_warnings`** (`:172`). If *no* descriptor carries a payload, nothing is said. Otherwise, for each invariant: no `checked_against` → "has no --checked-against, and this batch has payload-carrying descriptors …"; a `checked_against` whose exact string is not the `path` of any `file_registered` or `file_inspected` WAL record → "… names checked_against=…, but there is no record of that file ever being registered or shown during this batch -- the claim is unverified".

Two properties undercut the second warning's strength:

- **registering counts as inspecting.** `register` itself writes `file_registered`, so any file that was registered at all passes this test; the warning fires only for a name that was never registered or is spelled differently (`./spec.md` ≠ `spec.md`);
- despite "during this batch", the WAL scan is **project-wide** — a record from an earlier, unrelated batch satisfies it.

This matches the authors' own wording in `limitations.md` ("evidence of inspection, not of derivation"), but the practical strength is lower than the message suggests.

**`_rule_ref_consistency_warnings`** (`:152`). Each `rule_ref` is normalized with `re.sub(r"[^0-9a-zA-Z]", "", r).lower()`; descriptors whose *different spellings* share a normalized key are reported as "look like the same clause, written differently".

> **Verified (V28).** The normalization removes every non-alphanumeric character, so:
> ```
> rule_ref '1.11' and '11.1'              → both "111"     → warned as "the same clause"   (false positive)
> rule_ref '7.1' and '§7.1'               → both "71"      → warned                         (intended)
> rule_ref 'Section 7.1' and '7.1'        → "section71" vs "71" → NOT warned               (the case the docstring names)
> ```
> The warning is a hint about typing drift, not a reliable detector; treat it as noise-prone.

#### 45.8 `check_descriptor`

`check` (`:450`) fetches the descriptor with `next(x for x in … if …)` — an unknown ID raises a bare `StopIteration`, printed as `{"error": "StopIteration: "}` with exit 2 — and returns `engine._check_pre_state`'s verdict as `{"phase": "per_op", "result": "pass"/"fail", "detail": "live hash <h>"}`. It appends that record to `validation_log.jsonl` but, unlike the other validator functions, **does not touch the checkpoint**.

It is the *same comparison apply-time uses*, and nothing more. In particular it cannot tell whether a descriptor has **already been applied**: the pre-state of an `insert_after` is its anchor line, which does not change when the insert is applied.

> **Verified.** For an `insert_after` descriptor, `check` returns `pass` with the same `live hash` both *before* `apply-all` and *after* it. For a `replace_range` the hash changes after applying, so `check` then reports `fail` — which is "correct" in the sense that the pre-state no longer holds, but is not "something is wrong".

#### 45.9 `validate_post`

`validate_post` (`:494`):

```
1. unapplied = descriptors with status != "applied"            (pending AND undone)
   if any → log {"result":"fail","error":"N descriptor(s) not yet applied: [...]"}, checkpoint cause post_check, RETURN
            (status unchanged, locks kept)
2. for each touched file (every file_id appearing in any descriptor):
      checker = SYNTAX_CHECKERS.get(path.suffix)               (exact, case-sensitive suffix)
      none → "skipped (no checker registered for this file type)"
      else → (ok, message)
3. for each invariant:
      read the whole file with Path.read_text (universal newlines)
      balanced_pairs      → count each open/close character in the whole text; equal counts pass
      occurrence_count    → re.finditer(pattern, text) (default flags); optional comment filter;
                            drop matches whose START line is in accepted_matches; compare the count with expected_count
4. passed = all syntax ok AND all invariants ok
   data.status := "committed" if passed else "failed"; save descriptors.json
   release_locks(batch)
5. log the record; checkpoint cause post_check
```

Details that matter:

- **Syntax checkers** (`SYNTAX_CHECKERS`, `:486`): `.py` → `compile(source, path, "exec")`, which parses but does not execute or resolve names, and uses *the interpreter running the tool* — code in a syntax newer than that interpreter supports is reported as a `SyntaxError`. `.js` → `subprocess.run(["node", "--check", path], timeout=10)`; `FileNotFoundError` becomes `skipped -- 'node' binary not found`, a non-zero exit becomes a failure whose message is **the last line of stderr** (V10: with Node 22 that last line is just the version string `Node.js v22.22.0`; the useful text is higher up). A `TimeoutExpired` is not caught. Other suffixes — and files without a suffix — are skipped. The keys of the `syntax` object in the result are **absolute paths**.
- **Invariant matching** is over the **whole text**, not per line (V8). Lines are only used to compute the reported line number (`text.count("\n", 0, m.start()) + 1`) and the displayed snippet. `exclude_comments` looks at the line where each match *starts*. A match is "accepted" if that starting line number is in `accepted_matches`; accepted matches are excluded from `actual` but still listed with `accepted: true`.
- `raw_matches_before_exceptions` is the count **after** the comment filter and **before** `accept-match` — so it is not a raw count if `exclude_comments` is set.
- At most the first 20 matches are listed; `matches_truncated` is `raw_actual > len(listed)`.
- `balanced_pairs` ignores `expected_count`, `exclude_comments` and `accepted_matches`; the `pattern` argument is a string of open/close character pairs like `()[]{}`.
- An exception inside the loop — an invalid regex, a `LineNotFound` because the invariant's file is not registered — propagates **out of `validate_post` before the status and locks are touched**: the batch stays `validated`, the locks stay held, and the failure is visible only as the generic `{"error": "PatternError: …"}` (V8). An unregistered file can be repaired by registering it and running `validate-post` again; a bad regex cannot be repaired.
- Step 4 runs before the log append, so a crash between them could leave a `committed` batch without a `post` record in the validation log.

> **Verified.** `committed` is not terminal: running `validate-plan` on a committed batch passes (nothing is pending) and sets the status back to `validated`; and a committed batch accepts new descriptors with no complaint. An **empty** batch passes both validations and is marked `committed`.

#### 45.10 What the validator does not do

Each of these is a direct reading of the code, and each is the other side of a guarantee stated in earlier parts:

- it does **not** re-run the plan checks at apply time — only the per-descriptor hash comparison is repeated (V4: descriptors added after `validate-plan` are invisible to `apply-next`, because `apply_order` is a snapshot);
- it does **not** look at `dest` of a move/copy (V5);
- it does **not** check that blobs exist;
- it does **not** simulate the batch forward ([section 55](#55-stated-limitations-and-their-verification-status));
- it does **not** know about the other domino findings: a direct descriptor added after the last `sync-domino-queue` is not in the queue, so gate 6 never sees it (V20).

---

### 46. domino.py and inventory.py

Both modules implement the same pattern — *a durable queue whose completeness gates the plan* — and both are small enough to describe fully.

#### 46.1 `domino.py`

Data: `domino_queue.json` = `{"batch_id", "entries": [{finding_id, descriptor_id, status, linked_descriptors, had_candidates}]}`. A finding ID is `dm` + (entries so far + 1), four digits.

| Function | At | Behavior |
|---|---|---|
| `sync_queue(batch)` | :53 | for every descriptor with `provenance == "direct"` (**any status**) that is not yet in the queue, append a `pending` entry. Idempotent; never removes or duplicates. Writes the file even when nothing is added, which is what satisfies the `domino` gate. Returns `{added, total, pending}` |
| `_covered_positions(reg, batch)` | :85 | the set of `(file_id, position)` occupied by *any* descriptor of the batch (any status, any provenance), computed **now** from the current registry: the range for non-insert ops, the anchor line for an insert; an unresolvable reference is skipped silently |
| `_mechanical_candidates(reg, d)` | :109 | patterns: `[domino_hint]` (a **regex**) if the descriptor has one, else `re.escape(line.strip())` for each old line of the target with at least four non-blank characters; then `registry.scan_pattern` over **all registered files** for each pattern, de-duplicated by `(file_id, pos)` |
| `next_pending(batch)` | :140 | first `pending` entry → `{finding_id, descriptor_id, op, file_id, old_content, domino_hint, candidates, note}` where `candidates` = mechanical candidates minus covered positions. Read-only: writes nothing. `{"result": "done", …}` when none is pending |
| `resolve(batch, finding)` | :184 | see below |
| `_had_candidates` | :225 | recompute the candidates minus covered positions *now*; true if any remain |
| `status(batch)` | :234 | `{total, pending: [ids], traced, traced_with_candidates, traced_empty, ready_for_plan}` |

`resolve` has three outcomes, decided in this order:

1. entry already `traced` → `{"result": "skipped", … "already traced -- idempotent no-op"}`;
2. otherwise set `had_candidates` (computed now); if the **WAL already contains `domino_traced`** for this finding → recount linked descriptors, mark `traced`, save, checkpoint → `recovered`;
3. otherwise append `domino_start`, **recount** the descriptors with `provenance == "domino"` and `domino_of == <the finding's descriptor_id>`, append `domino_traced` with the count, mark `traced`, save, checkpoint (`domino_pending`, `domino_total`, cause `domino_op`) → `traced`.

The recount is the point of the design: the caller does not say how many cascades it found; the engine counts them.

Behaviors verified in the earlier parts, restated at code level:

- `domino_hint` is passed to `re.search` **unescaped**. A hint like `foo(` raises a regex error inside `next_pending` *and* inside `resolve` (through `_had_candidates`); the entry stays `pending`, no command edits a descriptor, and the batch is stuck (V9). On Python ≥ 3.13 the reported type is `PatternError`; on older versions it is `error`.
- a descriptor added **after** the last `sync-domino-queue` is not in the queue; `domino-status` says `ready_for_plan: true` and the gate passes (V20).
- `insert_after` has no old content, so unless it carries a `domino_hint` it produces no candidates.
- `had_candidates` is "were any candidates *left uncovered* when the finding was resolved" — **not** "were there candidates when you looked".
- the search reads every registered file from disk for every pattern: O(patterns × total lines).

#### 46.2 `inventory.py`

Data: `region_inventory.json` = `{"batch_id", "ranges": [{range_id, file_id, start, end, status, disposition, note, descriptor_ids}]}`. Range IDs: `ri` + four digits.

| Function | At | Behavior |
|---|---|---|
| `add_range(batch, file, start, end)` | :38 | validates with `ids_in_range` (file registered, both IDs live, ordered), appends a `pending` range. Does not forbid overlapping or duplicate ranges, and does not check that the ranges cover anything in particular. Writes **no WAL record and no checkpoint** |
| `next_pending(batch)` | :52 | the first `pending` range with its **current text** (`range_content`) |
| `resolve(batch, range, disposition, note, descriptor_ids)` | :70 | validates the disposition ∈ {`transferred_verbatim`, `transferred_with_edit`, `excluded`}; `transferred_with_edit` needs ≥ 1 descriptor ID; any descriptor IDs given must exist in the batch. Sets `status = "resolved"`, the disposition, note and IDs; saves; checkpoint (`inventory_pending`, `inventory_total`, cause `inventory_op`) |
| `status(batch)` | :97 | `{total, pending: […], resolved: count, ready_for_plan}` |

> **Verified (V29).** `resolve` does not look at the range's current status: resolving an already-resolved range **overwrites** its disposition, note and descriptor IDs silently, and there is no WAL record, so the earlier decision survives nowhere:
> ```
> inventory-resolve batch_0001 ri0001 --disposition excluded --note first
> inventory-resolve batch_0001 ri0001 --disposition transferred_verbatim --note second
> → region_inventory.json holds only  "disposition": "transferred_verbatim", "note": "second"
> ```
> For an assembly batch, where the inventory is the evidence that nothing was dropped, this makes the evidence rewritable. Keep your own copy of the dispositions if the audit matters.

---

### 47. cli.py

#### 47.1 Skeleton

`main()` (`cli.py:508`) builds one `argparse` parser with 38 sub-parsers, each bound to a `cmd_*` function with `set_defaults(func=…)`, then:

```python
args = p.parse_args()
try:
    args.func(args)
except SystemExit:
    raise
except Exception as e:
    _err(f"{type(e).__name__}: {e}")
```

`_out(obj, code)` prints `json.dumps(obj, indent=2, ensure_ascii=False, default=str)` and calls `sys.exit(code)`; `_err(msg)` is `_out({"error": msg}, 2)`. Every command ends through `_out`/`_err` — except `dry-run`, which prints plain text and simply returns (exit 0).

Three consequences:

- **Pretty-printed, multi-line JSON** on stdout for everything except `dry-run`, which prints plain text.
- **Two error shapes.** An exception a command catches itself becomes `{"error": "<message>"}` (no type name). Anything else is caught by the generic handler and becomes `{"error": "<Type>: <message>"}`. Both exit 2.
- **Tracebacks never appear**, so a program bug and a bad argument are indistinguishable by exit code. Argparse errors (a missing required option, a value outside `choices`) are different again: usage text on **stderr**, not JSON, exit 2.

The `choices=` checks are on `new-batch --shape`, `add-descriptor --severity` and `--provenance`, `add-invariant --severity` and `--type`, `inventory-resolve --disposition`. **`--op` is not a `choice`:** an unknown op reaches `engine.add_descriptor` and comes back as `{"error": "unknown op 'x'; must be one of […]"}`.

#### 47.2 What each command catches

This matrix explains which failures come back with a clean message and which as `Type: message`:

| Command(s) | Caught by the command itself (→ `{"error": message}`, exit 2) |
|---|---|
| `register`, `require-file`, `inventory-next`, `inventory-status`, `sync-domino-queue`, `domino-next`, `domino-status`, `validate-plan`, `check`, `validate-post`, `status`, `find-pattern`, `report`, `export-batch`, `checkpoint`, `resume` | nothing |
| `show-file`, `explain`, `dry-run` | an explicit "not registered" / "no descriptor" check |
| `new-batch`, `add-descriptor-template`, `add-category`, `close-category`, `set-category-scope`, `close-category-file`, `undo-descriptor`, `accept-match`, `add-invariant` | `DescriptorError` |
| `add-descriptor`, `move-across-files`, `copy-across-files` | `DescriptorError`, `LineNotFound`, `RangeInvalid` |
| `add-constraint`, `add-source-range` | `LineNotFound`, `RangeInvalid` |
| `inventory-resolve` | `InventoryError` |
| `domino-resolve` | `DominoError` |
| `apply-next`, `apply-all` | `Abort` → logged, **exit 1** (the only domain exception that exits 1) |
| `import-batch` | an explicit "already exists" check |

Everything not in that table goes to the generic handler. Notable examples: an unregistered path given to `register` as a directory (`IsADirectoryError`), a `--payload-file` that does not exist (`FileNotFoundError`), an unknown descriptor given to `check` (`StopIteration`), an uncaught `LineNotFound` raised mid-apply, and every regex error (`find-pattern`, `domino-next`, `validate-post`).

#### 47.3 `add-descriptor` details

- `--payload-file` is read with `Path.read_text("utf-8")` and **one** trailing `\n` is removed; `--payload-text` is used as given. If both are passed, **`--payload-file` wins** and the text is ignored.
- `--depends-on` is split with `.split(",")` and **not trimmed** (V26): `d0001, d0002` yields `["d0001", " d0002"]`, which fails only at `validate-plan` with a message that has a doubled space (`depends_on unknown descriptor  d0002`). Pass `d0001,d0002`.
- An empty `--depends-on ""` is falsy and gives `[]`; a trailing comma gives an empty-string dependency, which is "unknown" at plan time.
- No argument is cross-checked with the op: `--after` on a `replace_range` or `--dest` on an insert is stored and ignored.

#### 47.4 `apply-next` and `apply-all`

`apply-next` (`:270`): reads `apply_order`; if empty, `{"error": "no apply_order on this batch -- run validate-plan first"}` (exit 2); picks the **first descriptor in `apply_order` whose status is not `applied`** (so an `undone` one is picked again — V1); calls `apply_descriptor`; on `Abort` appends a `per_op` record with `result: "abort"` to the validation log, sets the checkpoint (`last_interrupt_cause: "abort"`) and exits 1 with `{"result": "abort", …}`. With nothing left it prints `{"result": "done", …}` and exits 0.

`apply-all` (`:296`) is the same in a loop that **reloads the descriptors every iteration**. It accumulates the per-descriptor results and prints them **once, at the end**. On the first `Abort` it prints what it has plus the abort entry and exits 1.

Two corollaries:

- With an empty `apply_order` (never validated) the loop body never runs and it prints `{"applied": []}` with exit 0 (V4).
- An exception that is *not* `Abort` ends the process through the generic handler **before anything is printed**, so the list of descriptors applied up to that point is lost to the caller (V30).

> **Verified (V30).** Descriptors: `d0001` replace `L1`; `d0002` `copy_range … --dest START` (accepted at add time); `d0003` replace `L3`.
> ```
> $ cli.py validate-plan batch_0001        → pass, apply_order [d0001, d0002, d0003]
> $ cli.py apply-all batch_0001
> {"error": "LineNotFound: START is not in the registry for f.txt"}                          [exit=2]
> $ cli.py status batch_0001               → "counts": {"applied": 1, "pending": 2}
> f.txt:  A  L2  L3
> ```
> The state on disk is correct (one applied, two pending); only the output is silent about the one that did apply. After any `apply-all` that exits 2, run `status`.

#### 47.5 `resume`

`cmd_resume` (`:477`) is read-only and works from the checkpoint alone:

1. no checkpoint → `{"detail": "no checkpoint -- nothing to resume, start with register/new-batch"}`;
2. a checkpoint without `active_batch` → the checkpoint plus a note;
3. otherwise load that batch's descriptors and compute `applied`, `total`;
4. suggestion: status `planning` → `validate-plan`; else if `applied < total` → `apply-next`; else → `validate-post` (whatever the status — hence V15: a `committed` batch is still told to run `validate-post`);
5. if the checkpoint's cause is `abort`: scan the validation log backwards for the latest record of this batch with `result == "abort"`; attach it as `last_abort` and replace the suggestion with the "investigate … do not just retry apply-next" text.

`resume` ignores `domino_pending` and `inventory_pending`: for a `planning` batch in the middle of domino tracing it says `validate-plan` — which will fail with `domino_incomplete`. Read the `checkpoint` object it prints.

#### 47.6 `report`

```
issues_by_severity[sev] += 1   for EVERY descriptor of every listed batch, any status; sev = descriptor.severity or "unspecified"
files_touched   = number of distinct file_ids among those descriptors
lines_before    = snapshot.json["lines"] of the FIRST listed batch that has a snapshot    (count at new-batch time)
lines_now       = live positions in the whole registry, every registered file
lines_delta     = lines_now − lines_before
```

So "issues" are *descriptors*, including pending and undone ones and cascade descriptors; and the line figures are **project-wide**, not per touched file: registering more files after the first batch was created inflates `lines_delta`.

#### 47.7 `export-batch` and `import-batch`

`export-batch` writes a gzip tar containing the batch directory (under its batch ID) and the **whole** `payloads/` directory (as `payloads`), to `--out` or `./<batch_id>.tar.gz`. It reads through `storage.batch_dir`, which creates the directory — exporting an unknown batch ID creates a phantom directory and an essentially empty archive.

`import-batch` extracts the archive into `.operational-platform/_import_tmp` with `tarfile.extractall` **with no extraction filter**, then for each top-level entry: `payloads` → merge blobs that do not already exist (rename); anything else → treated as a batch directory and renamed into `batches/`, refusing (with `{"error": "… already exists -- refusing to overwrite"}`) if that name exists; finally removes `_import_tmp`. Observations:

- the refusal path returns **without** removing `_import_tmp`, and `iterdir()` order is not defined, so `payloads` may already have been merged when the refusal happens;
- project-level files, the registry, the WAL and the lock table are **not** part of the archive; an imported `validated` batch holds no locks until it is validated again;
- on Python 3.12–3.13 the call emits a `DeprecationWarning` about the missing `filter`; extraction without a filter follows the archive's own member paths ([section 57](#57-trust-model-and-security-notes)).

#### 47.8 `dry-run`

`cmd_dry_run` (`:364`) deep-copies the registry through `json.loads(json.dumps(reg))`, loads the file's current lines, and replays — in `apply_order`, or in insertion order if there is none — every non-applied descriptor **of the named file**, using the same position primitives and text edits as the real apply, but **without any hash check**. Output: the resulting lines joined by `"\n"`, as plain text. Errors are not caught: an unresolvable ID in the replay (a deleted `dest`, say) ends in the generic handler. It reads and writes no state.

#### 47.9 The small commands

| Command | Implementation notes |
|---|---|
| `show-file` | prints `{pos, line_id, text}` per live ID, sorted by position; `text` is `null` if the registry has a position beyond the end of the file; appends `file_inspected` |
| `status` | counts per status and provenance; `--group-by a,b` builds a nested dictionary over descriptor fields, keys stringified (`"None"` for null) |
| `find-pattern` | `scan_pattern`; with `--file`, an unregistered file silently yields no matches |
| `explain` | `before` from `pre_payload_ref`, `after` from `payload_ref`: insert → only `after`; delete → only `before`; replace → both; **copy → `after` only**; move → neither |
| `require-file` | appends to `materials_manifest.json` (idempotent) and prints the manifest; checks nothing about the path until `validate-plan` |
| `checkpoint` | prints `checkpoint.json` verbatim, or `{"detail": "no checkpoint yet …"}` |

### 48. Concurrency, atomicity and crash windows

#### 48.1 What is atomic, and what is not

| Artifact | Written by | Atomic against a *process* crash | Durable against *power loss* |
|---|---|---|---|
| every JSON state file (registry, descriptors, invariants, checkpoint, locks, …) | write to `<name>.tmp`, then `Path.replace` | **yes** — old or new, never half | no — no `fsync` anywhere |
| `wal.jsonl`, `validation_log.jsonl` | `open(…, "a")` + one `write` of one line | effectively, for a short line; not guaranteed | no |
| payload blobs | `write_text` if the file is absent | **no** | no |
| **the managed files** | `write_text` (truncate, then write) | **no** | no |

There is **no locking** of any kind (no `flock`, no lock file, no `O_EXCL` — the only "locks" in the tool are the logical ID claims of [section 33](#33-cross-batch-locks), which guard against overlapping *plans*, not against simultaneous *processes*).

**Concurrent processes (Code-derived; not simulated).** Every command is *load whole file → modify → save whole file*. Two commands that overlap in time on the same project can therefore lose each other's updates (last writer wins on `registry.json`, `descriptors.json`, `checkpoint.json`), and two `apply-next` on the same batch can both pass the `status != "applied"` test and apply the same descriptor twice. **Run one command at a time per project.** An agent harness that parallelizes tool calls must serialize the calls to this tool.

#### 48.2 The crash harness

The windows below were not inferred; they were produced. `crash_sim.py` (a program written for this guide, with its output, in [D.5](#d5-the-crash-harness)) does, for each op and each window:

1. create a five-line file `L1…L5`, register it, create a batch with one descriptor, validate the plan;
2. monkey-patch one `storage` function to raise a private `Crash` exception at the chosen point of `apply_descriptor`: **A** `save_registry` (so the file write has happened and the registry save has not), **B** `wal_append` for the `op_applied` event (registry saved, WAL line not written), **C** the `save_descriptors` call that records `status: applied` (WAL written, status not);
3. call `apply_descriptor` again — the "restart" — and compare the final file with the result of an uncrashed run of the same descriptor.

Because the engine keeps no in-memory state between calls (everything is re-read from disk), a raised exception followed by a fresh call is equivalent to a killed process followed by a new command. What the harness does **not** model: a kill *during* a single write (a torn managed file), power loss, two crashes in a row, and a crash before step 1 or after step 7 of the apply sequence (which are harmless: nothing is on disk yet, or everything is).

The apply sequence, with the state on disk after each step:

| After… | managed file | `registry.json` | WAL | descriptor status |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| (nothing yet) | old | old | — | `pending` |
| 1. `op_start` | old | old | `op_start` | `pending` |
| 2. file written — **window A** | **new** | old | `op_start` | `pending` |
| 4. registry saved — **window B** | new | **new** | `op_start` | `pending` |
| 5. `op_applied` — **window C** | new | new | `op_start`, `op_applied` | `pending` |
| 6. status saved | new | new | … | `applied` (+ `created_ids`) |

#### 48.3 The verified results

Outcome of the **retry** (`apply-next` after the crash) — file contents after the retry are compared with the uncrashed expectation:

| Op | A — after file write, before registry save | B — after registry save, before WAL `op_applied` | C — after WAL `op_applied`, before status save |
|---|---|---|---|
| `insert_after` | **applied again** → `L1 L2 NEW NEW L3 L4 L5` ✗ | **applied again** → `L1 L2 NEW NEW L3 L4 L5` ✗ | recovered ✓ |
| `replace_range` | recovered ✓ | **abort** (file correct, batch stuck) | recovered ✓ |
| `delete_range` | **abort** (file correct) | **abort** (file correct) | recovered ✓ |
| `move_range` | **abort** (file correct) | applied — harmless repeat ✓ | recovered ✓ |
| `copy_range` | **applied again** → `L1 L2 L3 L4 L1 L1 L5` ✗ | **applied again** → `L1 L2 L3 L4 L1 L1 L5` ✗ | recovered ✓ |

Why each cell comes out the way it does (all follow from [44.4](#444-apply_descriptor-the-whole-algorithm)):

- **Window C is always safe.** The WAL says `op_applied`; `apply_descriptor` takes branch R1 and only reconciles the status.
- **`insert_after` and `copy_range`, A and B: silent duplication.** The pre-state hash that gates the retry is the hash of the **anchor line** (insert) or the **source range** (copy). The crashed run did not change either, so the hash still matches and the normal path runs a second time. This is the dangerous category: no error, no warning, wrong file.
- **`replace_range`, A: recovered.** The registry still has the old positions, so the pre-state hash no longer matches (the text there changed); the op is a positive-content op, the payload is found where it should be, and the registry is synchronized.
- **`replace_range`, B: abort.** The registry already tombstoned the old IDs; resolving the target raises `LineNotFound`, which `apply_descriptor` turns into an `Abort`. The *file is already correct* — the abort is a refusal to guess, but it leaves the descriptor `pending`.
- **`delete_range`, A and B: abort.** No post-state check exists for deletes; in A the hash at the old position now covers other text, in B the target IDs are tombstones. Again the file is correct and the descriptor stays `pending`.
- **`move_range`, A: abort; B: applied.** In A the registry is stale, so the hash mismatches and moves have no post-state check. In B the registry already reflects the move, the hash matches at the *new* position, and moving a block to "after `dest`" when it already sits after `dest` is a no-op — correct by construction, not by design.

An `abort` during recovery is a *terminal* state for the batch: the descriptor is neither applied nor retryable, `validate-post` refuses while it is pending, and the batch's locks stay held. The only exits are those described for V21 ([section 39.6](#396-abort-the-file-changed-under-the-plan)): hand-remove the lock entry and abandon the batch.

> **Documentation versus observation (V2).** `limitations.md` says delete and move have "a narrower crash-recovery window" and that the failure is an `abort` ("fails safe"), with one gap "between the file write and the registry write specifically, for a delete or a move". Observed: delete and move do abort and are safe, but (a) **`replace_range` also aborts in window B**, and (b) **`insert_after` and `copy_range` — the ops the document describes as the *well-protected* ones — duplicate silently in windows A and B**. The "positive content" idea only helps when the pre-state hash *changes* as a result of the operation, which is true for replace, not for insert and copy.

#### 48.4 What `recovered` proves — and what it does not

| Branch | Evidence it rests on | What can still be wrong |
|---|---|---|
| **R1** — WAL has `op_applied` | a *log record*, not the file | after an `undo` the record is stale: the retry reports `recovered` and marks the descriptor `applied` with the file unchanged (V1); `validate-post` then passes |
| **R2** — pre-state mismatch, post-state match | the *file content* equals the payload at the expected spot | a coincidence (the text happened to match) could be taken for a completed apply; rare |
| (both) | — | the new IDs minted by the interrupted run are not recorded: `created_ids` stays empty and the descriptor can never be undone (V24) |

The audit trail shows these retries differently: R2 appends `op_applied` with `"note": "backfilled"`; R1 appends nothing; a retry after window A/B of a delete or replace that aborts appends nothing but the `per_op` abort record in the validation log. A crashed attempt always leaves its `op_start`, so **a WAL with an `op_start` that has no later `op_applied` for the same descriptor** is the signature of an interrupted apply — except that a *successful* `apply` after an interrupted one also leaves the earlier orphan `op_start` behind (two `op_start`, one `op_applied`).

#### 48.5 After an unclean stop: a protocol

1. `resume` — read-only. Note `last_interrupt_cause` and `applied`/`total`.
2. `status <batch>` — the statuses on disk.
3. Look at the **tail of the WAL**: `tail -5 .operational-platform/wal.jsonl`. `op_start` with no `op_applied` after it: the stop happened in or before window B. `op_applied` but the descriptor is still `pending`: window C (safe).
4. Look at the **file**: `show-file`, or `git diff` if it is under version control. Is the descriptor's change present?
5. If the interrupted descriptor was an `insert_after` or `copy_range` **and its text is already in the file**, do **not** run `apply-next` — it would add the text a second time. Restore the file from version control, `register <file> --force`, and re-plan a fresh batch. If it was a `replace_range`, `delete_range` or `move_range` whose change is already in the file, `apply-next` will abort (or, for a move, repeat harmlessly): the file is right, and the remaining decision is how to close the batch (usually: abandon it and release its locks by hand).
6. If the change is **not** in the file, `apply-next` is safe.

Under all of this sits the first rule of the tool's own limitations page: *for anything you would genuinely regret losing, work on a version-controlled checkout.*

#### 48.6 Summary: what protects against what

| Hazard | Protection | Strength |
|---|---|---|
| positions drifting because of earlier edits | stable line IDs resolved at apply time | strong (by construction) |
| the file changing outside the tool | hash compare-and-swap before every write | strong for non-insert targets; checks only the anchor for inserts |
| two plans overlapping | conflict graph + cross-batch locks | strong for plan-time overlap; blind to `dest` of moves and to anything not yet validated |
| a crash mid-apply | WAL + post-state recognition | strong in window C; **inconsistent in A/B** (silent duplication for insert/copy, stuck batches for the rest) |
| a half-finished plan | per-batch gates (taxonomy, domino, inventory) | records that a mechanism was used, not that it was used well |
| a wrong plan | independent invariants at `validate-post` | as good as the invariants; whole-text regex semantics (V8) |
| concurrent processes | none | — |
| power loss | none (no `fsync`) | — |
| mistakes the tool cannot see | version control | yours to provide |

---
## Part VI — Complete CLI reference

This part documents all **38** subcommands of `scripts/cli.py`: syntax, arguments, behavior, output, exit codes, what each command writes, and the caveats that were verified. The semantics behind each command are explained in Parts III–V; this part is the lookup table. Outputs shown are real (from the "tour" run described in [Appendix D](#appendix-d--how-this-guide-was-verified)), **abridged**: the tool prints pretty-printed multi-line JSON, shown here compacted where that is clearer.

---

### 49. Conventions

#### 49.1 Invocation

```
python3 scripts/cli.py <command> [arguments]
```

Run it from the project you are editing (any directory below the project root works *once state exists* — see 49.5). The command name is the first argument; `-h` after a command prints its argparse usage. There is no `init` command and no global option.

#### 49.2 Output and exit codes

| Exit | Meaning |
|---:|---|
| `0` | the command ran. For `validate-plan`, `check` and `validate-post` it additionally means the result was `pass`. **Not** a promise that anything useful happened (`apply-all` on an unvalidated batch exits 0 with `{"applied": []}`) |
| `1` | a *reported* failure: `validate-plan`, `check` or `validate-post` returned `result: "fail"`, or `apply-next` / `apply-all` hit an `abort` |
| `2` | argparse rejected the command line (usage text on **stderr**), **or** an error JSON was printed: `{"error": "<message>"}` for errors the command catches, `{"error": "<Type>: <message>"}` for everything else ([section 47.1](#471-skeleton)) |

Every command prints **one JSON object** to stdout (pretty-printed, UTF-8, non-ASCII preserved) — except `dry-run`, which prints the simulated file as plain text. Messages are plain English strings; scripts should key on the `result` field and the documented keys, not on message text.

#### 49.3 Argument conventions

| Convention | Detail |
|---|---|
| `batch_id` | positional, `batch_0001` form. An unknown ID is **not** an error for most commands: it behaves as an empty "planning" batch and leaves a phantom directory (V13) |
| line IDs | `f_<10 hex>_l<5 digits>`, from `show-file` or from a descriptor's `created_ids`. Never type positions where an ID is expected |
| `START` | the literal string, valid for `--after` (insert) and `--dest` (move only — see the `copy_range` caution, V5) |
| paths | relative to the **project root**, one canonical spelling, no `./` (V3). The same string must be used in `register`, `--file`, `--checked-against`, `--files`, `--src-file`, `--dest-file`, `require-file` |
| comma lists | `--depends-on d0001,d0002`, `--files a.py,b.py`, `--descriptor-ids d0001,d0002`, `--batches b1,b2` — **no spaces** around commas (V26) |
| values starting with `--` | must use the `=` form: `--payload-text=--text`, `--domino-hint=--flag` |
| multi-line text | `--payload-file PATH` (one trailing newline stripped) or `--payload-text $'a\nb'`; `--payload-file` wins if both are given |
| `--op` | not an argparse choice: validated by the engine, so a bad value gives a normal `{"error": …}` |
| abbreviations | argparse accepts any **unambiguous prefix** of a long option (`--payload-f`, `--fil`). Always write the full name, and never build a wrapper that matches option names textually (m14) |

The "Writes" line of each command below names the state files it changes (all under `.operational-platform/`; see [Part VII](#part-vii--state-file-formats)). "WAL" is `wal.jsonl`, "VLOG" is `validation_log.jsonl`, "checkpoint" is `checkpoint.json`.

#### 49.4 Command index

| Group | Commands |
|---|---|
| Setup and inspection | [`register`](#501-register) · [`show-file`](#502-show-file) · [`find-pattern`](#503-find-pattern) · [`status`](#504-status) · [`explain`](#505-explain) · [`dry-run`](#506-dry-run) |
| Batches and descriptors | [`new-batch`](#507-new-batch) · [`add-descriptor`](#508-add-descriptor) · [`add-descriptor-template`](#509-add-descriptor-template) · [`move-across-files`](#5010-move-across-files-and-copy-across-files) · [`copy-across-files`](#5010-move-across-files-and-copy-across-files) |
| Taxonomy, constraints, materials | [`add-category`](#5011-add-category) · [`close-category`](#5012-close-category) · [`set-category-scope`](#5013-set-category-scope-and-close-category-file) · [`close-category-file`](#5013-set-category-scope-and-close-category-file) · [`add-constraint`](#5014-add-constraint) · [`require-file`](#5015-require-file) |
| Invariants | [`add-invariant`](#5016-add-invariant) · [`accept-match`](#5017-accept-match) |
| Domino queue | [`sync-domino-queue`](#5018-the-domino-commands) · [`domino-next`](#5018-the-domino-commands) · [`domino-resolve`](#5018-the-domino-commands) · [`domino-status`](#5018-the-domino-commands) |
