## Part VIII — Guarantees, limits and verified caveats

Parts I–VII describe how the tool is meant to work and how it was observed to work. Part VIII answers a different question: **what can you rely on, and what can you not?** It is the part to read before you let the tool near anything you would regret losing.

| Section | What it gives you |
|---|---|
| [54](#54-what-the-tool-guarantees) | The guarantees, each with its mechanism, the evidence behind it and the conditions under which it stops holding — followed by what the tool explicitly does *not* promise. |
| [55](#55-stated-limitations-and-their-verification-status) | The 23 limitations that the bundled `limitations.md` states about itself, each re-tested and given a verdict. |
| [56](#56-verified-behaviors-and-deviations-from-the-documentation) | The 31 numbered findings **V1 … V31** — behavior that differs from the documentation, or that the documentation never mentions — each with a reproduction, its impact and a workaround. |
| [57](#57-trust-model-and-security-notes) | Whom the tool trusts, and what that means for archives, paths, batch IDs and an agent harness. |

> **Evidence labels used in this part.** **Verified** means the behavior was produced by running the tool in a scratch project (CPython 3.13.16, Node.js v22.22.0; [Appendix D](#appendix-d--how-this-guide-was-verified)). **Code-derived** means it follows from reading the source and was not exercised as a scenario. A statement with neither label is a statement of the documentation, and says so.

---

### 54. What the tool guarantees

The honest summary fits in one sentence: **the tool guarantees that it will not apply an edit to text that differs from what you planned, and it keeps a trail of what it did — it does not guarantee that a half-finished operation can always be completed, repeated or undone.** The first half is strong and was observed to hold. The second half is where Part VIII spends most of its time.

#### 54.1 The guarantees

| # | Guarantee | Mechanism | Evidence | Where it stops holding |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **G1** | **Stable identity.** A line keeps its ID for as long as it exists, and an ID is never reused for different text. | A per-file `next_seq` counter; a deleted line becomes a `null` position (a tombstone) rather than disappearing; the lists are append-only ([§22](#22-files-and-lines-identity-that-never-changes), [§42](#42-registrypy)). | **Verified.** Registry invariants R1–R4 ([§53.1](#531-registryjson)) hold in every scratch project checked, including after simulated crashes, undo of every operation and moves ([§59.2](#592-a-read-only-state-auditor)). | When the file is edited outside the tool, registry and text drift apart ([§42.4](#424-how-registry-and-file-can-come-apart)). After `register --force`, which re-mints every ID of the file ([§50.1](#501-register)). After a `move_range` whose `dest` lies inside the moved block, where the file is rewritten *before* the error is raised (**V5**). |
| **G2** | **Compare-and-swap.** A descriptor is applied only if the live text of its target equals what was planned (`expect_hash`); otherwise nothing is written. | `_check_pre_state` runs before every write ([§25.3](#253-the-compare-and-swap-at-apply-time), [§44.4](#444-apply_descriptor-the-whole-algorithm)). | **Verified.** A file edited behind the plan's back produced `abort` with a hash detail and the file untouched ([§39.6](#396-abort-the-file-changed-under-the-plan)); the crash harness ([§48.3](#483-the-verified-results)). | `insert_after` hashes only its **anchor line** — so a stale registration whose anchor text coincides still passes (**V3**) — and an insert at `START` hashes nothing (`expect_hash` is the literal `"START"`). `dest` of a move or copy is never hashed (**V5**). The two `recovered` branches accept a WAL record (**V1**) or a text coincidence as proof of completion. `check` answers `pass` for an insert both before and after it was applied. |
| **G3** | **No apply without a passed plan.** | `apply_order` is written only by a passing `validate-plan`; `apply-next` refuses without it ([§45.1](#451-validate_plan-the-control-flow)). | **Verified.** `apply-next` on a batch that was never validated: `no apply_order on this batch -- run validate-plan first`, exit 2. | Descriptors added *after* the plan passed are invisible to `apply-next`/`apply-all` (**V4**). `apply-all` on a never-validated batch prints `{"applied": []}` and exits **0**. Re-validating a half-applied batch can fail (**V22**). |
| **G4** | **Overlapping targets need a declared order, and a declared order is obeyed.** | A conflict graph over *claimed ID sets*, a topological order and cycle detection ([§45.3](#453-what-a-descriptor-claims)–[§45.5](#455-the-topological-order)). | **Verified.** Two replaces of one line: `conflicts`. The same pair with `--depends-on`, in either direction: `apply_order` obeys it ([§39.2](#392-conflicts--and-why-a-declared-order-is-obeyed-not-judged)). | `dest` is not claimed (**V5**) and `START` is never claimed (**V17**). The *meaning* of the order is not judged: a plan can pass and the second descriptor still abort at apply time (limitation L4, [§55](#55-stated-limitations-and-their-verification-status)). |
| **G5** | **Protected zones are never targeted.** | Protected ranges are expanded to ID sets and intersected with each descriptor's claim ([§28.2](#282-how-it-is-enforced)). | **Verified**, including project-level constraints inherited by a later batch. | `dest` is not checked: a block can be moved *into* a protected zone (**V5**). The check is asymmetric at the edge: an insert anchored **on** a protected line is refused, an insert anchored on the line **before** the zone is allowed (neither modifies a protected line). |
| **G6** | **Validated plans exclude each other.** | `active_locks.json` holds the claimed IDs of every validated, unfinished batch; a second plan that overlaps is refused with `cross_batch_conflicts` ([§33](#33-cross-batch-locks)). | **Verified** (two batches on one line; the stale-lock case of [§39.6](#396-abort-the-file-changed-under-the-plan)). | A batch that has not passed `validate-plan` claims nothing. An aborted batch can never be closed and its locks block even a fresh re-plan (**V21**). A batch imported after it was applied leaves an empty lock entry (**V31**). |
| **G7** | **A batch is `committed` only after every descriptor is applied and the post-checks pass.** | `validate-post` refuses while any descriptor is not `applied`, then runs the syntax checkers and the batch's invariants ([§45.9](#459-validate_post)). | **Verified.** An unapplied descriptor → error and no status change; a syntax error → `failed`; invariants pass/fail. | It checks only what you declared (limitations L6, L7; **V8**, **V10**) and it *trusts descriptor statuses* — which can be wrong after an undo (**V1**) or an import (**V31**). An invalid invariant regex raises only here, after the work is done (**V8**). |
| **G8** | **There is a trail.** Every apply and undo is bracketed by WAL records; every plan, post and per-op check leaves a validation-log record; the checkpoint remembers the last phase for `resume`. | `wal_append`, `validation_log_append`, `save_checkpoint` ([§34](#34-the-audit-trail-wal-validation-log-and-checkpoint)). | **Verified.** The worked examples of Part IV, the crash simulations ([§48.4](#484-what-recovered-proves--and-what-it-does-not)) and the auditor's WAL patterns ([§59.2](#592-a-read-only-state-auditor)). | The trail is not tamper-evident and is not `fsync`ed. A *refused* undo still writes `undo_start` (**V25**). `inventory-resolve` overwrites an earlier decision and writes no record at all (**V29**). The trail records that a thing was done, not that it was done well. |
| **G9** | **Each JSON state file is replaced atomically.** A process crash leaves the old file or the new one, never half of each. | Write `<name>.tmp`, then `Path.replace` ([§43.2](#432-the-json-writer)). | **Code-derived.** The crash harness injects an exception *between* the writes of one command; it does not kill a process in the middle of a write. | The managed files and the payload blobs are written in place (`write_text`): not atomic. There is no `fsync` anywhere: nothing survives power loss by design ([§48.1](#481-what-is-atomic-and-what-is-not)). |
| **G10** | **Offline, deterministic, standard library only.** | The imports of all seven modules are `json`, `hashlib`, `re`, `os`, `time`, `pathlib`, `shutil`, `tarfile`, `argparse`, `typing` and — only inside the `.js` syntax check — `subprocess`. There is no network, `random` or `uuid` import. | **Code-derived** (every module read; the import lines searched). | Timestamps (`ts`, `updated_at`) differ between runs. If `node` is on the `PATH`, the tool runs it. |
| **G11** | **Planning fails closed.** A failing `validate-plan` changes no descriptor, takes no lock and writes no `apply_order`; it stops at the **first** failing gate. | `validate_plan` returns at the first failing gate ([§45.1](#451-validate_plan-the-control-flow), [§51](#51-the-validate-plan-diagnostic-catalog)). | **Verified**, gate by gate ([§51](#51-the-validate-plan-diagnostic-catalog)). | Only one gate is reported at a time, so a batch can need several rounds to reach a pass (**V11** is the order in which they run). A *passing* re-validation can flip a `committed` or `failed` batch back to `validated`. |
| **G12** | **Managed files change only through apply and undo.** | `storage.write_lines` is called from exactly nine places, all inside `engine.py`'s apply and undo helpers. | **Code-derived**, and **Verified** that read-only commands leave managed files byte-identical. | `insert_after START` on a path that does not exist *creates* the file and its parent directories (**V19**). Even read-only commands create `.operational-platform/` directories (**§43.1**), and a mistyped batch ID creates a directory (**V13**). |

> **Reading the table.** The "stops holding" column is not a list of rare accidents. Most entries are one command away from an ordinary session: `START` inserts, `move_range` with a `dest`, an `undo` followed by `apply-next`, a `register ./app.py`. Part IX ([§58](#58-best-practices)) turns them into working rules.

#### 54.2 What is *not* guaranteed

| Not guaranteed | Why it matters | What to do instead |
|---|---|---|
| **Isolation between concurrent processes.** | Every command loads whole files, modifies them and saves them whole; there is no lock of any kind ([§48.1](#481-what-is-atomic-and-what-is-not)). Two overlapping commands can lose each other's updates, and two `apply-next` on one batch can both apply the same descriptor. | Run **one command at a time per project.** An agent harness that parallelizes tool calls must serialize this tool. |
| **Atomicity across the four writes of one apply** (managed file, registry, WAL, descriptor status). | A crash between them leaves three possible half-states, and the engine's recognition of them is uneven: silent duplication for `insert_after`/`copy_range`, a stuck batch for the others (**V2**, [§48.3](#483-the-verified-results)). | After any unclean stop, follow the protocol of [§48.5](#485-after-an-unclean-stop-a-protocol) *before* the next `apply-next`. |
| **Durability.** | No `fsync`; a power cut can lose the last writes or leave a managed file truncated. | Work on a copy or under version control. |
| **Version control.** | The tool stores payload text and the text it replaced (for undo), not a history of the files. There is no "restore to the state before batch 3". | Use git (or any VCS) alongside. The limitations page says the same: *for anything you would genuinely regret losing, work on a version-controlled checkout.* |
| **Semantic correctness.** | The post-check proves that a `.py` file compiles, that a `.js` file passes `node --check`, and that the invariants **you wrote** hold. Nothing else. | Write invariants from the *source of truth* (the untouched spec), not from the result — that is what `--checked-against` nudges you toward ([§29.5](#295-the-independence-warnings)). |
| **Finding every cascade.** | Domino tracing finds candidates only where text is shared (limitation L8). | Treat the queue as a prompt for judgment, not as a proof of completeness ([§30.5](#305-what-the-gate-guarantees--and-its-hole)). |
| **Protection against edits made outside the tool.** | A hash check happens only at apply time and only for the text a descriptor touches. | Run `check` before `apply-next`; keep the working tree clean between planning and applying. |
| **Robustness against hostile input.** | Archives, batch IDs and paths are trusted ([§57](#57-trust-model-and-security-notes)). | Import only archives you made; keep untrusted text away from command arguments. |
| **Scale.** | Adding descriptors is quadratic in their number; an apply rewrites whole JSON files each time ([§41.5](#415-cost-model-and-measured-scale)). | Keep batches to a few hundred descriptors ([§40.9](#409-batch-size-and-several-batches-in-sequence)). |

#### 54.3 How the guarantees compose

A single edit passes through four layers of protection, and each one catches a different class of mistake:

```
plan time    : claimed-ID conflicts · protected zones · cross-batch locks · gates      (is the PLAN coherent?)
apply time   : compare-and-swap on the target's text                                    (is the FILE what we planned against?)
crash time   : WAL + post-state recognition                                             (did an earlier run already do this?)
post time    : syntax · invariants                                                      (is the RESULT acceptable?)
```

The weak joints are between the layers, not inside them. Plan-time checks look at *IDs*, apply-time checks look at *text*, and the two meet only at the anchor or range of each descriptor — which is exactly why `dest` (an ID that is neither claimed nor hashed) is the single most productive source of deviations in §56. Likewise the crash layer looks at the WAL and at the post-state text, and the two disagree about what "done" means after an undo (**V1**).

---

### 55. Stated limitations and their verification status

The bundled `references/limitations.md` is unusually candid — it opens with "Stated plainly rather than discovered the hard way" — and lists 23 limitations, each as a bold sentence followed by an explanation. This section takes them one at a time. Each was checked against the source and, where a scenario could settle it, run.

**Verdicts.**

| Mark | Meaning |
|---|---|
| ✔ | **Confirmed as stated.** |
| ✔+ | **Confirmed, and reality is worse or broader than stated** — the page understates the limitation. |
| ~ | **Partly wrong** — the statement is inaccurate in a way that changes what you should do. |
| ✘ | **Wrong.** (No limitation received this verdict.) |

Result: **14 ✔, 7 ✔+, 2 ~, 0 ✘** (tally below the table).

| # | Stated limitation (shortened) | Verdict | What was observed |
|---|---|---|---|
| **L1** | *Overlapping batches are detected, not scheduled.* Three edges: the lock is taken at plan time; the checkpoint is a single slot; there is no command to release a lock — the one sanctioned hand edit is deleting its entry from `active_locks.json`. | ✔+ | All three edges confirmed ([§33.3](#333-edges), [§39.5](#395-cross-batch-locks)). **Worse:** an aborted batch can never be closed, and its locks block a *fresh* batch that targets the same lines, so the hand edit is not an edge case but the only exit (**V21**). A batch imported after it was applied leaves an empty lock `{"batch_0001": []}` (**V31**). `resume` can suggest the wrong batch (**V15**). |
| **L2** | *Reversal exists per descriptor, not per batch.* No automatic undo; undo order is not checked; replace/insert/copy verify the live text first, delete/move do not; a crash mid-undo is not recovered. | ✔+ | Confirmed, including the order hazard: undoing an early descriptor while a later one built on it is allowed, and the batch can then never pass `validate-post`. **Not stated, all verified:** `undo` followed by `apply-next` reports a false `recovered` and leaves the file unchanged (**V1**); undoing a `replace_range` or `delete_range` poisons plan validation (**V12**); the undo of a `delete_range` can restore the block in the wrong place even when only one other descriptor is involved (**V23**); after any `recovered` outcome undo is impossible (**V24**); a refused undo still writes `undo_start` (**V25**). |
| **L3** | *`delete_range` and `move_range` have a narrower crash-recovery window* than insert/replace/copy; the gap is "between the file write and the registry write"; the failure is a safe `abort`. | **~** | The gap exists and is safe for delete and move. But the page's picture of *which* ops are protected is backwards: **`insert_after` and `copy_range` silently duplicate** their text in two crash windows, and `replace_range` aborts in one. There are **two** windows between the file write and the final status save (A and B), not one narrow gap (**V2**, [§48.3](#483-the-verified-results)). |
| **L4** | *No automatic detection of "descriptor B targets content descriptor A is about to create."* Declare it with `--depends-on`. | ✔ | Confirmed. A `replace_range` followed by an `insert_after` on the replaced line, ordered with `--depends-on`, **passes** `validate-plan` and then aborts at apply time (`target no longer exists in the registry … This batch needs re-planning, not a retry.`); the reverse order applies cleanly ([§39.2](#392-conflicts--and-why-a-declared-order-is-obeyed-not-judged)). |
| **L5** | *Cross-file moves are two descriptors,* one can apply and the other fail. | ✔ | Confirmed: `move-across-files` writes a `delete_range` and an `insert_after` ([§50.10](#5010-move-across-files-and-copy-across-files)); nothing ties them together except the order you give them. |
| **L6** | *Syntax checking covers `.py` and `.js` only;* `.js` is skipped if `node` is missing; other extensions are reported as skipped. | ✔ | Confirmed, with a documentation contradiction: `cli-reference.md` says only `.py` is wired up (**V10**). A `.js` failure is reported as the last line of Node's stderr — with Node 22 that is just the version banner `Node.js v22.22.0`. |
| **L7** | *Two invariant types;* `balanced_pairs` counts characters and knows nothing of nesting, strings or comments. | ✔ | Confirmed ([§29.2](#292-types-and-options), [§29.3](#293-evaluation-semantics-what-actually-runs)). `--type` accepts exactly `occurrence_count` and `balanced_pairs`. See **V8** for what "regex count" really means. |
| **L8** | *Domino tracing finds candidates, not verdicts, and only where there is shared text.* | ✔ | Confirmed. The search is a regex over the finding's `domino_hint` (or its old content), lines of three characters or fewer are ignored, and nothing is returned for a cascade with different wording ([§30.4](#304-how-the-candidate-search-works)). The documentation says "a literal or regex match"; it is **only** a regex (**V9**). |
| **L9** | *Domino tracing does not recurse.* | ✔ | Confirmed: a descriptor added with `--provenance domino` is never queued — `sync-domino-queue` answered `{"added": [], "total": 1, "pending": 1}` after one was added. |
| **L10** | *"Apply the more specific change before the more general one" is not mechanized* — and "order is **provably** irrelevant, by construction" for non-overlapping ranges. | **~** | The first half holds for the *line ranges*. The second half is too strong: the claim is only as good as the set of IDs the validator looks at, and **`dest` is not in it**. A plan that deletes a line and moves another block to *after* that line passes validation and raises `LineNotFound` at apply time; a move into a protected zone is accepted (**V5**). Two inserts at the same anchor conflict (good) but two inserts at `START` do not, and they stack in reverse order of application (**V17**). |
| **L11** | *Taxonomy and constraints can be project-wide; everything else is per-batch.* | ✔ | Confirmed; the practical consequence is **V14**: a project-level category forces every later batch to use or close it (`taxonomy_incomplete: ["SEC"]`), and nothing removes it. |
| **L12** | *One taxonomy entry, once declared, cannot be removed or renamed.* | ✔ | Confirmed: re-declaring a code is refused (`category 'TYPO' is already declared for this batch`), and no command whose name contains *remove, delete, rename, release* or *unlock* exists in the top-level help. |
| **L13** | *Invariant match listings cap at 20.* | ✔ | Confirmed: 25 matches → `actual: 25`, 20 listed, `matches_truncated: true`. |
| **L14** | *Line endings are preserved per file, but only one style per file;* mixed endings are normalized on the first edit. | ✔+ | Confirmed — and "mixed" is broader than `\r\n` versus `\n`. The line model is Python's `str.splitlines()`, so a form feed, a vertical tab, `\x1c`–`\x1e`, `\x85`, U+2028/U+2029 and a lone `\r` all **split lines** and are rewritten as the file's line ending on the first edit (**V7**). |
| **L15** | *`--exclude-comments` recognizes whole-line comments only* (`#`, `//`, `<!--`, `*`). | ✔ | Confirmed on a four-line file: a trailing `# old_name` still counted; a Markdown bullet `* old_name …` was wrongly excluded; `#` and `//` lines were excluded correctly. |
| **L16** | *Accepted exceptions are keyed by line number.* | ✔ | Confirmed, with a demonstration: after `accept-match` on line 2, a batch deleted that line and put a **new** `foo` on the new line 2; `validate-post` passed, listing the new text as `accepted: true` with the *old* reviewer's note attached. |
| **L17** | *`--checked-against` is evidence of inspection, not of derivation;* matched by exact path string. | ✔+ | Confirmed (`./spec.md` ≠ `spec.md`). **Broader:** the evidence is the *whole-project* WAL, so a file registered before the batch existed — and never shown or read — satisfies it, although the warning text says "during this batch" (**§56.9**). The warning is also the only thing the option does. |
| **L18** | *A shape gate checks that a mechanism was used, not that it was used well.* | ✔ | Confirmed: `--shape rename` passed with a domino queue of **zero** findings ([§32.2](#322-all-gates-in-the-order-validate-plan-runs-them)). |
| **L19** | *`--context` is checked once, when the descriptor is added.* | ✔ | Confirmed (code-derived): `_check_context` is called only from `add_descriptor`; the stored string is never read again. For `insert_after` it is checked against the **anchor** line, and for `START` against the empty string. |
| **L20** | *`dry-run` previews one file and skips the hash checks.* | ✔ | Confirmed (**V16**), and it prints plain text rather than JSON, so `dry-run` output cannot be piped into a JSON consumer. |
| **L21** | *Imported batches assume the destination registered the same files;* ids are not remapped; an existing batch id is refused. | ✔+ | All three confirmed. **Worse:** descriptor *statuses* travel with the batch. A batch exported **after** it was applied imports as `committed`/`applied` while the destination files are untouched, and `validate-post` then **passes** (**V31**). Batch numbering is *count + 1*, so an import can collide with a later `new-batch` (**V13**). |
| **L22** | *Descriptor templating is literal, per-line, and does not dedupe.* | ✔+ | Confirmed — a template descriptor on a line that another descriptor already targets surfaces as a `conflicts` entry at `validate-plan`. **Broader:** `--find ''` is accepted and matches **every** line (`"ab"` became `"XaXbX"`, **V27**). |
| **L23** | *Region inventory records a disposition, not that it was carried out.* | ✔+ | Confirmed: `transferred_with_edit` with `--descriptor-ids d0001` was accepted although `d0001` targets a *different file* than the range, and the plan passed. **Broader:** resolving an already-resolved range silently overwrites the earlier decision and writes no WAL record (**V29**). |

**Tally by verdict.** ✔ (14): L4, L5, L6, L7, L8, L9, L11, L12, L13, L15, L16, L18, L19, L20. ✔+ (7): L1, L2, L14, L17, L21, L22, L23. ~ (2): L3, L10.

#### 55.1 What the page gets right

Three things deserve credit, because they are what make the rest of the tool usable. First, the limitations page **names the honest answer for the dangerous cases**: "for anything you'd genuinely regret losing, work on a copy or a version-controlled checkout" is, after all the testing in this guide, still the correct summary advice. Second, the limitations that describe a **missing feature** (L5, L7, L9, L11, L12, L13, L15, L18) are accurate as stated. Third, **no limitation turned out to be milder than described** — the page errs in only two directions. In seven rows (✔+) it understates how much can go wrong. In the two rows marked **~** it makes a *positive* claim about safety — "it fails safe", "provably irrelevant" — that the tests did not bear out. When the page says "this does not work", believe it; when it says "this is safe", test it.

#### 55.2 What the page does not mention at all

The 31 findings of [§56](#56-verified-behaviors-and-deviations-from-the-documentation) include **eleven** that none of the 23 stated limitations describes: V3 (path spelling decides file identity), V4 (descriptors added after planning are ignored), V6 (an inverted range is accepted), V9 (an invalid `--domino-hint` wedges the domino commands), V18 (`skipped` cannot be produced from the CLI), V19 (registering a path that does not exist), V20 (a direct descriptor added after the last queue sync is not gated), V22 (re-validating a half-applied batch), V26 (`--depends-on` is not trimmed), V28 (`rule_ref` normalization) and V30 (`apply-all` reports nothing when a later descriptor raises). Most of them are *input-hygiene* issues — the tool accepts something it should reject, or fails late and loudly instead of early — which is a different kind of gap from the *design* limits the page lists. They are cheap to avoid once known; §58 turns each into a rule.
### 56. Verified behaviors and deviations from the documentation

This section is the register of everything that was found to behave differently from the bundled documentation — or that the documentation never mentions — numbered **V1 … V31**. The numbers are used throughout this guide (`V5` in Part III is the same `V5` here), so they will not change.

#### 56.1 How to read an entry

Every entry has the same five parts:

| Part | Content |
|---|---|
| **Docs say** | What the bundled documentation promises or implies, quoted from the file that says it. Where nothing is promised the entry says so. |
| **Observed** | What the tool actually did. |
| **Reproduce** | The commands and the real output, shortened. File IDs are a function of the path string (`f_` + the first ten hex digits of the SHA-256 of the path), so a file called `f.txt` is `f_e4723ca566` in *your* run too, and `a.txt` is `f_18b7cb099a`. |
| **Impact** | What goes wrong for a user. |
| **Workaround** | What to do instead, or how to notice. |

**Severity.**

| Level | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **High** | Can leave a **wrong file, or a wrong status, with no error at all** — the dangerous category. |
| **Medium** | A loud failure that strands a batch, a plan that fails late, or a silent change that is visible if you look. Recovery needs manual work, usually a new batch. |
| **Low** | A misleading message or passage of the documentation, an input accepted that should have been rejected, a cosmetic oddity. |

> **Why "a new batch" is so often the remedy.** The tool has **no command that removes a descriptor, an invariant, a constraint or a category, and none that edits a descriptor.** Once a batch holds a descriptor that can never validate, or a state that can never reach `validate-post`, the batch is finished — the plan lives in a new one. Several entries below are really *this* fact seen from different angles.

*Output conventions.* Output is shown as the tool printed it, except that short JSON objects are collapsed onto one line, absolute paths are shortened and `# …` comments are annotations added for this guide.

#### 56.3 Undo, redo and crash recovery

Six findings (V1, V2, V12, V23, V24, V25) concern the machinery that is supposed to make the tool *recoverable*. There are two causes. For V1 and V2 it is a design one: the WAL record and the *post-state* test were built to recognize an **interrupted apply**, and they are also being asked whether something was **reversed**, which they cannot know. For V12, V23 and V24 it is a data-model one: **undo is implemented as a new edit, not as a rollback** — restored text gets new IDs, and the position to restore to is an anchor remembered from planning time. [Section 44.4](#444-apply_descriptor-the-whole-algorithm) shows the algorithm; this section shows what falls out of it.

##### V1 — `undo-descriptor` followed by `apply-next` is a false `recovered`

**Docs say.** `file-formats.md`: *"A descriptor's `status` can now also be `undone`. Because `apply-next` treats anything not `applied` as pending, running it after an undo re-applies that descriptor -- an undo followed by `apply-next` is a redo."*

**Observed.** It does not re-apply. `apply_descriptor` looks at the WAL first, finds the `op_applied` record written by the **first** application, concludes that an earlier, interrupted run already did the work, and reconciles the status to `applied` without touching the file. The WAL has no way to say "…and then it was reversed": the R1 test asks only whether `op_applied` exists ([§44.4](#444-apply_descriptor-the-whole-algorithm), [§48.4](#484-what-recovered-proves--and-what-it-does-not)).

**Reproduce.** A five-line `notes.txt` (`alpha beta gamma delta epsilon`), one `replace_range` of line 2 with `BETA`:

```
$ cli.py apply-next batch_0001
{"result": "applied", "descriptor_id": "d0001"}                       # notes.txt: alpha / BETA / gamma …
$ cli.py undo-descriptor batch_0001 d0001
{"result": "reverted", "descriptor_id": "d0001"}                      # notes.txt: alpha / beta / gamma …
$ cli.py apply-next batch_0001                                        # the documented "redo"
{"result": "recovered", "descriptor_id": "d0001",
 "detail": "WAL shows this already completed; status reconciled, nothing re-applied"}
$ cat notes.txt                                                       # still "beta" — BETA never came back
$ cli.py status batch_0001      →  "counts": {"applied": 1}
$ cli.py validate-post batch_0001  →  "result": "pass"
```

**Impact.** The batch reports a descriptor as `applied` whose edit is **absent**; `validate-post` passes unless an invariant happens to mention the text; the batch becomes `committed`. Together with V31 this is one of two ways a clean-looking batch can be missing an edit without any crash or outside interference.

**Workaround.** Treat `undo-descriptor` as final. If the change is wanted after all, add a **new** descriptor in a **new** batch, against the restored lines' *new* IDs (`show-file`). The read-only auditor flags the state: *"undone, but its op_applied is still in the WAL"* ([§59.2](#592-a-read-only-state-auditor)).

##### V2 — Crash recovery is uneven across the five operations

**Docs say.** `limitations.md`: delete and move have *"a narrower crash-recovery window"* than insert, replace and copy, because the latter *"add positively-checkable content, so a crash … can be detected by reading back what's actually there"*; the one gap is a crash *"between the file write and the registry write specifically, for a delete or a move, with the WAL entry also not yet written"*, which ends in an `abort` — *"it fails safe"*. `cli-reference.md` says of `abort`: *"The file is left exactly as found."*

**Observed.** Crashes were injected at three points of one `apply_descriptor` call — **A** after the file write, before the registry save; **B** after the registry save, before the WAL `op_applied`; **C** after the WAL `op_applied`, before the status save — and the call was repeated ([§48.2](#482-the-crash-harness)):

| Op | A | B | C |
|---|---|---|---|
| `insert_after` | **applied again — duplicate** | **applied again — duplicate** | recovered |
| `replace_range` | recovered | **abort** | recovered |
| `delete_range` | **abort** | **abort** | recovered |
| `move_range` | **abort** | applied (harmless repeat) | recovered |
| `copy_range` | **applied again — duplicate** | **applied again — duplicate** | recovered |

So the page has the picture backwards: the ops it calls *well protected* (insert, copy) are the ones that **silently duplicate** their text; `replace_range` also aborts (in B); and the "narrow gap" is two windows. The abort messages blame the wrong party:

```
replace_range B: d0001: target no longer exists in the registry (f_e4723ca566_l00002 was deleted earlier
                 and is no longer addressable). This batch needs re-planning, not a retry.
delete_range  A: d0001: live content matches neither the expected pre-state (74da7275b116) nor a plausible
                 post-state. live hash 1ab05bcb1d04. Someone or something changed this file outside the batch
                 -- re-plan rather than retry.
```

In every aborting cell the file is **already in its intended final state**; the "outside change" is the tool's own interrupted run.

**Reproduce.** `crash_sim.py` ([§48.2](#482-the-crash-harness)); the dangerous cell:

```
insert_after  A: crash after file write, before registry saved
    file after crash: [L1 L2 NEW L3 L4 L5]
    retry -> applied; file: [L1 L2 NEW NEW L3 L4 L5]   expected: [L1 L2 NEW L3 L4 L5]   => MISMATCH
```

**Impact.** *High* for insert and copy (a wrong file, no error). *Medium* for the aborts: the descriptor stays `pending`, `validate-post` refuses, and the batch's locks stay held (V21).

**Workaround.** After any unclean stop do not run `apply-next` blindly; follow the protocol of [§48.5](#485-after-an-unclean-stop-a-protocol). The auditor reports an `op_start` without `op_applied` and an `op_start` logged twice ([§59.2](#592-a-read-only-state-auditor)).

##### V12 — Undoing a `replace_range` or `delete_range` poisons the batch

**Docs say.** `cli-reference.md`: *"The descriptor's status becomes `undone`."* `file-formats.md`: *"an undo followed by `apply-next` is a redo."*

**Observed.** Undoing a replace or a delete re-inserts the restored text under **new** IDs and tombstones the old ones ([§22.3](#223-how-ids-and-positions-change)). The undone descriptor still names the old IDs, so `validate-plan` can never pass again — and `validate-post` can never pass either, because the descriptor is `undone`, not `applied`. An undone `insert_after`, `copy_range` or `move_range` leaves the plan valid (its anchors are still live), but see V1 for what `apply-next` then does.

**Reproduce.** `n.txt` = `alpha beta gamma`; replace line 2 with `BETA`; apply; undo:

```
$ cli.py validate-plan batch_0001
{"phase": "plan", "batch_id": "batch_0001", "result": "fail",
 "schema_errors": ["d0001: f_953a374320_l00002 was deleted earlier and is no longer addressable"]}
$ cli.py show-file n.txt
{"file_id": "f_953a374320", "path": "n.txt", "lines": [{"pos": 1, "line_id": "f_953a374320_l00001", "text": "alpha"},
  {"pos": 2, "line_id": "f_953a374320_l00005", "text": "beta"}, {"pos": 3, "line_id": "f_953a374320_l00003", "text": "gamma"}]}
```

The restored `beta` is `…l00005`; the original `…l00002` and the replacement `…l00004` are both tombstones.

**Impact.** After an undo of a replace or delete the batch cannot be completed. There is no command to delete the dead descriptor.

**Workaround.** Treat such an undo as the end of the batch: put any further edits of that region into a **new** batch, addressed by the new IDs from `show-file`. Never rely on "undo, then re-validate".

##### V23 — Undo of a `delete_range` can restore the block in the wrong place

**Docs say.** `limitations.md`: *"for delete and move there is no such check (a delete's inverse re-inserts at the remembered anchor without confirming the neighbourhood is unchanged)."* The page frames the hazard as something *else* changing the file.

**Observed.** The hazard needs no outside party: another descriptor **of the same batch** is enough. `undo_anchor` — the line that sat directly above the block — is recorded when the descriptor is **added**, not when it is applied ([§53.3](#533-batchesiddescriptorsjson)). An insert applied earlier between that anchor and the block makes the anchor stale.

**Reproduce.** File `L1 L2 L3 L4`. `d0001` = `insert_after L1` with `X`; `d0002` = `delete_range L2..L3`.

```
$ cli.py apply-all batch_0001                  # file: L1 / X / L4
$ cli.py undo-descriptor batch_0001 d0002
{"result": "reverted", "descriptor_id": "d0002"}
$ cat f.txt                                    # L1 / L2 / L3 / X / L4      ← the file before d0002 was L1 / X / L2 / L3 / L4
```

**Impact.** *High.* The undo is reported as a success and the result is a plausible-looking file with two lines in the wrong order.

**Workaround.** Do not undo a `delete_range` (or a `move_range`) once any other descriptor has touched the lines around it. Restore from version control, or re-plan.

##### V24 — After any `recovered` outcome the descriptor can never be undone

**Docs say.** `cli-reference.md`: *"A descriptor applied before undo support existed carries no `created_ids`/`pre_payload_ref` and can't be undone."*

**Observed.** The same condition arises for **current** descriptors. `created_ids` is written only by the final status save of a *normal* apply. A descriptor that ended through either `recovered` branch has `created_ids: null`, and `undo-descriptor` refuses with a message about undo support that has nothing to do with the cause.

**Reproduce.** `crash_undo.py` ([Appendix D](#appendix-d--how-this-guide-was-verified)): crash, retry, then undo:

```
insert_after  C (crash after WAL op_applied): retry -> recovered  created_ids=None
              undo -> DescriptorError: d0001: missing created_ids, predates undo support
replace_range A (crash before registry save): retry -> recovered  created_ids=None
              undo -> DescriptorError: d0001: missing created_ids/pre_payload_ref, predates undo support
```

**Impact.** The one situation in which you most want an undo — a crash — is the one in which it is unavailable. The IDs minted by the interrupted run are not recorded anywhere.

**Workaround.** After a crash, undo by hand (version control), or write the inverse as a new descriptor in a new batch. The auditor flags `applied without created_ids`.

##### V25 — A refused undo still writes `undo_start`

**Docs say.** `limitations.md`: *"`undo_start` without `undo_applied` in the WAL tells you [a crash in the middle of an undo] happened."*

**Observed.** `undo_descriptor` writes `undo_start` **before** it checks that the live text still matches. A refused undo — which exits 2 with an error — therefore leaves the same WAL signature as an interrupted one.

**Reproduce.** Apply a replace, change the line outside the tool, then undo:

```
$ cli.py undo-descriptor batch_0001 d0001
{"error": "d0001: live content no longer matches what this descriptor produced -- something else changed it since,
 refusing to undo blind"}                                                                        # exit 2
$ tail -3 .operational-platform/wal.jsonl
{"ts": …, "event": "op_start",   "batch_id": "batch_0001", "descriptor_id": "d0001", "op": "replace_range"}
{"ts": …, "event": "op_applied", "batch_id": "batch_0001", "descriptor_id": "d0001"}
{"ts": …, "event": "undo_start", "batch_id": "batch_0001", "descriptor_id": "d0001"}
```

**Impact.** An orphan `undo_start` is inconclusive: it can mean a crash, or a refusal. Nothing was undone in the second case.

**Workaround.** Read the exit code and message of the undo call; use the file, not the WAL, to decide what state you are in.
