## Appendix C — Message catalog

Every message the tool can print — with the module, the function and the line it comes from — and the messages of the three programs of [Part IX](#part-ix--operating-guide). It is for the moment when a reply says something you do not recognize: search this page for a few words of it.

**How it was built.** Not by running the tool until it complained. A program, `extract_messages.py` ([D.6](#d6-the-guides-own-programs)), parses the seven modules with Python's own `ast` module and reports every string that is not a docstring or an `argparse` help text — the arguments of `raise`, of `Abort(…)` and of `_err(…)`, dictionary entries such as `"detail"` and `"error"`, items appended to the lists of failures and warnings, and the text half of `(ok, text)` returns. `gen_catalog.py` groups the result into the tables below. The extraction found **108** strings; **103** are messages, and 5 are not (three formats of generated IDs and two docstrings).

**Checked against the real runs.** `check_catalog.py` ([D.6](#d6-the-guides-own-programs)) turns every template into a pattern and compares it with every string that the scenarios of this guide actually printed in an `error` or `detail` field, or as an item of a failure list (the samples of [C.16](#c16-real-replies-verbatim) are part of that material). Nothing was left unexplained: what is not the catalog's is Python's own text ([C.15](#c15-messages-that-are-not-the-tools-own)) or data — a category code, a file name or an ID listed under a failure key. The check also runs the other way, and that half is the more modest one: of the **100** templates that can be tested (three that would match almost anything, and the five extracted strings that are not messages, are left out), **60** were printed by at least one recorded run and **40** were not — those are read from the source. Read the catalog as complete for the source and as verified for the 60.

```
distinct strings in the error / detail / failure-list fields of the real runs: 118
  matched a template of the catalog : 96
  Python's own text (C.15)          : 9
  data, not messages (category codes, file names, IDs) : 13
  unexplained                       : 0
templates of the catalog (not counting 3 that would match almost anything, nor 5 ID formats and docstrings): 100
  produced by at least one real run : 60
  known from the source only        : 40
```

**How to read a row.** The first column is a *template*: `{…}` is an expression of the source, shown as written — `{op!r}` prints the value with Python's `repr`, so a text in single quotes. *Appears as* names the exception or the field of the reply. *Source* is `module.function` and the line number **in the archive's files** — line numbers are those of this version of the tool (the code has no version constant). Messages that Python or `argparse` produce are in [C.15](#c15-messages-that-are-not-the-tools-own).

### C.1 How a message reaches you

| Shape | Looks like | Exit |
|---|---|---:|
| an error the command caught itself | `{"error": "'nope.txt' is not registered -- run register_file first"}` | 2 |
| any other exception, through the generic handler | `{"error": "PatternError: missing ), unterminated subpattern at position 1"}` | 2 |
| a failed check | `{"phase": "plan", "result": "fail", "<key>": [...], "detail": "..."}` — one failing key ([§51](#51-the-validate-plan-diagnostic-catalog)) | 1 |
| an abort | `{"result": "abort", "descriptor_id": "d0002", "detail": "…"}` | 1 |
| a normal result | `{"result": "applied", "descriptor_id": "d0001"}`, `done`, `recovered`, `reverted`, `traced`, `pass` | 0 |
| a command-line error | usage text and `cli.py <command>: error: …` on **stderr**, not JSON | 2 |
| a guard refusal ([§60.3](#603-the-guard-wrapper)) | `{"guard_error": "…"}` | 3 |

Which exceptions a command prints bare and which arrive as `Type: message` is the matrix of [§47.2](#472-what-each-command-catches). Scripts should key on `result`, the exit status and the documented keys — never on the wording below ([§49.2](#492-output-and-exit-codes), [§60.2](#602-the-contract-what-to-parse-when-to-continue-when-to-stop)).

| `{start_id}..{end_id} resolves to an inverted range ({ps}..{pe})` | `RangeInvalid` | `registry.ids_in_range`:107 |
| `move destination falls inside the block being moved` | `RangeInvalid` | `registry.apply_move`:187 |

### C.15 Messages that are not the tool's own

Some replies carry text that Python or `argparse` wrote. They reach you through the generic handler as `{"error": "<Type>: <message>"}`, or — for `argparse` — as usage text on stderr.

| Reply | When | Entry |
|---|---|---|
| `FileNotFoundError: [Errno 2] No such file or directory: '…'` | a `--payload-file`, or the archive of `import-batch`, does not exist | [§47.3](#473-add-descriptor-details) |
| `IsADirectoryError: [Errno 21] Is a directory: '…'` | `register .` or any directory | [§50.1](#501-register) |
| `UnicodeDecodeError: 'utf-8' codec can't decode byte 0xff in position 0: invalid start byte` | `register` of a file that is not UTF-8 | E10 |
| `StopIteration: ` (an empty message) | `check` with an unknown descriptor ID | [§50.21](#5021-check) |
| `PatternError: missing ), unterminated subpattern at position 1` | a regex that does not compile — `find-pattern`, `domino-next`, `domino-resolve`, `validate-post`. The type is `error` on Python before 3.13 | V8, V9 |
| `LineNotFound: …`, `RangeInvalid: …` | raised where no command catches them: `check`, `validate-plan` on an inverted range, `validate-post` on an unregistered file, a bad `dest` mid-apply | V5, V6, V8 |
| `usage: cli.py <command> [-h] …` and `cli.py <command>: error: argument --shape: invalid choice: 'nonsense' (choose from …)` | a value outside `choices=` — `--shape`, `--severity`, `--provenance`, `--type`, `--disposition` — or a missing required option, or a wrong type (`--expected-count many`) | [§47.1](#471-skeleton) |
| `cli.py: error: argument command: invalid choice: '…' (choose from …)` | an unknown command | [§49.1](#491-invocation) |

## Appendix D — How this guide was verified

This appendix is the record behind the word *verified*. It says what was read and what was run, in which environment and with which programs; what each mechanical check found; and — in [D.10](#d10-what-was-not-verified) — what was **not** checked. Everything in it can be repeated: the scripts of the scenarios are printed in [D.11](#d11-the-scenario-scripts), the programs in [D.5](#d5-the-crash-harness), [D.6](#d6-the-guides-own-programs) and [D.9](#d9-measurements), and the transcript of the reference run in [D.12](#d12-the-reference-tour).

| Section | What it holds |
|---|---|
| [D.1](#d1-what-verified-means) | the three levels of evidence, the procedure, and the rules the guide keeps about its own numbers |
| [D.2](#d2-the-environment) | the archive and its checksum, the machine, the interpreter, how the tool was invoked, and how the package was renamed |
| [D.3](#d3-the-scenarios) | the scenario scripts: how one is built, the full inventory, and whether the transcripts reproduce |
| [D.4](#d4-text-edge-cases) | the ten text edge cases (E1–E10), byte by byte |
| [D.5](#d5-the-crash-harness) | the crash harness: its results and the three programs |
| [D.6](#d6-the-guides-own-programs) | every program written for this guide: what it is for, and its source |
| [D.7](#d7-mechanical-checks) | the checks that a program made rather than a reader: identity, command names, the "Changes" column, state formats, the auditor, the guard's table, the catalog, the links |
| [D.8](#d8-tests-of-the-programs-of-part-ix) | the tests of the programs of Part IX — the auditor, the lock release, the guard, the driver |
| [D.9](#d9-measurements) | scale: what was measured, with which scripts, on what machine |
| [D.10](#d10-what-was-not-verified) | what was not verified, and how the guide says so |
| [D.11](#d11-the-scenario-scripts) | the listing of the scenario scripts and their helper |
| [D.12](#d12-the-reference-tour) | the complete transcript of the reference run |

### D.1 What verified means

The guide separates what was *seen* from what was *read*, and says which one a statement stands on.

| Level | What it means | Where it shows |
|---|---|---|
| **Verified** | The behavior was **produced**: a command or a program was run and its reply, its effect on disk or its output was recorded. A reader can repeat it with the scripts of this appendix. | the register of deviations ([§56](#56-verified-behaviors-and-deviations-from-the-documentation)), the crash windows ([§48](#48-concurrency-atomicity-and-crash-windows)), the formats of Part VII, every transcript |
| **Code-derived** | The behavior follows from **reading** the source — all seven modules were read line by line — and was not exercised. | marked *code-derived* wherever it occurs; [D.10](#d10-what-was-not-verified) says what falls under it |
| **Documented** | A claim of the archive's own documents, neither run nor contradicted. A sentence with no label is of this kind. | Part II, and wherever the text quotes the documents |

**The procedure was the same every time.**

1. A question came from reading the source or the documentation — *does an insert survive a crash between the file write and the registry write?*
2. A scenario script was written for it, in a project directory of its own ([D.3](#d3-the-scenarios)).
3. The transcript was read, not skimmed. Where a text editor could hide the answer — a final newline, a carriage return, a form feed — the bytes of the file were looked at with `od -c` ([D.4](#d4-text-edge-cases)).
4. When the tool did what its documentation says, that was recorded as *verified to work as documented* ([§56.10](#5610-what-was-verified-to-work-exactly-as-documented)). When it did not, an entry of the register was written: what the documentation says, quoted; what was observed; the commands that reproduce it; the impact; a workaround ([§56.1](#561-how-to-read-an-entry)).
5. An entry whose first explanation proved wrong was corrected, not removed. The guard of [§60.3](#603-the-guard-wrapper) is the example: its first version looked for an option by its spelling, and the abbreviation test ([D.8](#d8-tests-of-the-programs-of-part-ix)) showed that `argparse` accepts prefixes; the finding became m14.

**The guide keeps three rules about its own numbers.**

- A count in the text is *counted by a program* or *copied from a transcript*; it is not remembered. The number of fixture projects (174), the line counts of the programs, the 38 commands of the cheat sheet, the tables of the message catalog, the census of state files, the "Changes" column, the scenario inventory and the table of programs are generated; the program that joins the parts fills in the counts of fixtures, lines and links.
- A transcript is the output of a real run. The only edits are those listed in front of Part I ([About this guide](#about-this-guide)): shortened paths, trimmed long outputs, short objects collapsed onto one line, and `# …` comments added.
- What could not be checked is said so, in the place where the claim is made, and again in [D.10](#d10-what-was-not-verified).

### D.2 The environment

| Item | Value |
|---|---|
| Machine | Linux 6.18.44 on x86-64; 2 virtual CPUs (Intel Xeon at 2.10 GHz); 8 GB of memory; a private, disposable container — no other users and no real project |
| Interpreter | CPython **3.13.16** (main, Oct 1 2026, GCC 13.3.0) — the only Python on which the tool and the programs were *run* |
| Node.js | v22.22.0, present for the optional JavaScript syntax check of `validate-post` (`node --check`) |
| Shell and utilities | GNU bash 5.2.21; GNU coreutils 9.4 (`od`, `cat -A`); `bc` 1.07.1 (for timings) |
| Static analysis | `vermin` 1.9.2, for the "Python needed" column of [D.6](#d6-the-guides-own-programs) — an estimate from the text of a file, not a run |
| Network | none needed and none used: the tool imports only the standard library (`argparse`, `hashlib`, `json`, `os`, `pathlib`, `re`, `shutil`, `sys`, `tarfile`, `time`, `typing`, and `subprocess` once, for `node --check`) and none of its modules opens a connection |

**The tool that was run is the tool in the archive.** The archive of this edition, `operational-platform-a-2a.zip`, and the unpacked copies were compared file by file with SHA-256 ([D.7](#d7-mechanical-checks) shows the program):

Archive: **125,131 bytes**, SHA-256 `58d93e5774c1e483ab7efa77a7c8dd1196c64a60e5296be73246e2bb7228761e`.

| Compared | Files identical | Files that differ | Files missing from the unpacked copy | Files in the copy that the archive does not contain |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---|
| the archive (outer zip) | 5 | 0 | 0 | none |
| the nested `operational-platform.skill` | 12 | 0 | 0 | `operational-platform/scripts/__pycache__/cli.cpython-313.pyc`, `operational-platform/scripts/__pycache__/domino.cpython-313.pyc`, `operational-platform/scripts/__pycache__/engine.cpython-313.pyc`, `operational-platform/scripts/__pycache__/inventory.cpython-313.pyc`, `operational-platform/scripts/__pycache__/registry.cpython-313.pyc`, `operational-platform/scripts/__pycache__/storage.cpython-313.pyc`, `operational-platform/scripts/__pycache__/validator.cpython-313.pyc` |

The seven `__pycache__` files are not part of the archive: the interpreter wrote them next to the modules when it first ran them. Since the rename described [below](#how-the-package-was-renamed) no module was edited, patched on disk or instrumented. Where a test needed to interfere — the crash harness replaces one `storage` function for one call — it did so in memory, in a process of its own ([D.5](#d5-the-crash-harness)).

**How the tool was invoked.** Always `python3 -I …/cli.py`, with the project root as the working directory ([§6.3](#63-invocation--and-the-one-thing-the-docs-gloss-over)). Isolated mode (`-I`) makes the interpreter ignore every `PYTHON…` variable and the user's site directory, and keeps the current directory off `sys.path`, so that a file that happens to sit in a project directory — a `json.py`, say — cannot replace a module of the standard library. `cli.py` puts its own directory on the path (its line 19), which is why it works under `-I`; the programs of this guide that import the tool do the same with a directory given as an argument. Every scenario starts from `rm -rf` of its own project directory, so a re-run starts clean.

**Timings.** The machine is a shared virtual machine with two CPUs. Each measurement was made once, with `date` and `bc` ([D.9](#d9-measurements)); read the numbers as orders of magnitude and as ratios, not as benchmarks.

#### How the package was renamed

The archive was delivered with **several names for one thing**: a tool called `llm-assembler` (the skill, its folder, its `.skill` package and the state directory `.llm-assembler/`), a project called "LLM Operational Platform", and file names that carry them. This edition of the guide uses **one name, Operational Platform**, in file names and in text. The renamed archive was made from the delivered one by `rename_package.py` ([D.6](#rename_packagepy)), which only reads the delivered archive. This subsection, with the two reports of that program that it quotes, and the listing of the program are the only places in the guide where the delivered names are written out.

**The rules.**

- **File names.** `llm-assembler` and `llm-os` become `operational-platform`; `llm-operational-platform-task-execution-methodology` becomes `operational-platform-task-execution-methodology`.
- **Text.** The tool's name, the state directory's name and the project's name all become Operational Platform: as the identifier `operational-platform` inside a code span, a code block or the target of a link (so `.llm-assembler/` becomes `.operational-platform/`), and as the name "Operational Platform" in running text. "LLM Operational Platform" loses its first word.
- **Rewritten whole.** Five paragraphs explained how the delivered names differed from one another — the opening of the README and of the two methodology documents, the README's note on names, and the heading of the tool's own document, which the archive holds twice. After the rename they say that there is one name.
- **Left alone.** Words that are not names: "assembly" and "assembled" say what the tool does, not what it is called.

**What changed, file by file.**

The delivered archive (125,314 bytes, SHA-256 `12c09a809756d332a5f958d44cd3af3d38b72a050fec27f8fa4e5bf593c7ca3e`) holds 5 files, one of which (the package) holds 12 more. The lines of `operational-platform/scripts/storage.py` that differ (`-` as delivered, `+` renamed):

```diff
--- llm-assembler/scripts/storage.py
+++ operational-platform/scripts/storage.py
@@ -2 +2 @@
-storage.py -- all filesystem I/O for llm-assembler lives here, and nowhere
+storage.py -- all filesystem I/O for Operational Platform lives here, and nowhere
@@ -8 +8 @@
-State layout, rooted at STATE_DIR (".llm-assembler/" inside the project
+State layout, rooted at STATE_DIR (".operational-platform/" inside the project
@@ -11 +11 @@
-    .llm-assembler/
+    .operational-platform/
@@ -47 +47 @@
-STATE_DIRNAME = ".llm-assembler"
+STATE_DIRNAME = ".operational-platform"
@@ -52 +52 @@
-    .llm-assembler/ walking upward from `start` (default: cwd). If none
+    .operational-platform/ walking upward from `start` (default: cwd). If none
```

**Residue.** None of the old names is left in a file name or in a text of the renamed archive.

One string of one module is more than a docstring: `STATE_DIRNAME`, **the name of the directory in which a project keeps its state**. It is the one change that a running tool can see. A project that was made by the delivered tool, and holds a `.llm-assembler/`, is therefore not recognized by the renamed one — and the renamed tool does not complain: it reports a batch that does not exist and starts a new, empty state beside the old one (V13). Carrying such a project over takes one command, `mv .llm-assembler .operational-platform`, run in the project root while no one is using the tool, because no file of the state contains the name of the tool. Nor does an archive that `export-batch` makes, so a batch exported by the delivered tool imports into the renamed one as it is. `rename_package.py carry-over` checked both on a small project, with the delivered tool unpacked from the delivered archive:

| Step | Result |
|---|---|
| The delivered tool registers a file, opens a batch, adds one descriptor, plans, exports the batch and applies it | 10 files of state under `.llm-assembler/` |
| Files of that state that contain the old name | **0** of 10 |
| The renamed tool is asked for the batch in a copy that still has `.llm-assembler/` | `status` `planning`, `counts` `{}` — the answer for a batch that does not exist; and a new `.operational-platform/` appears, holding `.operational-platform/batches`, `.operational-platform/batches/batch_0001`, `.operational-platform/payloads` |

After `mv .llm-assembler .operational-platform` in another copy, the same four commands were run by the delivered tool on the copy that kept its directory and by the renamed tool on the copy whose directory was renamed (the path of the project is masked as `<project>`, that of the tool as `<cli.py>`):

| Command | Exit codes | Same reply |
|---|:--:|:--:|
| `status batch_0001` | 0 and 0 | yes |
| `show-file list.txt` | 0 and 0 | yes |
| `validate-post batch_0001` | 0 and 0 | yes |
| `status batch_0001` | 0 and 0 | yes |

The batch that the delivered tool exported before it applied it (the archive holds the batch's files and the payloads, and no name of the tool) was then imported into two more copies of the project, which held the registered file and no batch — by the delivered tool in the copy that kept its directory, and by the renamed tool in the copy whose directory was renamed:

| Command | Exit codes | Same reply |
|---|:--:|:--:|
| `import-batch batch_0001.tar.gz` | 0 and 0 | yes |
| `status batch_0001` | 0 and 0 | yes |
| `validate-plan batch_0001` | 0 and 0 | yes |
| `apply-all batch_0001` | 0 and 0 | yes |
| `validate-post batch_0001` | 0 and 0 | yes |
| `show-file list.txt` | 0 and 0 | yes |

**Is the renamed tool the same tool?** The syntax trees say that its code is. The scenarios say that it behaves so. The 42 scenario scripts of this edition are those of the first edition of this guide, which was written under the delivered names, changed by the same rules (`rename_package.py map`) — and in one other way: `sc_minor.sh` had shared the project name `m1` with `sc_moves.sh`, so that whichever ran later left its state there; it now has a project of its own. They were run on the renamed tool, each in a new directory, by `repro_check.py` ([D.6](#repro_checkpy)), and what they printed was compared with the transcripts that the delivered tool had printed, after the names in those transcripts had been changed by the same rules:

**42** scenario scripts were run again in a new directory. **41** printed exactly what the recorded transcript says (after the root directory, the time stamps, the dates of `ls -l` and the size of `wal.jsonl` were normalized); **1** printed the same text apart from the point named below; **0** differ.

| Script | Result | Where |
|---|---|---|
| `sc_trust.sh` | identical apart from file IDs | an ID hashes a path that contains the root |

After that, every transcript of this guide was recorded again on the renamed tool, the fixture projects were rebuilt, the benchmarks of [D.9](#d9-measurements) were repeated, and every generator and check of [D.6](#d6-the-guides-own-programs) was run again on the new results. [D.3](#d3-the-scenarios) says whether the new transcripts reproduce.

### D.3 The scenarios

A *scenario* is a short, deterministic sequence of commands in a project directory of its own, written to answer one question and read afterwards. Scenarios are grouped into **scenario scripts**, `sc_NAME.sh`, which print their own headings.

#### How a scenario script is built

The helpers are in `lib.sh` ([D.11](#d11-the-scenario-scripts)); a script `source`s it.

| Helper | What it does |
|---|---|
| `newproj NAME` | removes `$S/projects/NAME` if it exists, creates it empty and changes into it — the tool is always run from the project root, and a scenario never inherits another's state |
| `run ARGS…` | prints `$ cli.py ARGS…`, runs the command through `python3 -I`, prints the reply and `[exit=N]`; the transcripts are made of these |
| `quiet ARGS…` | runs a command and discards its reply — for setting a state up |
| `fid PATH` | registers the path (it is idempotent) and returns its `file_id`, from which a script builds line IDs such as `${F}_l00003` |
| `show PATH` | prints a file with the line ends made visible (`cat -A`, the `$` at the end of a line shown as ⏎) |

Each scenario announces itself with `##### CODE: title`. The *code* is the scenario's own label — `C1`, `E4`, `GD3`, `V31`, `L17` — and it is what the labels of the guide refer to: **E1–E10** are the text edge cases ([D.4](#d4-text-edge-cases)), **LINT-A–LINT-D**, **GD1–GD5**, **DR1–DR4**, **RL1–RL4** and **AB-A/AB-B** are the tests of the programs of Part IX ([D.8](#d8-tests-of-the-programs-of-part-ix)), and a code that repeats the number of a deviation or a limitation (`V20`, `L13`) is the scenario that produced it. A script's **transcript** is what it prints, standard output and standard error together.

#### The inventory

The table is **generated** from the scripts and from their transcripts by `gen_scenarios.py` ([D.6](#gen_scenariospy)): the headings come from the transcript — so that a heading inside a loop shows once per pass, with its real values — the project names from the calls of `newproj`, and the number of replies from the lines of the transcript that start with `$ `. A script may run more commands silently, to set a state up, so the last column counts what was *recorded*, not what was run. The script names link to their listings in [D.11](#d11-the-scenario-scripts).

**42** scenario scripts; **163** scenarios that announce themselves with a heading; **589** commands whose reply is recorded in a transcript (a script may run more commands silently, to set a state up).

The fixtures that all of them left behind — 174 project directories that hold a state directory — are what the census of formats and the sweep of the auditor read.

#### Do the transcripts reproduce?

A transcript that cannot be reproduced is an anecdote. `repro_check.py` ([D.6](#repro_checkpy)) runs every scenario script again, in a new directory, on a fresh copy of the tool, and compares what it prints with the transcript that this guide quotes. Four things are normalized in both texts, because they differ from run to run *by design*: the root directory, the time stamps that the tool writes (`"ts"` and `"updated_at"`), the dates that `ls -l` prints, and the size that `ls -l` prints for `wal.jsonl` — the file holds floating-point time stamps, and their printed length is not the same in every run (a repeated run of `sc_export.sh` printed 99 bytes where the transcript says 98). The six lines `run N: …` of `sc_lockorder.sh` are masked too: their point is that the orders differ. A script that still differs is compared again in two weaker ways — with every file ID masked, and with the lines sorted — and the report says which.

**42** scenario scripts were run again in a new directory. **40** printed exactly what the recorded transcript says (after the root directory, the time stamps, the dates of `ls -l` and the size of `wal.jsonl` were normalized); **2** printed the same text apart from the point named below; **0** differ.

| Script | Result | Where |
|---|---|---|
| `sc_conflict.sh` | identical apart from the order of lines | the first line that differs is line 290 |
| `sc_trust.sh` | identical apart from file IDs | an ID hashes a path that contains the root |

The two points that the run shown above reports are understood, and neither is a defect of a transcript:

- **`sc_conflict.sh`** prints `active_locks.json`, and the order in which that file lists the IDs of a claimed range can differ from one process to the next. The tool builds the list from a *set* of strings, and Python randomizes string hashes per process. So a new run reproduces the recorded order only when the random orders happen to agree. `conflict_runs.py` ([D.6](#conflict_runspy)) ran the script twenty more times and compared each run with the transcript:

```
run  1: same lines, another order
run  2: identical
run  3: identical
run  4: same lines, another order
run  5: identical
run  6: identical
run  7: identical
run  8: same lines, another order
run  9: same lines, another order
run 10: same lines, another order
run 11: same lines, another order
run 12: same lines, another order
run 13: same lines, another order
run 14: identical
run 15: identical
run 16: same lines, another order
run 17: identical
run 18: identical
run 19: same lines, another order
run 20: same lines, another order
20 runs: 9 identical, 11 with the same lines in another order, 0 different
```

Which of the two you get, you cannot choose — the report above may therefore list this script or not. Nothing reads the order, so the locks are not affected; it is the minor finding **m15** ([§56.9](#569-minor-findings)), and `sc_lockorder.sh` is its scenario. Its own transcript:

```
##### M15: the same plan validated in six fresh projects -- the order of the IDs that active_locks.json stores
run 1: 00004 00002 00003 00001
run 2: 00002 00003 00001 00004
run 3: 00003 00002 00004 00001
run 4: 00001 00002 00003 00004
run 5: 00004 00003 00002 00001
run 6: 00003 00001 00004 00002
every run wrote the same four IDs: True
all six runs wrote the same order: False
```

- **`sc_trust.sh`** registers a file by an *absolute* path (its scenario T2 is the finding S3 of [§57.2](#572-findings)). A file ID is the hash of the path as it was typed ([§22.1](#221-file-identity)), so a different root gives a different ID.

**In the first edition of this guide, the first run of this check also found two recorded outputs that no longer matched the programs they quote**, and both were refreshed before that edition was assembled. The sample of the auditor's report for the `guard` project ([§59.2](#592-a-read-only-state-auditor)) no longer matched the project as it stood: the project holds a pending descriptor and two more blobs than the recorded report showed, so the fresh report has one more warning. And the transcript of the plan lint (`sc_lint.sh`) predated a change to the wording of one message of `state_audit.py` — the message about `^` and `$` without `(?m)` now names the effect that depends on the invariant's expected count. Neither changed a conclusion of the guide; both show why a transcript is checked against the program that made it, not only against the memory of having made it. In this edition every transcript was recorded afresh on the renamed tool, and the run shown above found no case of that kind.

### D.4 Text edge cases

The tool's idea of a line is Python's `str.splitlines()`, and a file is written back as its lines joined by one line ending, plus a final one ([§22.5](#225-what-a-line-is)). That is a claim about *bytes*, so it was tested on bytes. `sc_edge.sh` ([D.11](#sc_edgesh)) builds every file with `printf`, never with an editor; runs one edit through the whole path — register, add a descriptor, `validate-plan`, `apply-all`; and prints the result with `od -c` (or with `cat -A`, whose `$` is shown as ⏎), so that a missing final newline, a carriage return or a form feed cannot hide in the display.

| Case | The file before | The edit | What the bytes showed |
|---|---|---|---|
| E1 | `one⏎two` — no final newline | replace line 1 with `ONE` | `ONE⏎two⏎`: a final newline was **added** |
| E2 | `one␍⏎two␍⏎` — CRLF | replace line 1 with the two LF lines `ONE` and `ONE-b` | `ONE␍⏎ONE-b␍⏎two␍⏎`: the payload was written with the file's own ending; the registry holds `line_ending: crlf` |
| E3 | `a␌b⏎c⏎` — a form feed inside a line | `register`, `show-file`, then replace line 3 with `C` | **three** lines were registered, not two; the result is `a⏎b⏎C⏎`: the form feed became a newline |
| E4 | `one⏎two⏎` | insert after line 2 with `--payload-text $'X\n'` | `one⏎two⏎X⏎⏎`: a blank line appeared |
| E5 | `one⏎two⏎three⏎` | replace line 2 with an empty payload | `one⏎⏎three⏎`: one empty line, not a deletion |
| E6 | `a␍⏎b⏎c⏎` — mixed endings | replace line 1 with `A` | `A␍⏎b␍⏎c␍⏎`: lines that no descriptor targeted were changed |
| E7 | no file at all | `register brand/new.txt`, then insert after `START` | `register` succeeded with 0 lines; the apply **created** the file, with the lines `hello` and `world` |
| E9 | `one⏎two⏎three⏎` | two `--payload-file`s: `P1⏎P2⏎` after line 1 and `Q1⏎Q2⏎⏎` after line 3 | exactly one trailing newline is stripped: `P1`, `P2`; and `Q1`, `Q2` plus one blank line |
| E10 | a file that starts with the bytes `FF FE 00` | `register` | `UnicodeDecodeError: 'utf-8' codec can't decode byte 0xff in position 0: invalid start byte`, exit 2 |

(`⏎` is LF, `␍⏎` is CRLF, `␌` is a form feed.) There is no E8: the numbering has a gap. The table is the table of [§56.4](#564-identity-and-the-line-model) — the entries V7 and V19, with their consequences and workarounds — seen from the other side; the transcript below is what it was made from. For E1, E2, E4, E5, E6 and E9 the setup commands ran silently, so the transcript shows the bytes alone; E3, E7 and E10 also print the replies.

### D.5 The crash harness

[§48.2](#482-the-crash-harness) explains the method and [§48.3](#483-the-verified-results) the results; this section holds the evidence and the programs.

`crash_sim.py` does, for each of the five operations and each of three windows, what a killed process would have done — without killing one. It calls `engine.apply_descriptor` with one function of `storage` replaced, in memory, by a function that raises a private `Crash` exception at the chosen point: **A** `save_registry` (the managed file has been written; the registry has not been saved), **B** `wal_append` for the `op_applied` event (the registry is saved; the WAL line is not written), **C** the `save_descriptors` call that records `status: applied` (the WAL says `op_applied`; the descriptor still says `pending`). It then calls `apply_descriptor` again — the "restart" — and compares the file with the file that an uncrashed run of the same descriptor produced in a project of its own (`projects/crash/expected_OP`). Each crashed run has a project of its own too (`projects/crash/OP_A`, `OP_B`, `OP_C`), and four of them are among the samples of the auditor shown in [§59.2](#592-a-read-only-state-auditor).

Because the engine keeps nothing in memory between calls — every call re-reads the state from disk — an exception followed by a fresh call is equivalent to a killed process followed by a new command. That is the argument, and it is also the limit: the harness stops *between* two writes, never in the middle of one ([D.10](#d10-what-was-not-verified)).

**Reading the output.** Each block is one operation; each pair of lines is one window. `crashed=True` says that the injected failure was reached; the first file is what was on disk after the crash; `retry -> RESULT` is what the second call to `apply_descriptor` returned — `applied`, `recovered`, or an `Abort` that the program prints as `abort (fail-safe)`; the second file is what was on disk after the retry, and `expected` is the file of the uncrashed run.

```

```

Of the 15 retries, 6 ended `recovered`, 4 ended in an `abort`, and 5 were `applied` a second time. Eleven left the file exactly as an uncrashed run would. **Four left duplicated text and reported success** — `insert_after` and `copy_range`, windows A and B — which is the silent duplication of V2. The fifth `applied` (`move_range`, window B) is a repeat that changes nothing, and the four aborts leave a correct file but a descriptor that can never be applied ([§39.6](#396-abort-the-file-changed-under-the-plan)).

Two companion programs use the same technique:

- `crash_msgs.py` prints the full text of the `Abort` for the four retries that end in one (`replace_range` B, `delete_range` A and B, `move_range` A); the output is in [C.16](#c16-real-replies-verbatim).
- `crash_undo.py` asks what a *recovered* crash leaves behind — whether the descriptor can still be undone — and found V24: it cannot, because `created_ids` is written only by the last status save of a normal apply ([§44.7](#447-verified-undo-after-a-recovered-crash-is-impossible)). Its output is in [C.16](#c16-real-replies-verbatim) as well.

#### `crash_sim.py`

```python
"""Simulate a process crash at three points inside engine.apply_descriptor and
then retry, for every op. Usage: python3 -I crash_sim.py <scripts_dir> <work_dir>"""
import sys, os, shutil, pathlib
scripts_dir, base = sys.argv[1], sys.argv[2]
sys.path.insert(0, scripts_dir)
import engine, registry, storage, validator

class Crash(Exception):
    pass

TEXT = "L1\nL2\nL3\nL4\nL5\n"

def setup(name):
    p = pathlib.Path(base) / name
    shutil.rmtree(p, ignore_errors=True); p.mkdir(parents=True)
    os.chdir(p)
    (p / "f.txt").write_text(TEXT)
    registry.register_file("f.txt")
    fid = registry.file_id_for("f.txt")
    lid = lambda n: f"{fid}_l{n:05d}"
    b = engine.new_batch()
    return p, b, lid

def add(op, b, lid):
    if op == "insert_after":
        return engine.add_descriptor(b, op, "f.txt", after=lid(2), payload_text="NEW")
    if op == "replace_range":
        return engine.add_descriptor(b, op, "f.txt", start=lid(2), end=lid(2), payload_text="NEW2")
    if op == "delete_range":
        return engine.add_descriptor(b, op, "f.txt", start=lid(2), end=lid(3))
    if op == "move_range":
        return engine.add_descriptor(b, op, "f.txt", start=lid(2), end=lid(2), dest=lid(4))
    if op == "copy_range":
        return engine.add_descriptor(b, op, "f.txt", start=lid(1), end=lid(1), dest=lid(4))

def content(p): return (p / "f.txt").read_text().replace("\n", " ").strip()

def expected(op):
    p, b, lid = setup("expected_" + op)
    d = add(op, b, lid)
    assert validator.validate_plan(b)["result"] == "pass"
    engine.apply_descriptor(b, d["descriptor_id"])
    return content(p)

CRASH_POINTS = {
    "A: crash after file write, before registry saved": ("save_registry", None),
    "B: crash after registry saved, before WAL op_applied": ("wal_append", "op_applied"),
    "C: crash after WAL op_applied, before descriptors.json status": ("save_descriptors", "after_wal"),
}

def run(op, label, target, arg):
    p, b, lid = setup(f"{op}_{label[0]}")
    d = add(op, b, lid)
    did = d["descriptor_id"]
    assert validator.validate_plan(b)["result"] == "pass"
    orig = getattr(storage, target)
    state = {"seen_wal": False}
    def patched(*a, **k):
        if target == "save_registry":
            raise Crash()
        if target == "wal_append":
            if a and isinstance(a[0], dict) and a[0].get("event") == arg:
                raise Crash()
            return orig(*a, **k)
        if target == "save_descriptors":
            # only crash on the save that records status=applied
            data = a[1]
            if any(x["descriptor_id"] == did and x["status"] == "applied" for x in data["descriptors"]):
                raise Crash()
            return orig(*a, **k)
    setattr(storage, target, patched)
    try:
        engine.apply_descriptor(b, did)
        crashed = False
    except Crash:
        crashed = True
    finally:
        setattr(storage, target, orig)
    after_crash = content(p)
    try:
        r = engine.apply_descriptor(b, did)
        outcome = f"{r['result']}"
    except engine.Abort as e:
        outcome = "abort (fail-safe)"
    except Exception as e:
        outcome = f"EXCEPTION {type(e).__name__}"
    after_retry = content(p)
    exp = expected(op)
    verdict = "OK" if after_retry == exp else "MISMATCH"
    print(f"  {label}\n      crashed={crashed}  file after crash: [{after_crash}]\n"
          f"      retry -> {outcome}; file: [{after_retry}]  expected: [{exp}]  => {verdict}")

for op in ["insert_after", "replace_range", "delete_range", "move_range", "copy_range"]:
    print(f"\n{op}")
    for label, (target, arg) in CRASH_POINTS.items():
        run(op, label, target, arg)
```

#### `crash_msgs.py`

```python
"""Print the Abort detail produced when a retry follows a crash inside apply_descriptor.
Usage: python3 -I crash_msgs.py <scripts_dir> <work_dir>"""
import sys, os, shutil, pathlib
scripts_dir, base = sys.argv[1], sys.argv[2]
sys.path.insert(0, scripts_dir)
import engine, registry, storage, validator

class Crash(Exception):
    pass

def setup(name):
    p = pathlib.Path(base) / name
    shutil.rmtree(p, ignore_errors=True); p.mkdir(parents=True)
    os.chdir(p)
    (p / "f.txt").write_text("L1\nL2\nL3\nL4\nL5\n")
    registry.register_file("f.txt")
    fid = registry.file_id_for("f.txt")
    return p, engine.new_batch(), (lambda n: f"{fid}_l{n:05d}")

def add(op, b, lid):
    if op == "replace_range":
        return engine.add_descriptor(b, op, "f.txt", start=lid(2), end=lid(2), payload_text="NEW2")
    if op == "delete_range":
        return engine.add_descriptor(b, op, "f.txt", start=lid(2), end=lid(3))
    if op == "move_range":
        return engine.add_descriptor(b, op, "f.txt", start=lid(2), end=lid(2), dest=lid(4))

def run(op, window, target, arg):
    p, b, lid = setup(f"msg_{op}_{window}")
    did = add(op, b, lid)["descriptor_id"]
    assert validator.validate_plan(b)["result"] == "pass"
    orig = getattr(storage, target)
    def patched(*a, **k):
        if target == "save_registry":
            raise Crash()
        if target == "wal_append":
            if a and isinstance(a[0], dict) and a[0].get("event") == arg:
                raise Crash()
            return orig(*a, **k)
    setattr(storage, target, patched)
    try:
        engine.apply_descriptor(b, did)
    except Crash:
        pass
    finally:
        setattr(storage, target, orig)
    try:
        r = engine.apply_descriptor(b, did)
        print(f"{op:13s} {window}: {r['result']}")
    except engine.Abort as e:
        print(f"{op:13s} {window}: ABORT  {e}")

run("replace_range", "B", "wal_append", "op_applied")
run("delete_range", "A", "save_registry", None)
run("delete_range", "B", "wal_append", "op_applied")
run("move_range", "A", "save_registry", None)
```

#### `crash_undo.py`

```python
"""After a recovered crash, can the descriptor still be undone? (created_ids is
only written by the final save_descriptors of a normal apply.)
Usage: python3 -I crash_undo.py <scripts_dir> <work_dir>"""
import sys, os, shutil, pathlib, json
scripts_dir, base = sys.argv[1], sys.argv[2]
sys.path.insert(0, scripts_dir)
import engine, registry, storage, validator

class Crash(Exception):
    pass

def setup(name):
    p = pathlib.Path(base).resolve() / name.replace(" ", "_").replace("(", "").replace(")", "")
    shutil.rmtree(p, ignore_errors=True); p.mkdir(parents=True)
    os.chdir(p)
    (p / "f.txt").write_text("L1\nL2\nL3\nL4\nL5\n")
    registry.register_file("f.txt")
    fid = registry.file_id_for("f.txt")
    return p, engine.new_batch(), (lambda n: f"{fid}_l{n:05d}")

def content(p): return (p / "f.txt").read_text().replace("\n", " ").strip()

def scenario(op, label, target, arg):
    p, b, lid = setup(f"undo_{op}_{label}")
    if op == "insert_after":
        d = engine.add_descriptor(b, op, "f.txt", after=lid(2), payload_text="NEW")
    else:
        d = engine.add_descriptor(b, op, "f.txt", start=lid(2), end=lid(2), payload_text="NEW2")
    did = d["descriptor_id"]
    assert validator.validate_plan(b)["result"] == "pass"
    orig = getattr(storage, target)
    def patched(*a, **k):
        if target == "save_registry":
            raise Crash()
        if target == "wal_append":
            if a and isinstance(a[0], dict) and a[0].get("event") == arg:
                raise Crash()
            return orig(*a, **k)
        if target == "save_descriptors":
            if any(x["descriptor_id"] == did and x["status"] == "applied" for x in a[1]["descriptors"]):
                raise Crash()
            return orig(*a, **k)
    setattr(storage, target, patched)
    try:
        engine.apply_descriptor(b, did)
    except Crash:
        pass
    finally:
        setattr(storage, target, orig)
    r = engine.apply_descriptor(b, did)
    data = storage.load_descriptors(b)
    dd = data["descriptors"][0]
    try:
        u = engine.undo_descriptor(b, did)
        undo = u["result"]
    except Exception as e:
        undo = f"{type(e).__name__}: {e}"
    print(f"{op:13s} {label}: retry -> {r['result']:9s} created_ids={dd['created_ids']}  undo -> {undo}")

scenario("insert_after", "C (crash after WAL op_applied)", "save_descriptors", "after_wal")

scenario("replace_range", "A (crash before registry save)", "save_registry", None)
scenario("replace_range", "C (crash after WAL op_applied)", "save_descriptors", "after_wal")
```

### D.6 The guide's own programs

Besides the scenario scripts, the guide rests on programs that were written for it. None is part of the archive. All of them are written in Python with the standard library only, and every path they use is an argument. The generators and the checks read text, JSON or a zip file and write only the output file they are given; the harnesses write only in the working directory they are given; the programs of Part IX act on the project root they are given, as their sections say; `rename_package.py` writes a new archive and the folders into which it is unpacked, and in its `carry-over` mode it also runs the *delivered* tool, in a directory of its own. The programs that **import the tool's own modules** — and so run the tool's code — are marked in the table; run those only on a copy of the tool that you trust. Run any of them as `python3 -I`; `rebuild.sh` starts the generators, the checks and the harnesses from an empty directory and checks at the end that it is still empty.

The table of facts is **generated** by `gen_program_table.py`: the number of lines, the modules imported (and whether each belongs to the standard library, by `sys.stdlib_module_names`), whether the program starts other processes, and the lowest Python that `vermin` says the file needs. `vermin` knows modules, functions and syntax; it cannot see a method called on an object, so the generator also looks for the few methods newer than 3.7 that these programs could have used — which is how the guard's use of `Path.is_relative_to` (3.9) shows up. The column is an *estimate*: every program was *run* on CPython 3.13.16 only.

**27** programs, **3,702** lines in all. Every import is from the standard library. **7** of them import modules of the tool itself (so they run the tool's code: use them only on a copy of the tool that you trust); **8** start other processes; the rest only read and write files.

#### Rebuilding the evidence

`rebuild.sh` runs the generators and checks in a **new** directory and compares each result byte for byte with the copy that this guide embeds. It does not rebuild the transcripts of the scenario scripts — `repro_check.py` compares those, after normalizing what differs by design — nor the benchmarks, whose numbers are timings.

```bash
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# rebuild.sh -- regenerate the generated parts of this guide's evidence in a NEW directory and compare each with the
# copy that the guide embeds. Written for this guide; not part of the original archive.
#
#   ARCHIVE=/path/to/operational-platform-a-2a.zip VERMIN=/path/to/vermin bash rebuild.sh WORK_DIR NEW_DIR
#
# WORK_DIR  holds scripts/ (the guide's programs), outputs/ (the stored results), projects/ (the fixtures that the scenario
#           scripts left behind), operational-platform-skill-extracted/ and operational-platform-extracted/ (the unpacked archive).
# NEW_DIR   is created empty. Every program writes there; nothing in WORK_DIR is touched.
# Not rebuilt here: the transcripts of the scenario scripts (repro_check.py compares them, after normalizing the values
# that differ by design), the benchmarks (their numbers are timings) and the one-off test of check_guard_table.py.
set -u
W=$(cd "$1" && pwd)
N=$2
TOOL=$W/operational-platform-skill-extracted/operational-platform
VERMIN=${VERMIN:-vermin}
mkdir -p "$N/empty" "$N/out" "$N/work" || exit 1
N=$(cd "$N" && pwd)
cd "$N/empty" || exit 1                       # every program runs from an empty directory; see the last line
P() { python3 -I "$W/scripts/$1" "${@:2}"; }
same() { if cmp -s "$W/outputs/$1" "$N/out/$1"; then echo "same        $1"; else echo "DIFFERENT   $1"; fi; }

P gen_cheatsheet.py "$TOOL/scripts" "$N/out/cheatsheet_commands.md" "$N/out/cheatsheet_synopses.md" >/dev/null
same cheatsheet_commands.md; same cheatsheet_synopses.md

P extract_messages.py "$TOOL/scripts" > "$N/out/messages_raw2.tsv";                same messages_raw2.tsv
P gen_catalog.py "$N/out/messages_raw2.tsv" "$N/out/catalog_tables.md" >/dev/null; same catalog_tables.md
P gen_catalog_programs.py "$W/scripts" "$N/out/catalog_programs.md" >/dev/null;    same catalog_programs.md
P check_catalog.py "$N/out/messages_raw2.tsv" "$W/outputs" > "$N/out/check_catalog.txt"; same check_catalog.txt

P check_docs_vs_cli.py "$TOOL/scripts/cli.py" "$TOOL/SKILL.md" "$TOOL/references/cli-reference.md" \
  "$TOOL/references/file-formats.md" "$TOOL/references/limitations.md" "$TOOL/references/methodology-mapping.md" \
  > "$N/out/check_docs_vs_cli.txt";                                                 same check_docs_vs_cli.txt
P check_guard_table.py "$TOOL/scripts" "$W/scripts/asm_guard.py" > "$N/out/check_guard_table.txt"; same check_guard_table.txt
if [ -n "${ARCHIVE:-}" ]; then
  P check_tool_identity.py "$ARCHIVE" "$W/operational-platform-extracted" "$W/operational-platform-skill-extracted" "$N/out/tool_identity.md" >/dev/null
  same tool_identity.md
fi

P crash_sim.py "$TOOL/scripts" "$N/work/crash" > "$N/out/crash_sim.txt";            same crash_sim.txt
P crash_msgs.py "$TOOL/scripts" "$N/work/crash_msgs" > "$N/out/crash_msgs.txt";    same crash_msgs.txt
P crash_undo.py "$TOOL/scripts" "$N/work/crash_undo" > "$N/out/crash_undo.txt";    same crash_undo.txt

P changes_check.py "$TOOL/scripts" "$N/work/changes" "$N/out/changes_check.md" >/dev/null; same changes_check.md
P schema_census.py "$W/projects" "$N/out/schema_census.md" >/dev/null;             same schema_census.md
P audit_sweep.py "$W/projects" "$W/scripts/state_audit.py" "$N/out/audit_sweep.md" >/dev/null; same audit_sweep.md
P gen_scenarios.py "$W/scripts" "$W/outputs" "$N/out/scenario_inventory.md" >/dev/null; same scenario_inventory.md
P gen_program_table.py "$W/scripts" "$VERMIN" "$N/out/program_table.md" >/dev/null; same program_table.md

# no program may have written to the directory it was started in
if [ -z "$(ls -A "$N/empty")" ]; then echo "the working directory is still empty"; else echo "DIRTY       the working directory is not empty"; fi
```

#### `gen_cheatsheet.py`

Imports `cli.py`, replaces `parse_args` so that `cli.main()` hands over the parser instead of running, and reads the synopsis of every sub-command from it. The one-line purposes and the "Changes" column are written by hand in the program, which **refuses to run** if the parser has a command that the table lacks or the other way round.

````python
"""Build the command table of Appendix A (the cheat sheet) from the tool's real argument parser.

Usage: python3 -I gen_cheatsheet.py SCRIPTS_DIR OUT_TABLE.md OUT_SYNOPSES.md

The synopsis of every sub-command (positionals, required options, optional options, flags, choices) is read
from the parser that cli.py builds, with parse_args replaced so that nothing runs. The one-line purposes and the
"changes" column are written by hand below, and the script REFUSES to produce a table if the parser has a command
that has no hand-written entry or the other way round -- so the table cannot drift from the tool.
It imports cli.py, so run it only on code you trust."""
import argparse
import sys
from pathlib import Path

scripts_dir, out_table, out_syn = sys.argv[1], sys.argv[2], sys.argv[3]
sys.path.insert(0, scripts_dir)

captured = {}


def fake_parse(self, *a, **k):
    captured["p"] = self
    raise SystemExit(0)


argparse.ArgumentParser.parse_args = fake_parse
sys.argv = ["cli.py", "status"]
import cli

try:
    cli.main()
except SystemExit:
    pass
subs = [a for a in captured["p"]._actions if isinstance(a, argparse._SubParsersAction)][0].choices

# group, purpose, what it changes ("-" = nothing under .operational-platform/ except that a first call creates the directory)
INFO = {
    "register": ("Setup and inspection", "bring a file under management: give every line a permanent ID", "registry, WAL"),
    "show-file": ("Setup and inspection", "print every live line with its position and ID (this is what makes a file count as inspected)", "WAL"),
    "find-pattern": ("Setup and inspection", "per-line regex search over registered files; positions are the current ones", "-"),
    "status": ("Setup and inspection", "descriptor counts by status and provenance, the apply order; `--group-by` nests them by any descriptor field", "-"),
    "explain": ("Setup and inspection", "the old text and the new text of one descriptor (which of them exists depends on the operation)", "-"),
    "dry-run": ("Setup and inspection", "print one file as it would look after all its non-applied descriptors (plain text, no hash checks)", "-"),
    "new-batch": ("Batches and descriptors", "open a batch; optionally declare its shape (which gates it must pass)", "batch files"),
    "add-descriptor": ("Batches and descriptors", "add one edit (insert, delete, replace, move, copy) to a batch", "blobs, descriptors"),
    "add-descriptor-template": ("Batches and descriptors", "one replace descriptor for every line that contains a string", "blobs, descriptors"),
    "move-across-files": ("Batches and descriptors", "move a range to another file: a delete plus an insert, two descriptors", "blobs, descriptors"),
    "copy-across-files": ("Batches and descriptors", "copy a range to another file: one insert, the source is untouched", "blobs, descriptors"),
    "add-category": ("Taxonomy, constraints, materials", "declare a finding category (per batch, or `--project`)", "taxonomy"),
    "close-category": ("Taxonomy, constraints, materials", "record that a category was checked and nothing was found", "taxonomy"),
    "set-category-scope": ("Taxonomy, constraints, materials", "declare which files a category must be checked in", "taxonomy"),
    "close-category-file": ("Taxonomy, constraints, materials", "close one file of a scoped category", "taxonomy"),
    "add-constraint": ("Taxonomy, constraints, materials", "protect a range of lines from every edit (per batch, or `--project`)", "constraints"),
    "require-file": ("Taxonomy, constraints, materials", "declare a file that must be registered before the plan can pass", "materials"),
    "add-invariant": ("Invariants", "declare a post-condition: a regex count over the whole file, or balanced pairs", "invariants"),
    "accept-match": ("Invariants", "accept one remaining match of an invariant, by line number, with a note", "invariants"),
    "sync-domino-queue": ("Domino queue", "put every direct descriptor that is not yet queued into the domino queue", "domino queue"),
    "domino-next": ("Domino queue", "the first pending finding, with the candidate lines its hint still finds (read-only)", "-"),
    "domino-resolve": ("Domino queue", "mark one finding traced; recounts the linked descriptors itself", "domino queue, WAL, checkpoint"),
    "domino-status": ("Domino queue", "counts: pending, traced, traced with candidates left, ready for plan", "-"),
    "add-source-range": ("Region inventory", "declare a source range that must be accounted for", "inventory"),
    "inventory-next": ("Region inventory", "the first pending range with its current text (read-only)", "-"),
    "inventory-resolve": ("Region inventory", "give a range its disposition: transferred as is, with an edit, or excluded", "inventory, checkpoint"),
    "inventory-status": ("Region inventory", "counts: total, pending, resolved, ready for plan", "-"),
    "validate-plan": ("Validation and apply", "run the eleven gates; on pass fix the apply order and take the locks", "validation log, checkpoint; on pass also descriptors, locks"),
    "check": ("Validation and apply", "compare one descriptor's expected hash with the live text — the test apply uses (read-only apart from the log)", "validation log"),
    "apply-next": ("Validation and apply", "apply the first descriptor of the order that is not `applied`, then stop", "files, registry, descriptors, WAL, checkpoint (validation log on abort)"),
    "apply-all": ("Validation and apply", "loop of `apply-next` until `done` or the first abort; prints one reply at the very end", "files, registry, descriptors, WAL, checkpoint (validation log on abort)"),
    "validate-post": ("Validation and apply", "needs every descriptor applied; checks syntax and invariants, sets `committed` or `failed`, releases the locks either way", "descriptors, locks, validation log, checkpoint"),
    "undo-descriptor": ("Reversal", "reverse one applied descriptor through its inverse", "files, registry, descriptors, WAL"),
    "checkpoint": ("Session and reporting", "print `checkpoint.json` as it is (read-only)", "-"),
    "resume": ("Session and reporting", "checkpoint, status of the active batch, applied/total and a suggested next command (read-only)", "-"),
    "report": ("Session and reporting", "files touched, issues by severity and the line delta for the listed batches", "-"),
    "export-batch": ("Transport", "pack the batch directory and the whole payload store into a `.tar.gz` (default `./<batch_id>.tar.gz`)", "the archive only"),
    "import-batch": ("Transport", "unpack an archive; the batch comes back **with the statuses it had when exported** (V31)", "batch files, blobs"),
}

missing = sorted(set(subs) - set(INFO))
extra = sorted(set(INFO) - set(subs))
if missing or extra:
    sys.exit(f"table out of date: parser-only {missing}, table-only {extra}")


# Display names for the values of options (the parser's own names are the upper-cased destinations: FILE, SRC_FILE ...).
# Which options exist, which are required, which are flags and which have choices still comes from the parser.
VALUE_NAMES = {
    "--op": "OP", "--file": "PATH", "--src-file": "PATH", "--dest-file": "PATH", "--checked-against": "PATH",
    "--payload-file": "PATH", "--payload-text": "TEXT", "--start": "LINE_ID", "--end": "LINE_ID",
    "--after": "LINE_ID|START", "--dest": "LINE_ID|START", "--dest-after": "LINE_ID",
    "--depends-on": "D1,D2", "--category": "CODE", "--code": "CODE", "--domino-hint": "REGEX",
    "--domino-of": "DESCRIPTOR_ID", "--context": "TEXT", "--rule-ref": "TEXT", "--description": "TEXT",
    "--note": "TEXT", "--reason": "TEXT", "--pattern": "REGEX", "--expected-count": "N", "--line": "N",
    "--files": "PATH,PATH", "--descriptor-ids": "D1,D2", "--batches": "BATCH_ID,BATCH_ID",
    "--find": "TEXT", "--replace": "TEXT", "--group-by": "FIELD,FIELD", "--out": "FILE.tar.gz",
}
POSITIONAL_NAMES = {"archive": "FILE.tar.gz"}

# where each command is described in Part VI
LINKS = {
    "register": "50.1", "show-file": "50.2", "find-pattern": "50.3", "status": "50.4", "explain": "50.5",
    "dry-run": "50.6", "new-batch": "50.7", "add-descriptor": "50.8", "add-descriptor-template": "50.9",
    "move-across-files": "50.10", "copy-across-files": "50.10", "add-category": "50.11",
    "close-category": "50.12", "set-category-scope": "50.13", "close-category-file": "50.13",
    "add-constraint": "50.14", "require-file": "50.15", "add-invariant": "50.16", "accept-match": "50.17",
    "sync-domino-queue": "50.18", "domino-next": "50.18", "domino-resolve": "50.18", "domino-status": "50.18",
    "add-source-range": "50.19", "inventory-next": "50.19", "inventory-resolve": "50.19",
    "inventory-status": "50.19", "validate-plan": "50.20", "check": "50.21", "apply-next": "50.22",
    "apply-all": "50.22", "validate-post": "50.23", "undo-descriptor": "50.24", "checkpoint": "50.25",
    "resume": "50.25", "report": "50.26", "export-batch": "50.27", "import-batch": "50.27",
}
SECTION_SLUGS = {
    "50.1": "501-register", "50.2": "502-show-file", "50.3": "503-find-pattern", "50.4": "504-status",
    "50.5": "505-explain", "50.6": "506-dry-run", "50.7": "507-new-batch", "50.8": "508-add-descriptor",
    "50.9": "509-add-descriptor-template", "50.10": "5010-move-across-files-and-copy-across-files",
    "50.11": "5011-add-category", "50.12": "5012-close-category",
    "50.13": "5013-set-category-scope-and-close-category-file", "50.14": "5014-add-constraint",
    "50.15": "5015-require-file", "50.16": "5016-add-invariant", "50.17": "5017-accept-match",
    "50.18": "5018-the-domino-commands", "50.19": "5019-the-inventory-commands",
    "50.20": "5020-validate-plan", "50.21": "5021-check", "50.22": "5022-apply-next-and-apply-all",
    "50.23": "5023-validate-post", "50.24": "5024-undo-descriptor", "50.25": "5025-checkpoint-and-resume",
    "50.26": "5026-report", "50.27": "5027-export-batch-and-import-batch",
}
assert set(LINKS) == set(INFO), sorted(set(LINKS) ^ set(INFO))
fallback_names = []

def metavar(a):
    if a.choices:
        return "{" + ",".join(str(c) for c in a.choices) + "}"
    if not a.option_strings:
        return POSITIONAL_NAMES.get(a.dest, a.dest.upper())
    flag = a.option_strings[0]
    if flag in VALUE_NAMES:
        return VALUE_NAMES[flag]
    fallback_names.append(flag)
    return a.dest.upper()


def pieces(name, sp):
    pos, req, opt = [], [], []
    for a in sp._actions:
        if isinstance(a, argparse._HelpAction):
            continue
        if not a.option_strings:
            pos.append(metavar(a))
            continue
        flag = a.option_strings[0]
        piece = flag if a.nargs == 0 else f"{flag} {metavar(a)}"
        if a.required:
            req.append(piece)
        else:
            opt.append(f"[{piece}]")
    return [name] + pos + req + opt


def wrap(parts, width=96, indent=6):
    """greedy wrap on piece boundaries, so an option is never split from its value"""
    out, cur = [], "cli.py"
    for p in parts:
        if len(cur) + 1 + len(p) > width and cur.strip():
            out.append(cur)
            cur = " " * indent + p
        else:
            cur = cur + " " + p
    out.append(cur)
    return "\n".join(out)


GROUP_ORDER = ["Setup and inspection", "Batches and descriptors", "Taxonomy, constraints, materials", "Invariants",
               "Domino queue", "Region inventory", "Validation and apply", "Reversal", "Session and reporting",
               "Transport"]
assert set(GROUP_ORDER) == {v[0] for v in INFO.values()}, "group list out of date"

table = ["| Command | What it does | Changes | Entry |", "|---|---|---|---|"]
syn_blocks = []
total = 0
for g in GROUP_ORDER:
    table.append(f"| **{g}** | | | |")
    block = [f"# {g}"]
    for n in INFO:
        if INFO[n][0] != g:
            continue
        ref = LINKS[n]
        table.append(f"| `{n}` | {INFO[n][1]} | {INFO[n][2]} | [§{ref}](#{SECTION_SLUGS[ref]}) |")
        block.append(wrap(pieces(n, subs[n])))
        total += 1
    syn_blocks.append("\n".join(block))
assert total == len(subs) == 38, (total, len(subs))
Path(out_table).write_text("\n".join(table) + "\n", encoding="utf-8")
Path(out_syn).write_text("```\n" + "\n\n".join(syn_blocks) + "\n```\n", encoding="utf-8")
print(f"{total} commands -> {out_table}, {out_syn}")
if fallback_names:
    print("options without a display name:", sorted(set(fallback_names)))
````

#### `extract_messages.py`

Parses the seven modules with `ast` and imports nothing from them. Prints one tab-separated row per message-like string — module, function, line, kind, text — to standard output.

```python
"""Extract every message-like string of the tool's own source, with its module, function and line.
Usage: python3 -I extract_messages.py SCRIPTS_DIR     (parses the source as text; imports nothing from it)

Reports every string constant or f-string that is not a docstring and not an argparse help= text,
is at least 12 characters long and contains a space.  Strings joined with + or % are reported as
one.  f-string expressions are shown as {expression}.  Each row: module, function, line, kind, text.
kind says where the string sits: raise X, Abort, a dict entry (reply['key']), a call (.append(),
_err(), ...), a return, an assignment, or 'other'."""
import ast
import sys
from pathlib import Path

root = Path(sys.argv[1])


def render(node):
    if isinstance(node, ast.Constant) and isinstance(node.value, str):
        return node.value
    if isinstance(node, ast.JoinedStr):
        out = []
        for v in node.values:
            if isinstance(v, ast.Constant):
                out.append(str(v.value))
            elif isinstance(v, ast.FormattedValue):
                conv = {115: "!s", 114: "!r", 97: "!a"}.get(v.conversion, "")
                spec = (":" + (render(v.format_spec) or "")) if v.format_spec is not None else ""
                out.append("{" + ast.unparse(v.value) + conv + spec + "}")
        return "".join(out)
    if isinstance(node, ast.BinOp) and isinstance(node.op, (ast.Add, ast.Mod)):
        l = render(node.left)
        if l is None:
            return None
        r = render(node.right) if isinstance(node.op, ast.Add) else ""
        if r is None:
            return None
        return l + r
    return None


class V(ast.NodeVisitor):
    def __init__(self, mod):
        self.mod, self.fn, self.rows, self.done = mod, [], [], set()

    def emit(self, node, kind):
        if id(node) in self.done:
            return
        text = render(node)
        if text is None or len(text) < 12 or " " not in text:
            return
        for sub in ast.walk(node):
            self.done.add(id(sub))
        self.rows.append((self.mod, ".".join(self.fn) or "<module>", node.lineno, kind, text))

    def visit_FunctionDef(self, n):
        body = n.body
        if body and isinstance(body[0], ast.Expr) and isinstance(body[0].value, ast.Constant):
            self.done.add(id(body[0].value))               # docstring
        self.fn.append(n.name)
        self.generic_visit(n)
        self.fn.pop()

    def visit_Raise(self, n):
        if isinstance(n.exc, ast.Call):
            for a in n.exc.args:
                self.emit(a, "raise " + ast.unparse(n.exc.func))
        self.generic_visit(n)

    def visit_Call(self, n):
        name = ast.unparse(n.func)
        for kw in n.keywords:
            if kw.arg == "help":
                for sub in ast.walk(kw.value):
                    self.done.add(id(sub))
        if name.endswith("Abort"):
            for a in n.args:
                self.emit(a, "Abort")
        elif name.endswith(".append") or name in ("_err",):
            for a in n.args:
                self.emit(a, name + "()")
        self.generic_visit(n)

    def visit_Dict(self, n):
        for k, v in zip(n.keys, n.values):
            if isinstance(k, ast.Constant) and isinstance(k.value, str):
                self.emit(v, f"reply['{k.value}']")
        self.generic_visit(n)

    def visit_Return(self, n):
        if isinstance(n.value, ast.Tuple) and len(n.value.elts) == 2:
            self.emit(n.value.elts[1], "return (ok, text)")
        self.generic_visit(n)

    def visit_Assign(self, n):
        self.emit(n.value, "assignment")
        self.generic_visit(n)

    def visit_JoinedStr(self, n):
        self.emit(n, "other")

    def visit_Constant(self, n):
        if isinstance(n.value, str):
            self.emit(n, "other")

    def visit_BinOp(self, n):
        self.emit(n, "other")
        self.generic_visit(n)


rows = []
for p in sorted(root.glob("*.py")):
    tree = ast.parse(p.read_text(encoding="utf-8"))
    v = V(p.stem)
    for ch in tree.body:                       # module docstring is the first statement
        pass
    if tree.body and isinstance(tree.body[0], ast.Expr) and isinstance(tree.body[0].value, ast.Constant):
        v.done.add(id(tree.body[0].value))
    v.visit(tree)
    rows.extend(v.rows)
rows.sort(key=lambda r: (r[0], r[2]))
for r in rows:
    print("\t".join([r[0], r[1], str(r[2]), r[3], r[4].replace("\n", "\\n")]))
```

#### `gen_catalog.py`

Turns the rows of `extract_messages.py` into the grouped tables of Appendix C. The titles of the groups and the notes under them are written by hand in the program, which reports how many strings it extracted, skipped and catalogued, and how many were left over.

```python
"""Turn the raw extraction of extract_messages.py into the grouped tables of Appendix C.
Usage: python3 -I gen_catalog.py MESSAGES.tsv OUT.md"""
import sys
from collections import OrderedDict

rows = []
for line in open(sys.argv[1], encoding="utf-8"):
    mod, fn, ln, kind, text = line.rstrip("\n").split("\t")
    rows.append((mod, fn, int(ln), kind, text.replace("\\n", " ")))

SKIP = lambda r: (r[4].startswith(("d{", "dm{", "ri{")) or "    " in r[4])           # ID formats and docstrings

AS = {
    "raise DescriptorError": "`DescriptorError`", "raise LineNotFound": "`LineNotFound`",
    "raise RangeInvalid": "`RangeInvalid`", "raise InventoryError": "`InventoryError`",
    "raise DominoError": "`DominoError`", "raise Abort": "`Abort` (`result: abort`)",
    "Abort": None, "reply['detail']": "`detail`", "reply['note']": "`note`", "reply['error']": "`error`",
    "_err()": "`error`", "shape_gaps.append()": "`shape_incomplete` item",
    "errs.append()": "`schema_errors` item", "conflicts.append()": "`conflicts` item",
    "violations.append()": "`protected_zone_violations` item", "gaps.append()": "`unit_category_matrix_incomplete` item",
    "warnings.append()": "`warnings` item", "errors.append()": "`schema_errors` item",
    "return (ok, text)": "`detail` / `syntax` value", "assignment": "value", "other": "value",
    "reply['suggested_next_command']": "`suggested_next_command`",
}
OVERRIDE = {
    ("validator", 238): "`cross_batch_conflicts` item",
    ("validator", 121): "`schema_errors` item (the text of the exception raised while resolving the target, after the descriptor ID)",
    ("cli", 500): "`suggested_next_command` (after an abort)",
    ("validator", 513): "`syntax` value",
    ("validator", 483): "`syntax` value",
    ("validator", 167): "`warnings` item",
    ("validator", 604): "`invariants[]` `detail` (`balanced_pairs`)",
    ("domino", 163): "`note` of `domino-next`",
    ("engine", 556): "internal -- not printed",
    ("engine", 557): "internal -- not printed",
    ("engine", 532): "`detail` of `check`; inside the abort text",
    ("engine", 541): "`detail` of `check`; inside the abort text",
    ("validator", 59): "`detail` of the `shape_incomplete` failure",
    ("engine", 452): "`detail` of `skipped` (never produced by the CLI, V18)",
    ("engine", 486): "WAL `note`",
}

GROUPS = [
    ("C.2", "Addressing lines (the registry)",
     "Raised by every command that resolves a line ID. `add-constraint`, `add-source-range`, `add-descriptor` and the two cross-file commands catch `LineNotFound` and `RangeInvalid` and print the bare message; anywhere else (a mid-apply abort aside, see C.7) the same text arrives as `LineNotFound: …` ([§47.2](#472-what-each-command-catches)).",
     lambda r: r[0] == "registry"),
    ("C.3", "Opening a batch and adding descriptors",
     "The checks of `engine.add_descriptor`, in the order they run ([§44.3](#443-add_descriptor-the-checks-in-order)), then the two small \"not found\" checks of the commands that read a descriptor or a file.",
     lambda r: (r[0] == "engine" and r[1] in ("new_batch", "add_descriptor", "_check_context", "_require", "_find")) or (r[0] == "cli" and r[1] in ("cmd_show_file", "cmd_explain", "cmd_dry_run"))),
    ("C.4", "Taxonomy, invariants and reviewed exceptions",
     "`DescriptorError` is caught by each of these commands and printed bare ([§47.2](#472-what-each-command-catches)).",
     lambda r: r[0] == "engine" and r[1] in ("add_invariant", "add_category", "close_category", "set_category_scope", "close_category_file", "accept_match")),
    ("C.5", "The domino queue and the region inventory", "",
     lambda r: r[0] in ("domino", "inventory")),
    ("C.6", "`validate-plan`",
     "The gate failures are objects `{\"phase\": \"plan\", \"result\": \"fail\", \"<key>\": [...], \"detail\": ...}`; the table lists the strings that appear as list items or as `detail`, in the order of the gates ([§51](#51-the-validate-plan-diagnostic-catalog)). A fifth kind, `warnings`, comes with a *pass*.",
     lambda r: r[0] == "validator" and r[1] in ("validate_plan", "_schema_errors", "_build_conflict_graph", "_protected_zone_violations", "_cross_batch_lock_conflicts", "_unit_category_matrix_gaps", "_invariant_independence_warnings", "_rule_ref_consistency_warnings")),
    ("C.7", "`apply-next` and `apply-all`",
     "The two `Abort` messages are the only exceptions of the domain that exit 1 ([§39.6](#396-abort-the-file-changed-under-the-plan), [§44.4](#444-apply_descriptor-the-whole-algorithm)). `check` prints the text of the pre-state comparison as its `detail`.",
     lambda r: (r[0] == "engine" and r[1] in ("apply_descriptor", "_check_pre_state", "_check_post_state")) or (r[0] == "cli" and r[1] == "cmd_apply_next")),
    ("C.8", "`undo-descriptor`", "All `DescriptorError`, printed bare ([§44.6](#446-undo_descriptor)).",
     lambda r: r[0] == "engine" and r[1] == "undo_descriptor"),
    ("C.9", "`validate-post` and the syntax checks", "",
     lambda r: r[0] == "validator" and r[1] in ("validate_post", "_check_python_syntax", "_check_node_syntax", "_check_balanced_pairs")),
    ("C.10", "Session, archives and the generic handler", "",
     lambda r: r[0] == "cli" and r[1] in ("cmd_resume", "cmd_checkpoint", "cmd_import_batch", "main")),
]


def code(text):
    n = 1
    while "`" * n in text:
        n += 1
    pad = " " if text.startswith("`") or text.endswith("`") else ""
    return "`" * n + pad + text.replace("|", "\\|") + pad + "`" * n


out, used = [], set()
rows2 = [r for r in rows if not SKIP(r)]
for gid, title, intro, pred in GROUPS:
    ORDER = {m: i for i, m in enumerate(["engine", "validator", "domino", "inventory", "registry", "cli"])}
    sel = sorted((r for r in rows2 if pred(r)), key=lambda r: (ORDER[r[0]], r[2]))
    for r in sel:
        used.add(r)
    out.append(f"### {gid} {title}\n")
    if intro:
        out.append(intro + "\n")
    out.append("| Message (`{…}` is an expression of the source) | Appears as | Source |")
    out.append("|---|---|---|")
    for mod, fn, ln, kind, text in sel:
        a = OVERRIDE.get((mod, ln)) or AS.get(kind) or kind
        out.append(f"| {code(text)} | {a} | `{mod}.{fn}`:{ln} |")
    out.append("")
left = [r for r in rows2 if r not in used]
print(f"{len(rows)} extracted, {len(rows) - len(rows2)} skipped (ID formats, docstrings), {len(rows2) - len(left)} catalogued, {len(left)} left over", file=sys.stderr)
for r in left:
    print("LEFT OVER:", r, file=sys.stderr)
open(sys.argv[2], "w", encoding="utf-8").write("\n".join(out))
```

#### `gen_catalog_programs.py`

The same for the programs of Part IX: it parses their source with `ast` and tabulates the findings of the auditor, the refusals and remarks of the guard, the stops of the driver and the messages of the lock release.

```python
"""Tables of Appendix C for the guide's own programs.
Usage: python3 -I gen_catalog_programs.py SCRIPTS_DIR OUT.md   (SCRIPTS_DIR holds state_audit.py, asm_guard.py, driver.py, release_lock.py)"""
import ast
import sys
from pathlib import Path

root = Path(sys.argv[1])


def render(node):
    if isinstance(node, ast.Constant) and isinstance(node.value, str):
        return node.value
    if isinstance(node, ast.JoinedStr):
        out = []
        for v in node.values:
            if isinstance(v, ast.Constant):
                out.append(str(v.value))
            elif isinstance(v, ast.FormattedValue):
                conv = {115: "!s", 114: "!r", 97: "!a"}.get(v.conversion, "")
                spec = (":" + (render(v.format_spec) or "")) if v.format_spec is not None else ""
                out.append("{" + ast.unparse(v.value) + conv + spec + "}")
        return "".join(out)
    if isinstance(node, ast.BinOp) and isinstance(node.op, ast.Add):
        l, r = render(node.left), render(node.right)
        return l + r if l is not None and r is not None else None
    return None


def code(text):
    n = 1
    while "`" * n in text:
        n += 1
    pad = " " if text.startswith("`") or text.endswith("`") else ""
    return "`" * n + pad + text.replace("|", "\\|") + pad + "`" * n


def calls(path, pred):
    tree = ast.parse(path.read_text(encoding="utf-8"))
    out = []
    for n in ast.walk(tree):
        if pred(n):
            out.append(n)
    out.sort(key=lambda n: n.lineno)
    return out


out = []

# ---- the auditor: note(level, message)
p = root / "state_audit.py"
rows = []
for n in calls(p, lambda n: isinstance(n, ast.Call) and isinstance(n.func, ast.Name) and n.func.id == "note" and len(n.args) == 2):
    lv = n.args[0]
    if isinstance(lv, ast.Constant):
        level = lv.value
    elif isinstance(lv, ast.IfExp):
        level = f"{lv.body.value} or {lv.orelse.value}"
    else:
        level = "?"
    msg = render(n.args[1])
    if msg is None:
        continue
    rows.append((level, msg, n.lineno))
rank = {"ERROR": 0, "WARN": 1, "INFO": 2}
out.append("### C.11 The state auditor (`state_audit.py`)\n")
out.append("One line per finding: the level, then the message. `{tag}` is the descriptor or invariant the finding is about (`batch_0001/d0001`). The messages are listed in the order the checks run; the order of the *output* is by level.\n")
out.append("| Level | Message (`{…}` is an expression of the source) | Line |")
out.append("|---|---|---:|")
for level, msg, ln in rows:
    out.append(f"| {level} | {code(msg)} | {ln} |")
out.append("")
for s in ("no .operational-platform directory under {root}",):
    pass
out.append("Besides the findings, the program prints `no .operational-platform directory under <root>` and exits 2 when there is no state, and a last line `-- checked N file(s), N blob(s), N batch(es), N WAL record(s), N validation record(s): N error(s), N warning(s), N info`.\n")

# ---- the guard
p = root / "asm_guard.py"
refuse = []
for n in calls(p, lambda n: isinstance(n, ast.Raise) and isinstance(n.exc, ast.Call) and ast.unparse(n.exc.func) == "Refuse"):
    refuse.append((render(n.exc.args[0]), n.lineno))
tree = ast.parse(p.read_text(encoding="utf-8"))
direct = []
for n in ast.walk(tree):
    if isinstance(n, ast.Dict):
        for k, v in zip(n.keys, n.values):
            if isinstance(k, ast.Constant) and k.value == "guard_error":
                direct.append((render(v), n.lineno))
advice = [(render(n.args[0]), n.lineno) for n in calls(p, lambda n: isinstance(n, ast.Call) and ast.unparse(n.func) == "notes.append")]
out.append("### C.12 The guard (`asm_guard.py`)\n")
out.append("A refusal is `{\"guard_error\": \"…\"}` on stdout and exit 3; a remark is a line `# guard: …` on stderr after a command that ran.\n")
out.append("| Message (`{…}` is an expression of the source) | Kind | Line |")
out.append("|---|---|---:|")
for msg, ln in sorted(refuse + direct, key=lambda r: r[1]):
    if msg:
        out.append(f"| {code(msg)} | refusal | {ln} |")
for msg, ln in advice:
    out.append(f"| {code(msg)} | remark | {ln} |")
out.append("")

# ---- the driver
p = root / "driver.py"
stops = [(render(n.exc.args[0]), n.lineno) for n in calls(p, lambda n: isinstance(n, ast.Raise) and isinstance(n.exc, ast.Call) and ast.unparse(n.exc.func) == "Stop")]
prints = []
for n in calls(p, lambda n: isinstance(n, ast.Call) and ast.unparse(n.func) == "print" and n.args):
    m = render(n.args[0])
    if m and " " in m and len(m) > 12 and not m.startswith("    "):
        prints.append((m, n.lineno))
out.append("### C.13 The driver (`driver.py`)\n")
out.append("A stop is printed as `STOP: …` and the program exits 1; everything else is progress on stdout.\n")
out.append("| Message (`{…}` is an expression of the source) | Kind | Line |")
out.append("|---|---|---:|")
allrows = sorted([(l, "stop", m) for m, l in stops] + [(l, "progress", m) for m, l in prints])
for ln, kind, msg in allrows:
    out.append(f"| {code(msg)} | {kind} | {ln} |")
out.append("")

# ---- release_lock
p = root / "release_lock.py"
rl = []
for n in calls(p, lambda n: isinstance(n, ast.Call) and ast.unparse(n.func) == "print" and n.args):
    m = render(n.args[0])
    if m and " " in m:
        rl.append((m, n.lineno))
out.append("### C.14 The lock helper (`release_lock.py`)\n")
out.append("| Message (`{…}` is an expression of the source) | Line |")
out.append("|---|---:|")
for msg, ln in rl:
    out.append(f"| {code(msg)} | {ln} |")
out.append("")
Path(sys.argv[2]).write_text("\n".join(out), encoding="utf-8")
print(f"auditor {len(rows)}, guard {len(refuse) + len(direct)} refusals + {len(advice)} remarks, driver {len(allrows)}, release_lock {len(rl)}", file=sys.stderr)
```

#### `check_catalog.py`

Reads every `*.txt` transcript in a directory, collects the strings that appear in an `error` or `detail` field or as an item of a list of failures, and matches each against the templates of the catalog. Then it counts, the other way round, how many templates were produced by a real reply at all.

